coins_engraved.reverse: Mars in quadriga right, holding trophy, shield, reins and spear; C.ABVRI below, ROMA in exergue

completed.family_note: The Aburii were a plebeian gens first attested in the mid-second century BC. Two moneyers are known: C. Aburius Geminus (Crawford 244, 134 BC), who struck a denarius with Mars in a quadriga and a bronze quadrans with a prow reverse, and M. Aburius M.f. Geminus (Crawford 250, 132 BC), who produced denarii featuring Sol driving a quadriga. Both issues were struck at Rome. The gens is otherwise little attested in literary sources, though Livy records members serving as praetor and as diplomatic legates.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini identifies two members of the gens from his coins: C. Aburius Geminus and M. Aburius Geminus. He cites Livy to connect M. Aburius to a praetorship and C. Aburius to a legation sent to Masinissa and Carthage. He correctly reads the GEM abbreviation as Geminus (or Gemellus) and notes the three value dots on the bronze quadrans as tribus notis signatus. He calls the prow type ratitus, deriving the term from ratis (ship), following standard antiquarian etymology.

coins_engraved.obverse: Draped female bust right (Luna or Diana); crescent behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Three standing female figures (triple cult statue)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini interprets the three standing female figures on the reverse as the Heliades — the sisters of Phaethon transforming into larch trees — connecting the cognomen Lariscolus to larix (larch). Modern scholarship identifies the reverse figures as a triple Diana. He cites this as a striking interpretive case.

completed.family_note: The Accoleii were a plebeian gens known from a single moneyer, P. Accoleius Lariscolus, who struck denarii in 43 BC (Crawford 486/1). The obverse depicts a bust of Diana Nemorensis, while the reverse shows a triple cult statue of Diana, Hecate, and Selene supporting a beam with five cypress trees. The type references the famous sanctuary of Diana at Nemi (Aricia). The cognomen Lariscolus may derive from a toponym or from larix (larch tree), though the connection remains debated.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini interprets the reverse figures not as the triple Diana but as the Heliades, the sisters of Phaethon, transforming into larch trees, connecting the cognomen Lariscolus to larix. This is a characteristically mythological reading that modern scholarship has rejected in favour of the Diana Nemorensis identification. He does not cite specific ancient sources for this family beyond the coin evidence itself, reflecting the gens's obscurity in literary sources.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Asklepios right, wearing tainia
coins_engraved.reverse: Serpent-entwined staff (rod of Asklepios); MN·A·CILI

coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini calls this primo aereo nummo (the first bronze coin) of the Acilii and derives the nomen Acilius from Greek akesimos (healer), connecting the gens to Aesculapius. He attributes the coin to a quaestor serving in Sicily during the Hannibalic war.

coins_engraved.reverse: Standing female figure (Valetudo) leaning on column, holding snake; MN.ACILIVS.III.VIR.VALETV
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini connects the Salutis and Valetudinis legend types to the temples of Salus and Valetudo on the Quirinal. He identifies the moneyer Mn. Acilius Glabrio as tresvir monetalis, reading the III.VIR.VALETV legend on the reverse.

completed.family_note: The Acilii were a plebeian gens, with the Glabrio branch being the most prominent. Mn. Acilius Glabrio defeated Antiochus III at Thermopylae in 191 BC. The coinage includes Mn. Acilius M.f. Balbus (Crawford 271/1, 125 BC), who struck denarii with Roma/Jupiter quadriga types within a distinctive myrtle wreath border signifying an ovation, and Mn. Acilius Glabrio (Crawford 442/1a, 49 BC), whose denarii show Salus (Valetudo) feeding a serpent, referencing the family's association with the cult of Salus on the Quirinal. An early bronze coin with Aesculapius imagery is also attributed to the gens.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini derives the nomen Acilius from the Greek akesimos (healer), connecting the gens to Aesculapius and healing cults. He identifies the myrtle crown on the reverse of Crawford 271/1 as signifying an ovation and notes the consul with M. Porcius Cato in 639 AUC. For the Glabrio denarius, he connects the Salutis/Valetudinis types to the temples on the Quirinal. He admits uncertainty about the fourth denarius on the plate (quarto denario mihi quidem obscurum est), tentatively attributing it to Mn. Acilius Glabrio who triumphed over the Aetolians.

coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Denarius of P. Aelius Paetus (Crawford 233/1). Obverse: helmeted head of Roma right with value mark behind. Reverse: the Dioscuri on horseback galloping right, P·PAETVS below and ROMA on a tablet in exergue. A standard Roman-magistrate Dioscuri type within Orsini's Aelia commentary.

Allius Bala as an Aelius. He cites Sophocles' Trachiniae in connection with Diana's stag-drawn chariot on the reverse.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right
coins_engraved.reverse: Dioscuri galloping right; C·AL below; ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini uncertain ("incertum ad quem spectet"), tentatively C. Ailius. His note that silver coinage did not yet exist is incorrect — the denarius was introduced in 211 BC and Crawford 75/1b is dated 209-208 BC. Notably, this coin was struck in Sicily during the Second Punic War, making it one of the earliest Roman denarii and a military issue — not a Rome mint coin. The X (denarius value mark) appears on the actual coin but was not engraved by Orsini. The Sicilian mint context is historically significant: Roman forces were consolidating control of Sicily after Marcellus's capture of Syracuse (212 BC), and field coinage was needed to pay troops.

coins_engraved.reverse: Biga of stags right; C.ALLI behind

He reads the Dioscuri reverse as a standard magistrate type.

completed.family_note: The Aelii were a plebeian gens of great antiquity, with the Paeti, Lamiae, and Tuberones among their principal branches. P. Aelius Paetus (Crawford 233/1, 138 BC) struck denarii with the standard Roma/Dioscuri type. Under Augustus, Q. Aelius Lamia served as IIIvir monetalis (RIC I 324, 18 BC), striking dupondii with AVGVSTVS TRIBVNIC POTEST, while L. Aelius Lamia struck quadrantes as IIIIvir monetalis (RIC I 420-421, 9 BC). C. Allius Bala (Crawford 336/1, 92 BC), whose distinctive Diana/stag biga denarius is grouped here by Orsini, is now generally assigned to a separate gens Allia.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini equates the Aelia gens with the Allia known from Capitoline monuments, treating C. Allius Bala as an Aelius. He identifies P. Aelius Paetus as praetor anno DL and relates the anecdote from Valerius Maximus (V.v) that a woodpecker (Picus Martius) landed on his head while he served as Praetor Urbanus. He cites Sophocles' Trachiniae in connection with Diana's stag-drawn chariot on the Bala denarius. For the Augustan bronzes, he discusses Q. and L. Aelius Lamia as IIIviri and IIIIviri monetales, noting the simpulum type on the quadrantes.

completed.family_note: The Aemilii were one of Rome's greatest patrician gentes, with the Lepidi, Paulli, Scauri, and Bucae among their principal branches. The coinage is extensive: M. Aemilius Scaurus and P. Plautius Hypsaeus (Crawford 422/1, 58 BC) struck denarii showing King Aretas of Nabataea kneeling beside a camel, commemorating Scaurus's eastern campaigns. L. Aemilius Lepidus Paullus (Crawford 415/1, 62 BC) produced multiple die variants celebrating his ancestor's triple triumph over Perseus of Macedon, with the reverse showing TER and captives. M. Aemilius Lepidus (Crawford 419, 61 BC) struck types showing the Basilica Aemilia, the equestrian statue commemorating his ancestor's youthful heroism (AN.XV), and his role as tutor of Ptolemy (TVTOR REG ALEXANDREAE). The triumvir M. Aemilius Lepidus struck portrait denarii as IMP and PONT.MAX (Crawford 495/2, 43 BC), and L. Aemilius Buca struck denarii bearing Caesar's portrait (Crawford 480/4, 44 BC).
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini devotes four plates to the Aemilii, the most extensive treatment of any gens in the letter A, with detailed historical commentary drawing on Cicero, Pliny, Plutarch, and Appian. He discusses the Aretas denarius in relation to Scaurus's aedileship and Nabataean submission. For the Paullus types, he explains TER as triple triumph and identifies Perseus and his sons as captives. He discusses the Basilica Aemilia and the clupei (shields) displayed there, the equestrian statue honouring the young Lepidus who killed an enemy and saved a citizen at age fifteen (citing Valerius Maximus III.1), and the Puteal Scribonianum on the Libonis type. His treatment of the triumvir Lepidus and L. Aemilius Buca is briefer, focusing on their political roles.

coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini debates whether the Afranii were patrician or plebeian, ultimately classifying them as plebeian. He reads the S as the praenomen Spurius and notes this abbreviation is paralleled in the Postumii. He connects Sp. Afranius to the Republican biga denarius type.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Helmeted Roma head facing right; winged helmet; possible control mark behind neck.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Victory or charioteer in biga galloping right; S·AFRA in field; ROMA in exergue.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Janus bifrons
coins_engraved.reverse: Prow right; S.AFRA above
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes this Janiform as (Crawford 206/2) as the bronze companion to the denarius. He reads the S.AFRA legend and identifies Sp. Afranius as the issuer, treating both coin 1 and coin 2 as monuments of the same moneyer.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Janus head (double-faced, facing both left and right); marks above.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Prow of ship facing right; S·AFRA above or in field.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare male head right; Iberian legend behind (appears as ARSA or similar)
coins_engraved.reverse: Horseman galloping right, wearing helmet, holding spear/lance; Iberian legend in exergue below
coins_engraved.identification: Bolskan (Hispania Citerior) AR denarius, c. 150–100 BC — ACIP 1412–1417; CNH pp. 210–212
coins_engraved.orsini_error: Orsini misattributes a Bolskan (Iberian, Hispania Citerior) denarius to gens Afrania, reading the north-eastern Iberian script as the Latin name AFRA; the coin is not Roman. An understandable error — Iberian script was not deciphered until 1922 — but a genuine misattribution.
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this Iberian horseman type to L. Afranius serving as Cn. Pompey's legate in Hispania during the Sertorian campaigns. He connects the reverse cavalry scene to L. Afranius's military role in Spain, drawing on Livy and Appian for the context.

completed.family_note: The Afranii were a plebeian gens. The earliest coin placed here (Crawford 206/1, c. 150 BC — a Roma/Victory-biga denarius with prow bronzes) is signed SAFRA; in modern scholarship the moneyer is an otherwise-unknown 'Safra', not an Afranius (the Sp. Afranius reading is Orsini's antiquarian interpretation of the legend). L. Afranius, Cn. Pompey's legate in Hispania during the Sertorian War (c. 75 BC), is associated with an Iberian horseman type bearing the legend HISPANORVM. The gens produced a consul in 60 BC, L. Afranius, who later commanded Pompeian forces in Spain during the Civil War.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini discusses whether the Afranii were patrician or plebeian, ultimately classifying them as plebeian. He reads the S on the denarius as the praenomen Spurius, noting this abbreviation also appears in the Postumii. He attributes the Iberian horseman type to L. Afranius serving as Cn. Pompey's legate in Hispania, connecting it to the Sertorian campaigns. His treatment is relatively brief, reflecting the limited literary evidence for the gens.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bust of Venus, right, draped and wearing diadem. C·CAESAR IMP·COS·ITER
coins_engraved.reverse: Trinacrus, left, placing right foot on prow and holding triskeles in right hand and cloak in left hand. A·ALLIENVS PRO·COS
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the obverse bust as Persephone, patron goddess of Sicily, and interprets the reverse Trinacrus as tria crura (three legs), the heraldic emblem of the island. He cites Hirtius (the continuator of Caesar's Gallic commentaries) as the source for Allienus as praetor governing Sicily.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Helmeted head (Roma?) facing right; moneyer name partially visible around rim.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Standing figure facing left or right; holding spear or standard; partial legend at right.
coins_engraved.specimen_shared_reason: same catalogue type cross-listed under multiple gentes (joint-moneyer issue or sub-variant); one museum specimen serves all

completed.family_note: The Allieni were a minor gens known primarily from A. Allienus, who served as praetor and proconsul of Sicily under Caesar in 49 BC. His denarius (Crawford 457/1, 49 BC) features a diademed head of Persephone on the obverse and the Trinacrus (the three-legged symbol of Sicily) on the reverse, clearly referencing his Sicilian command. The coin was struck at a Sicilian mint. No other members of the gens held significant magistracies.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini reads the obverse head as Venus (Veneris caput), referring it to Caesar and the origin of the gens Iulia, and explains the reverse Trinacrus as tria crura, the heraldic emblem of the island. He cites Hirtius (the continuator of Caesar's commentaries) as the source for Allienus serving as praetor governing Sicily. His treatment is brief, limited to a single coin with minimal prosopographic discussion, reflecting the gens's obscurity in the ancient sources.

coins_engraved.obverse: Draped female bust right; legend around C·ANNI·T·F·T·N·PRO·COS·EX·S·C
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory in quadriga right; Q above; C·TARQVITI·P·F in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies C. Annius T.f. T.n. as holding proconsular authority against Sertorius and reads the caduceus and scales as symbols of peace and justice in his command. He cites Sallust's Historiae for the Sertorian context of the Spanish campaigns.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Laureate female bust right (Anna Perenna); S.C behind; caduceus before
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Victory in biga right; C.ANNIVS.T.F.T.N / PRO.COS below

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate female bust right; S.C behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory in quadriga right; L.FABI.L.F / HISP below
coins_engraved.moneyer: C. Annius / L. Fabius L.f. Hispaniensis
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the joint issue with L. Fabius Hispaniensis, noting the proconsular command against Sertorius. He reads the Victory in quadriga as a military memorial type and connects the L.FABI.L.F / HISP legend to the joint magistracy in Spain.

coins_engraved.obverse: Simpulum and lituus; SILIVS ANNIVS LAMIA around
coins_engraved.reverse: Large S·C in centre; III·VIR / A·A·A·F·F around
coins_engraved.moneyer: L. Aelius Lamia, P. Silius, C. Annius
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes C. Annius as part of the college of L. Aelius Lamia, P. Silius, and C. Annius as IIIIviri A.A.A.F.F. He treats the simpulum reverse as marking the pontifical dimension of the Augustan moneyer college.

coins_engraved.reverse_ai: S.C large in centre; III.VIR / A.P.F around

coins_engraved.reverse: S.C large in centre; III·VIR / A.A.A.F.F around
coins_engraved.moneyer: L. Aelius Lamia, P. Silius, C. Annius
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini records the joint issue of Lamia, Silanvs, and C. Annius with the dextrarum iunctio obverse and S.C reverse. He connects the IIII.VIR A.A.A.F.F. legend to the Augustan monetary reform and the clasped hands to concordia imagery.

coins_engraved.reverse_ai: S.C large in centre; IIII.VIR / A.A.A.F.F around

coins_engraved.obverse: Single draped female bust right; legend around C·ANNIVS·T·F·T·N·PRO·COS
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory in quadriga right; HISP above; L·FABI·LF in exergue
coins_engraved.moneyer: C. Annius T.f.T.n. / C. Tarquitius P.f.
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the joint issue of C. Annius with C. Tarquitius P.f., citing Sallust's Historiae for Tarquitius's presence in Spain under Pompeian command. He reads the Victory quadriga as part of the anti-Sertorian military series.

coins_engraved.reverse_description: Quadriga galloping right; charioteer; HISP·Q above or in field; L·FABI·LF in exergue.

coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Victory in quadriga right; C.TARQVITI.P.F in exergue

completed.family_note: The Annii were a plebeian gens. C. Annius T.f. T.n. (Crawford 366, 82 BC) struck denarii as proconsul with authority against Sertorius in Spain, featuring Anna Perenna on the obverse and Victory in a biga or quadriga on the reverse, with joint issues naming quaestors L. Fabius Hispaniensis and C. Tarquitius P.f. Under Augustus, C. Annius served as IIIIvir monetalis alongside L. Aelius Lamia and P. Silius (RIC I 420-421, 9 BC), striking bronze quadrantes with simpulum/lituus and clasped-hands types.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini identifies C. Annius T.f. T.n. as holding proconsular authority against Sertorius, reading the caduceus and scales as symbols of peace and justice. He discusses the joint issues with L. Fabius Hispaniensis and C. Tarquitius, citing Sallust's Historiae for the latter. For the Augustan quadrantes, he notes the college of three IIIIviri monetales and interprets the clasped hands with caduceus as symbolising concordia and peace. His prosopographic treatment connects the gens to various literary references without extended historical discussion.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Jupiter in quadriga right; C.ANTES below, ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini equates the Antestia gens with Antistia and notes the spelling variation across inscriptions and manuscripts. He reads GRAG as a dimidiatum cognomen Graecum (half-Greek name), interpreting it as Gragulus rather than Gragus.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right
coins_engraved.reverse: Two horsemen (the Dioscuri) galloping right; ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies C. Antestius tentatively as the consul mentioned by Dio (book XLVII) paired with M. Licinius. He notes this horseman/Dioscurus type as the primary Antestian monument on the plate.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Helmeted head of Roma right
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Horseman (Dioscurus) galloping right; ROMA below

coins_engraved.obverse: Head right with star or control mark
coins_engraved.reverse: Two horsemen (the Dioscuri) galloping right, stars above; C·ANTESTI below; ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini groups this as a die variant of the C. Antestius denarius, treating coins 2 and 3 as two specimens of the same issue. He confirms C.ANTESTI in the legend and reads the horseman reverse as a Dioscurian type.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head right with star or control mark
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Horseman in biga right; C.ANTESTI / ROMA below

completed.family_note: The Antestii (also spelled Antistii) were a plebeian gens. L. Antestius Gragulus (Crawford 238/1, 136 BC) struck denarii with a Roma/Jupiter quadriga type bearing the cognomen GRAG on the obverse. C. Antestius (Crawford 219/1e, 146 BC) produced earlier denarii with the standard Roma/Dioscuri reverse. The gens is attested in various literary sources, and members held minor magistracies through the Republic. The spelling Antestius and Antistius appear interchangeably in inscriptions and manuscripts.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini equates the Antestia gens with Antistia, noting the variation in spelling across inscriptions and manuscripts. He notes the abbreviated cognomen GRAG (dimidiatum cognomen) but states he could not determine what it stands for (reperire adhuc non potui). For C. Antestius, he tentatively identifies the moneyer as the consul mentioned by Dio (book XLVII), paired with M. Licinius. He groups two die variants of the C. Antestius denarius together. His discussion is moderate in length, focused mainly on identifying the moneyers and their magistracies.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right (Augustus?); legend around
coins_engraved.reverse: Column or altar with priestly implements; ANTISTIVS.REGINVS around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies C. Antistius Reginus from Caesar's Bellum Gallicum (book VI) as the probable father of this moneyer, but explicitly withholds certainty: 'in re tam dubia nihil audeam affirmare'. He does not attribute the pontifical implements to this coin; those appear on coin 2 (the Vetus denarius).

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right (Augustus?); legend around
coins_engraved.reverse: COS / IMP.CAESAR.AVG legend; implements
coins_engraved.identification: RIC I (2nd ed.) Augustus 410 — C. Antistius Reginus
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the pontifical instruments on the reverse of this denarius as evidence of Antistius Vetus's pontificate: 'Instrumenta pontificalia, quae in altera denarii parte impressa sunt, Antistii pontificatum indicant', citing Velleius lib. II. He notes C. Antistius Vetus as consul with D. Laelius Balbus, anno DCCXLVII, and quotes the Pliny epigramma (lib. XXXI, cap. I).
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Clear laureate or bare head right within circular legend. Text reads VELVS·III·VIR around top, ANTISTIVS around bottom. Portrait is clean and detailed — a young male head facing right with neat short hair.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Clear circular field. At top: COS. In centre field: IMP·CAESAR·AVG (two lines). Below: XI (number). No figural scene — purely textual/epigraphic reverse with legend arranged in multiple register.

completed.family_note: The Antistii were a plebeian gens with the Reginorum and Veterum branches. C. Antistius Reginus served as IIIvir monetalis under Augustus (RIC I 410, 13 BC), striking denarii with Augustus's portrait and pontifical implements (simpulum, lituus, tripod, patera) on the reverse. C. Antistius Vetus, consul in 6 BC with D. Laelius Balbus, struck Augustan bronzes. Both issues are imperial rather than Republican, making this one of the gentes represented in Orsini only by Augustan coinage.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini identifies C. Antistius Reginus from Caesar's Bellum Gallicum (book VI), tentatively connecting the Augustan moneyer to the Caesarian officer of the same name — but explicitly hedges: 'in re tam dubia nihil audeam affirmare', leaving the identification as probable rather than certain. He discusses the pontifical instruments on the reverse of the SECOND denarius (the Vetus coin, coin 2), not the Reginus coin: 'Instrumenta pontificalia, quae in altera denarii parte impressa sunt, Antistii pontificatum indicant', connecting them to Velleius lib. II on Antistius Vetus as 'consularis atq. pontificis'. For C. Antistius Vetus he notes the consulship with D. Laelius Balbus, anno DCCXLVII, and cites Pliny lib. XXXI, cap. I. He closes with the Praeneste inscription for L. Antistius C.F. Aemilia.Vetus, Augur.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare male head right; RESTIO behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Standing figure (Hercules) holding club and trophy
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini states that Restio's portrait appears on this first denarius ('cuius imago in primo denario impressa est') and discusses him as the author of the lex sumptuaria, citing Gellius and Macrobius. He makes no specific claim about the Hercules reverse being emblematic of sumptuary legislation.

coins_engraved.obverse: Jugate (conjoined) laureate heads of the Dei Penates right; DEI PENATES (D.E.I. / PENATES) legend; C.ANTI behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Hercules holding cornucopia and patera
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini states that the Penates images are on the REVERSE ('in altera secundi denarii parte') of this coin, not the obverse. He presents two possible reasons for their inclusion — family origin from Lanuvium (citing Varro and Paedianus) or Restio's law touching on religion — but commits to neither ('fortasse'). He does not describe the other side's figure as Hercules here, nor link Hercules to the household cult.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Bare male head right (Penates per Orsini); C.ANTI behind
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Hercules holding cornucopia and patera

coins_engraved.obverse: Bucranium (bull skull) facing; C.ANTIVS above
coins_engraved.reverse: Flaming altar (thymiaterion); RESTIO around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini connects the bull's head crowned with a garland ('bouis caput insula redimitum') to the Saecular Games (Saeculares ludi), at which this animal was sacrificed, and infers that a member of the Restio family served as quindecemuir at those games. He mentions no capis, lituus, or other implements; the coin is identified only by the bull's head and its Saecular-games connection.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Bucranium (bull skull) facing; C.ANTIVS above
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Capis (ritual jug) and lituus; RESTIO below

completed.family_note: The Antii were a plebeian gens. C. Antius C.f. Restio (Crawford 455, 47 BC) struck three distinct denarius types: one with jugate heads of the Dei Penates and Hercules with club on the reverse, another with a portrait head and Hercules with trophy, and a third showing a bucranium with garlanded horns and a lighted sacrificial altar. The cognomen Restio derives from the tribune C. Antius Restio who carried the famous lex Antia sumptuaria, a sumptuary law restricting extravagant banqueting. The coin types emphasise religious and sacrificial themes.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini identifies C. Antius C.f. Restio as the tribune who carried the lex sumptuaria, noting 'cuius imago in primo denario impressa est'. He cites Agellius [Gellius] lib. II, cap. XXIV and Macrobius lib. III on the law. For coin 2 (the Dei Penates type), Orsini says only that the Penates images on the reverse are 'fortasse' (perhaps) those of the Dei Penates, giving two alternative explanations but committing to neither: either because the family originated from Lanuvium (citing Varro and Paedianus, where Penates were worshipped) or because Restio's law pertained to religion. For coin 3, Orsini connects the bull's head (bouis caput insula redimitum) to the Saecular Games (Saeculares ludi), at which that animal was sacrificed, and infers a member of the Restio family served as quindecemuir at those games.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head of M. Antonius right; M·ANT·IMP·AVG·III·VIR·R·P·C·M·NERVA·PROQ·P
coins_engraved.reverse: Bare head of L. Antonius right; L·ANTONIVS·COS
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini opens his Antonian section citing Plutarch, Dio, and the Philippics. He reads this denarius as a joint issue between M. Antonius and a fellow triumvir and discusses Antony as Pontifex, noting the augural and pontifical legends.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right with slight drapery; legend around partially visible
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory standing right on globe, holding wreath and palm; legend around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini connects the Victory on globe to Antony's claim of universal dominion. He draws on Velleius's account of Antony as Liber Pater (Dionysus) and reads the reverse as a triumviral propaganda monument.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Small head right facing slightly, within a circular flan. Very little legend visible around border — partially ANTONIA text at top of plate provides context but not legible on coin itself. Portrait is a bare head right, slightly draped at neck.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Clearly shows a standing winged figure (Victory) on a globe or base, holding a wreath in extended right hand and a palm branch in left. Legend reads: PIETAS (above figure) and COS (below or beside). The figure is well-rendered in classical style.
coins_engraved.specimen_refetch_qa: Specimen reverse is a PIETAS.COS type (Pietas standing, PIETAS COS in exergue), not the Victory-on-globe of Crawford 516

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right; M·ANTONIVS / III·VIR·R·P·C around
coins_engraved.reverse: Pietas standing facing beside a lighted altar; PIETAS / COS in fields
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini reads IMP.TERT and PIETAS.COS as establishing Antony's third imperatorship and his claim to Pietas. He connects the trophy reverse to Antony's eastern campaigns and cites Plutarch and Appian on the triumvir's military career.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Clear large coin image. Obverse shows bare head right within circular legend. Text clearly legible: IMP around top left, then continuing ANTONIVS·IMP·III·VIR·R·P·C around the portrait. Head is facing right with strong Roman features.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Standing winged figure, lightly draped, holding objects. Text: PIETAS above and COS beside/below. The figure appears to be Victory or Pietas standing right, holding a long object (palm?) and small round object.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Laureate head right; legend around: IMP.TERT.C... (partially legible)
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Trophy of arms; legend: PIETAS.COS

coins_engraved.obverse: Head wearing petasus right; C·ANTONIVS·M·F·PRO·COS around
coins_engraved.reverse: Priestly implements: simpulum, aspergillum, axe, apex; legend: PONTIFEX
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini's Dionysiac/Sol observations (pp. 18–19) are made collectively about the plate, not coin-by-coin. He cites Velleius on Antony presenting himself as Liber Pater ('cũ ante nouũ fe Liberũ patrem appellari iufisset... curru uelut Liber pater uectus esset Alexãdriae,' p. 19) and Dio lib. XLVIII on Antony as Osiris/Dionysus ('Aυτòς μἐν ὅσιρις & διονύσιος,' p. 19). These general remarks illuminate the plate as a whole. Individual comments attributing Sol iconography to coins 5 and 6 specifically, or Liber Pater to coin 7, are inferences, not Orsini's coin-by-coin statements. The comments for coins 4–7 should reflect that Orsini's Dionysiac/solar text applies to the plate generally ('Ad primũ uero & reliquos, spectãnt illa ex lib. l').
coins_engraved.observed_obverse: Bare head right, clean-shaven male portrait in profile. Legend readable around the rim: M·ANTINVM·M·F and PROCOS visible at bottom. Portrait faces right with short hair, classical Roman style. No symbols or attributes visible beyond the bust.
coins_engraved.observed_reverse: Four priestly implements arranged in a row within the coin field: from left, a simpulum (ladle), an aspergillum (sprinkler), an axe (securis), and an apex (priest's cap with spike). Legend reads PONTIFES (PONTIFEX) along the bottom. The implements are clearly engraved and identifiable. This matches the catalog description well.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Legend around: M.ANTINVM.M.F.PROCOS; bare head right
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Priestly implements: simpulum, aspergillum, axe, apex; legend: PONTIFEX

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head facing right; legend around: III.VIR.R.P.C.COS.DESIG.ITER.ET.TERT
coins_engraved.reverse: Nude male figure (Sol) standing facing, right arm raised holding object; legend around: M.ANTONIVS.M.F.M.N.AVGVR.IMP.TER
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the Sol figure on the reverse as part of Antony's Dionysiac-solar iconography. Drawing on Velleius, he discusses Antony's identification with Liber Pater and connects this type to the eastern solar cult in Antony's ideology.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right; legend: IMP
coins_engraved.reverse: Temple facade with four columns; radiate head of Sol within temple; legend: III VIR R.P.C. arranged around temple
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this temple-reverse type with radiate Sol within the façade as evidence of Antony's eastern religious associations. He reads the IMP legend as establishing imperatorship and connects the Sol imagery to Antony's Hellenistic divine claims.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right; no legend clearly visible
coins_engraved.reverse: Radiate and draped bust right (Sol/Helios type); legend around: M·ANTONIVS·III·VIR·R·P·C
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini reads the radiate Sol bust on the reverse as part of Antony's sustained identification with eastern solar and Dionysiac deities. He connects this to Plutarch's account of Antony presenting himself as a new Dionysus in the east.

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head right; legend around partially legible
coins_engraved.reverse: Cista (cista mystica / altar) with a small bust above it, flanked by two coiled serpents; legend around: III VIR R P C
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes this eastern issue of M. Antonius and records the double-head obverse as a joint issue. He draws on Appian and Dio for the context of Antony's eastern command and reads the laureate heads as establishing his triumviral authority.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Large, clear engraving of coin. Obverse shows head right within full circular legend. Text reads: M·ANTONIVS·IMP·COS·DES·ITER·ET·TER around the portrait. Portrait is a well-defined bare head facing right, slightly idealised.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Very clear reverse showing priestly implements: a tall ritual stand or tripod with a serpent coiling up it. Flanking objects — possibly simpulum left and lituus right. Legend: III·VIR around one side, R·P·C on the other.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Laureate head right; legend around partially legible
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Laureate head right (smaller); legend around partially visible

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right; legend partially visible
coins_engraved.reverse: Double cornucopia; ΑΥΤΟ / ΚΡΑ (Greek)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini records this eastern issue with a double cornucopia and the Greek legend ΑΥΤΟ/ΚΡΑ (autokrator).
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Bare head right, largely unlegended on this engraving — the obverse appears to show only the portrait with perhaps a faint border. Portrait is clean and depicts a mature male head right.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Very distinctive: a large round-bottomed amphora or cantharus (jug with two handles) prominently displayed. To the left of the jug: what appears to be a lituus or curved staff. Text reads: AYTO / KPA (Greek letters — ΑΥΤΟΚΡΑ[ΤΩΡ] = 'Autokrator/Imperator'). This is Greek-legend reverse!

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head right; legend around M·ANTONIVS·IMP·COS·DESIG·ITER·ET·TERT
coins_engraved.reverse: Statue figure atop a cista, flanked by two coiled serpents; legend around III·VIR·R·P·C
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini gives no individual comment on this cistophorus. His general discussion of Antony's eastern coins (pp. 19–21) concerns Dionysiac/Osiris imagery and the Armenia Devicta types; no coin-specific description of a cista mystica figure is offered anywhere in the Antonia section.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Two busts facing right — jugate portrait pair. The pair are close together and both are bare-headed. Legend around reads: M·ANTONIVS·IMP·COS·DES·ITER·ET·TER (partially). The portraits are male and female — man slightly in front, woman behind.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Standing figure with priestly implements — a tripod with serpent, or possibly trophy-like structure. Similar in concept to coin 8. Legend around with ANTO readable.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Bare head right; legend around partially visible
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Trophy with captured arms; legend around partially legible
coins_engraved.orsini_comment_ai: [QA: this note may describe a different type — flagged for review] Orsini discusses the Armenia Devicta types, connecting Antony's trophy reverse to the capture of Artavasdes of Armenia in 34 BC. He cites Plutarch and Dio on the Armenia campaign as the high point of Antony's eastern conquests.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare/laureate head of Mark Antony right, Armenian tiara behind; legend around: ANTONI.ARMENIA.DEVICTA
coins_engraved.reverse: Draped bust right (possibly Cleopatra); legend around: REGINAE.REGVM.FILIORVM.REGVM (partially legible)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini records this as the Cleopatra joint issue and notes the full titulature CLEOPATRAE REGINAE REGVM FILIORVM REGVM on the reverse. He draws on Plutarch and Dio for the political significance of Antony's union with Cleopatra.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Two bare heads facing right (jugate busts); legend around: ARMENIA.DEVICTA (partially legible)
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Draped bust right (possibly Cleopatra); legend around: REGINAE.REGVM.FILIORVM.REGVM (partially legible)

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right; legend: M.ANTO.IMP
coins_engraved.reverse: Bare head right; legend: CAESAR.DIC (portrait of Caesar)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this early joint issue of M. Antonius with a Caesar portrait, treating M.ANTO.IMP and CAESAR.DIC as establishing the triumviral relationship. He cites the Philippics for the period before Caesar's assassination.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Large clear portrait of male head right. Legend clearly: M·ANTO·IMP around. Head has strong features, short hair, clean-shaven face. Tiny lituus visible behind head.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Different male portrait facing right — clearly a different person, younger or differently featured. Legend: CAESAR·DIC clearly readable. Small jug/praefericulum visible to left of portrait.

coins_engraved.obverse: Single bare head right; legend around: M ANT IMP AVG III VIR R P C M BARBAT P
coins_engraved.reverse: Bare head right; legend around: CAESAR.IMP.PONT.III.VIR.R.P.C.
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini reads the jugate busts as a joint triumviral issue and connects the CAESAR.IMP.PONT.III.VIR.R.P.C legend to the reconstitution of Roman authority after Philippi. He draws on Appian's Bella Civilia for the triumviral settlements.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Two bare heads right (jugate busts of Antony and another); legend around: M.ANT.IMP.AVG.III.VIR.R.P.C.M.BARBAT (partially legible)
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Bare head right; legend around: CAESAR.IMP.PONT.III.VIR.R.P.C.

coins_engraved.obverse: Single bare head right; legend around: M ANT IMP AVG III VIR R P C L GELLI Q P
coins_engraved.reverse: Bare head right; legend around: CAESAR.IMP.PONT.III.VIR.R.P.C.
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the joint issue of Antony and Octavian (M.ANT.IMP and CAESAR.IMP) as a monument to the Second Triumvirate. He cites Appian and Dio on the Perusine war period and the uneasy alliance between the two triumvirs.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Two jugate male heads right. Legend clearly readable around: M·ANT·IMP·ANG·III·VIR·R·P·C·L·GELLO·P (or similar — the text L·GELLO is clearly visible). Both heads are bare.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Single bare head right, younger-looking. Legend: CAESAR·IMP·PONT·III·VIR·R·P·C clearly around portrait.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Two bare heads right (jugate busts); legend around: M.ANT.IMP.AVG.III.VIR.R.P.C.M.GELLO.P (partially legible)
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Bare head right; legend around: CAESAR.IMP.PONT.III.VIR.R.P.C.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head of Mark Antony right; M·ANTON·IMP·III·VIR·R·P·C
coins_engraved.reverse: Bare head of Octavian right; CAESAR·IMP·PONT·III·VIR·R·P·C
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Crawford 517/2 (M. Barbatius, 41 BC): two facing bare heads — M. Antonius (M·ANTON·IMP·III·VIR·R·P·C) and Octavian (CAESAR·IMP·PONT·III·VIR·R·P·C) — a monument to the short-lived triumviral concord between Antony and Octavian, NOT a jugate Antony/Cleopatra type. (Re-identified from the former 543/1.)
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Two bare heads right (jugate busts); legend around: M.ANTON.IMP.III.VIR.R.P.C.AVG (partially legible)
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Bare head right; legend around: CAESAR.IMP.PONT.IIII.VIR.R.P.C. (partially legible)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment_ai: Orsini reads the jugate busts as representing M. Antonius and a fellow triumvir with the CAESAR.IMP.PONT.IIII.VIR legend establishing the fourth consulship. He connects this to Antony's command in the east and cites Plutarch on the period.
coins_engraved.specimen_shared_reason: same catalogue type cross-listed under multiple gentes (joint-moneyer issue or sub-variant); one museum specimen serves all

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right; legend around: ANT... IMP... III.VIR.R.P.C.
coins_engraved.reverse: Prow of galley right; legend: AHENOBARVS.IMP; star above; legend below: CN.DOMITI (partially legible)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus prow issue as part of the Antonian series. He notes the AHENOBARVS.IMP galley reverse as marking fleet command and connects it to the build-up of Antony's naval forces before Actium.
coins_engraved.specimen_shared_reason: same catalogue type cross-listed under multiple gentes (joint-moneyer issue or sub-variant); one museum specimen serves all

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right; legend around: IMP.TER.ANTONIVS.AVG.VR.COS.DES...
coins_engraved.reverse: Legend in two lines within plain field: M.SILANVS.AVG / Q.PRO.COS.
coins_engraved.identification: Crawford 542/1 — Mark Antony with M. Silanus as quaestor pro consule, 33 BC
coins_engraved.moneyer: M. Junius Silanus (quaestor pro consule under M. Antonius)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes M. Silanus as quaestor pro consule under M. Antonius and reads the legend M.SILANVS.AVG / Q.PR as establishing his subordinate command. He discusses the IMP.TER legend as marking Antony's third imperatorship.

coins_engraved.obverse: Jug (praefericulum) between lituus and other priestly implements; legend around: III.VIR.R.P.C. / M.ANTON (partially legible)
coins_engraved.reverse: Augural/priestly implements: lituus (left), jug/praefericulum (center) and winged caduceus (right); legend around: M ANTON IMP ITER (AVGVR)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini reads the priestly implements (jug, lituus) on the obverse and caduceus between cornucopiae on the reverse as emblems of Antony's pontifical office and claim to peace and plenty. He connects this to Antony's augurate.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: No portrait — purely object/symbol reverse. Shows: lituus (curved augural staff) on left, then a tall jug (praefericulum or capis) in centre-right. Legend around: III·VIR·R·P·C on one side, M·ANTON on the other.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: More complex scene: a jug prominently in centre-left, a caduceus (winged staff with serpents) on the right, with additional symbols. Legend: FRANC·SIMP·ITER (partially readable) — possibly IMP·ITER visible.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Jug (praefericulum) between lituus and other priestly implements; legend around: III.VIR.R.P.C. / M.ANTON (partially legible)
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Caduceus between two cornucopiae; legend around partially legible, includes IMP and ITER

coins_engraved.obverse: Bearded head right; legend around: ANTO.COS.III.IMP.IIII
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory standing right, holding wreath and palm; legend around: SCARPVS.IMP / ANTONIO.AVG
coins_engraved.identification: Crawford 546/2b — M. Pinarius Scarpus for Mark Antony, Cyrenaica, 31-30 BC
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies M. Pinarius Scarpus as a Caesarian/Antonian officer serving in Cyrenaica. He reads ANTO.COS.III.IMP.IIII and the Victory reverse as establishing Antony's authority in North Africa in the last phase before Actium.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right; legend around: M.ANTONIVS.AVG.IMP
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory standing right within laurel wreath, holding trophy; legend partially visible
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this colonial/provincial issue as part of Antony's provincial programme. He reads M.ANTONIVS.AVG.IMP on the obverse and connects the Victory with trophy reverse to Antony's military command in the eastern provinces.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Clear, large portrait. Male head right, well-defined. Legend: R·P·C·M·ANTONIVS·AVG·IMP around — at bottom partially. The head is distinctive — pronounced nose, heavy features, clearly Antony's typical portrait type.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Standing winged figure (Victory) within a laurel wreath border. Victory holds a wreath and palm branch. The wreath frames the entire scene. No text visible within the wreath other than the figure.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right; ANTON·AVG·IMP·III·COS·DES·III·III·V·R·P·C (partially legible)
coins_engraved.reverse: Legend in field: ANTONIVS / AVG.IMP.III (text only within plain circle)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes the ANTONIVS / AVG.IMP.III legend and discusses this text-field reverse as an unusual Antonian issue. He connects it to the broader series of Antonian moneta struck in the east from 38 BC.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Large, clear portrait. Male head right within legend. Text legible: ANT·AVG·IMP·III·COS·DES·III·III·V·R·P·C around — this is a very full and legible legend.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Purely epigraphic — text only in field within plain circle/border. Two lines: ANTONIVS / AVG·IMP·III. No figural elements whatsoever.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Bare head right; legend around: ANTONIVS.AVG.IMP.III.COS.DESIG.III.III.V.R.P.C. (partially legible)
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Legend in field: ANTONIVS / AVG.IMP.III (text only within plain circle)

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare male head right (Antony); no legend clearly visible
coins_engraved.reverse: Galley/ship right; legend above: L.BIBVLVS
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini makes no comment on this coin in the Antonia section. He explicitly defers all discussion of Bibulus to the Calpurnia gens entry: 'De Bibulo, Fonteio, & Atratino, qui & ipsi Antonianarum partium fuerunt, non est hic locus scribendi: sed in Calpurnia, Fonteia, & Sempronia gentibus...diligenter à nobis indicabuntur.'
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Female or feminine portrait head right. Lightly drawn, with hair styled back in a bun or tied back. No legend clearly visible around this portrait — the border is plain. Head appears to be a female portrait.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Very distinctive: a warship (galley) facing right with oar-bank visible and stern ornament. Text above the galley: L·BIBVLVS clearly legible. The galley is a typical Roman warship (trireme type) drawn in detail.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Female head right with hair tied back (possibly Octavia); no legend clearly visible
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Galley/ship right; legend above: L.BIBVLVS
coins_engraved.specimen_shared_reason: same catalogue type cross-listed under multiple gentes (joint-moneyer issue or sub-variant); one museum specimen serves all

coins_engraved.obverse: Single bare male head in profile; no clearly legible legend
coins_engraved.reverse: Galley/ship right; legend: L.BIBVLVS (partially visible)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini makes no comment on this coin in the Antonia section. He explicitly defers all discussion of Bibulus to the Calpurnia gens entry: 'non est hic locus scribendi.'
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Two jugate male heads facing right — both bare. They are close together, side by side. No legend legible in engraving around the busts. Heads look male, not male/female.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Galley (warship) right with oar-banks. Text: L·BIBVLVS clearly above. Below the galley: A (control letter?). Very similar to coin 22 reverse.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Two male jugate heads left; no clearly legible legend
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Galley/ship right; legend: L.BIBVLVS (partially visible)
coins_engraved.specimen_shared_reason: same catalogue type cross-listed under multiple gentes (joint-moneyer issue or sub-variant); one museum specimen serves all

coins_engraved.obverse: Two heads right (jugate busts); legend around: ...PIVS.CAPI.TO.PRO.PR (partially legible)
coins_engraved.reverse: Galley/ship right; legend around: M.ANT.IMP... COS.DESIG.ITER.ET.TER (partially legible)
coins_engraved.moneyer: M. Antonius and C. Asinius Gallus (Capito, propraetor)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini makes no individual comment on this coin. He defers discussion of Bibulus, Fonteius, and Atratinus to other gentes entries ('non est hic locus scribendi: sed in Calpurnia, Fonteia, & Sempronia gentibus...diligenter à nobis indicabuntur,' p. 22). No text on pp. 18–27 individually discusses Capito or attributes a 'jugate heads' reading to Orsini for this coin.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Two jugate male heads right. Text legend clearly readable: L·[VS]·CAPITO·PRO·PR around — and on the other side of obverse: M·ANT·IMP·[COS]... The portraits show two bare-headed males.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Galley (warship) facing right — clearly the prow and oar-banks visible. Legend around: M·ANT·IMP·COS·DESIG·ITER·ET·TERT (partially). The galley has a distinctive artemon (foreyard).

coins_engraved.obverse: Two jugate heads (same direction, overlapping); legend above: M.AT.IMP.TER.COS
coins_engraved.reverse: Marine creature (hippocampus or dolphin) with small Victory figure; legend around: L·ATRATINVS
coins_engraved.identification: RPC I, 1459 — Mark Antony and Octavia, with L. Sempronius Atratinus, fleet coinage, Achaea, 36 BC; bare head of Antony right + Octavia / quadriga of hippocamps with L·ATRATINVS·AVGVR
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini makes no comment on this coin in the Antonia section. He explicitly defers discussion of Atratinus to the Sempronia gens entry: 'De Bibulo, Fonteio, & Atratino...non est hic locus scribendi.'
coins_engraved.observed_obverse: Two facing busts confronted at center: a male bust on the left and a female bust on the right, both shown in profile facing each other. The male appears bearded or with heavier features; the female has a more delicate profile. Legend around the upper border partially legible; letters visible include what appears to be M·AT and IMP. The composition shows both figures from the chest up facing inward.
coins_engraved.observed_reverse: A sea creature (hippocampus or sea-horse with fish tail) facing left, carrying a small winged Victory figure seated on its back. The Victory appears to hold a wreath or small object. Legend around the border partially visible; letters consistent with L·ATRATINVS. The creature's body curves across the coin field. Matches catalog description of marine creature with Victory.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Two heads facing each other (man and woman); legend above: M.AT.IMP.TER.COS
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Marine creature (hippocampus or dolphin) with small Victory figure; legend around: L·ATRATINVS

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head; capis (jug) in field before the face; CAESAR·DIC
coins_engraved.reverse: Bare head right; legend around: M.ANTO.IMP... R.P.C. (partially legible)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini reads this as a joint issue of M. Antonius and Octavian, noting CAESAR.DIC and M.ANTO.IMP as the paired legends. He connects the lituus on the obverse to Antony's augurate and discusses the early triumviral period before the break.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Clear portrait of male head right with lituus (curved augural staff) visible behind head. Portrait has laurel wreath (small) or simply a bare head. Legend: CAESAR·DIC clearly visible around. Small jug/vessel also visible.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Male portrait facing right (bare head). Legend clearly: M·ANO·IMP·R·C (partially — reading M·ANT·IMP·R·P·C). A small lituus visible behind this head too.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Bare head right with lituus behind; legend: CAESAR.DIC (partially visible)
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Bare head right; legend around: M.ANTO.IMP... R.P.C. (partially legible)

coins_engraved.obverse: Bird (eagle) standing, jug before it; legend above: M.ATINI
coins_engraved.reverse: Priestly implements (simpulum, aspergillum, securis, apex); LEP·IMP around
coins_engraved.identification: Crawford 489/3 — M. Aemilius Lepidus (as triumvir), 42 BC
coins_engraved.moneyer: M. Aemilius Lepidus and M. Antonius (joint triumviral issue)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the priestly implements (simpulum, aspergillum, securis, apex) on the reverse as emblems of M. Aemilius Lepidus's pontifical authority (Pontifex Maximus). He reads this joint Lepidus/Antonius issue within his extended treatment of triumviral coinage.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Bird walking left; M·V·IMP around; lituus left, jug right
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Priestly implements (simpulum, aspergillum, securis, apex); LEP·IMP around

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right; no legend clearly visible
coins_engraved.reverse: Lion walking right; legend above: INAQ; legend below: LVGV; A and XL in field
coins_engraved.moneyer: L. Munatius Plancus (for M. Antonius, at Lugdunum)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the lion as the emblem of the Lugdunum colony and identifies L. Munatius Plancus as involved in the colony's foundation (citing Dio XLV). He reads the lion as 'coloniae uetus insigne, à quo fortasfse nomen id, quod nunc uocatur traxit' (p. 23). He does not read or interpret the legend INAQ visible in the engraving, and does not identify it as a place name.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Female head right — wearing what appears to be a Phrygian-style cap or helmet, or possibly a helmet with a small crest. Distinctive profile with pointed chin. No clear legend visible on this obverse crop.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Lion walking right — powerful, clearly rendered. Text around: INAQ (above) / DVN (possibly), A· on left, ·XL on right, LVGV below. The INAQ·DVN / A·XL / LVGV text is a key identifier.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right; legend partially visible
coins_engraved.reverse: Lion walking right; legend above: ANTONI; legend below: IMP
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini reads the lion walking right with ANTONI / IMP as Antony's Lugdunum-type issue, discussing the lion as the emblem of the colony. He draws on Appian and Dio for the Lugdunum foundation and Antony's role in the Gallic command.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Small female head right wearing a winged helmet or cap. Possibly Victory helmeted, or IIIvir badge. Legend: III·VIR (top) and R·P·C (right side) visible around a small portrait. Very similar in style to coin 28 obverse.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Lion walking right. Text: ANTONI above lion, A·XLI (left and right flanking), IMP below. This is very similar to coin 28 but with slightly different legend.

coins_engraved.obverse: Jug and bird (eagle or raven) standing right; legend: M.A.IMP (partially legible)
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory, right, crowning trophy
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the jug and raven/eagle obverse and the Victory crowning trophy reverse as emblems of Antony's augural and military authority. He reads the M.A.IMP legend and connects the bird to Antony's augurate office.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Symbols/implements only — no portrait. Shows: a lituus (curved augural staff) on left, a tall jug (praefericulum/urceus) in centre, and a bird (possibly a raven or eagle) walking right. Legend: M·A·IMP (around).
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Victory walking right — wings spread, holding a wreath in extended right hand. She appears to be crowning something or walking purposefully. Possibly a shield at her feet.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right; legend around: M.ANT.AVGVR.III.VIR.R.P.C.
coins_engraved.reverse: Trophy of arms with shield and spear; legend: IMP.TER (with additional symbols)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini reads M.ANT.AVGVR.III.VIR.R.P.C as establishing Antony as augur and triumvir. He connects the trophy of arms with shield and spear to IMP.TER (third imperatorship) and discusses this within his account of Antony's Armenia campaign.

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head right; legend around: IMP.TER.ANTONIVS.AVGVR.COS.DES (partially legible)
coins_engraved.reverse: Trophy with captive at base; legend around: ...IMP... III.VIR.R.P.C. / ...ITER.ET.TER (partially legible)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes IMP.TER.ANTONIVS.AVGVR on the obverse and reads the trophy with captive as commemorating the Armenia campaign of 34 BC. He cites Plutarch and Dio on the capture of Artavasdes and connects the Armenia Devicta imagery to Antony's claims.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Large, clear portrait of male head right. Full circular legend clearly readable: ANTONIVS·AVGVR·COS·DES (top arc) and ITER·[ET·TER?] (bottom arc). Strong portrait with defined features — Antony's recognisable profile.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Priestly/ritual object — appears to be a tall ornate structure with a crown or radiate object on top, with wings or feathers at sides. Possibly an apex (priestly cap with olive branch) or decorated thymiaterion (incense stand). Legend: IMP·TER (top), III·VIR·R·P·C (bottom arc).

coins_engraved.obverse: Veiled head of Concordia right; legend partially visible around
coins_engraved.reverse: Two hands clasped round a winged caduceus (dextrarum iunctio); legend partially visible
coins_engraved.identification: Crawford 529/4b — Mark Antony and Octavian; Head of Concordia right, veiled / Two hands clasped round caduceus; AR quinarius, 39 BC
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this quinarius type as part of the concordia series with clasped hands (dextrarum iunctio). He connects the caduceus to peace negotiations and reads the Concordia imagery as commemorating the reconciliation between Antony and Octavian at Misenum (39 BC).
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Female head right, veiled or with garland in hair. Clear depiction — this appears to be a female deity (possibly Pietas, or Octavia, or a goddess). Legend around: III·VIR (at top left), R·P·C (at right).
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Two figures clasping hands — dextrarum iunctio (handshake/concordia scene). Text around: M·ANTONS·C·CAESAR (or M·ANT·[VS]·C·CAESAR). The reverse shows two standing figures joining right hands — a classic concordia type.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Bare head right; legend partially visible around
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Mounted horseman right (equestrian figure); legend partially visible

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right; legend CAESAR IMP
coins_engraved.reverse: Caduceus with wings; legend ANTONIVS IMP
coins_engraved.identification: Crawford 529/2a — M. Antonius and Octavian, 41 BC
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini reads this joint Antony/Octavian quinarius as a monument to the triumviral concordia. He notes CAESAR IMP and ANTONIVS IMP as the paired legends and connects the caduceus reverse to the pact of Misenum (39 BC) discussed in Appian.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of M. Antonius right; lituus behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Caduceus between two cornucopiae on globe; M·ANT·IMP III·VIR·R·P·C
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini reads the caduceus between cornucopiae on globe as symbolising Antony's claim to peace and plenty. He notes M·ANT·IMP III·VIR and discusses the head of Antony with lituus (augurate symbol) as the obverse type.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Bare male head right — a slightly younger or more idealised portrait than Antony's usual. Possibly Octavian? No clear legend on obverse in this crop.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Central object: a caduceus (winged staff with intertwined serpents) with cups or pateras hanging from it, and an anchor below. Legend: M·ANT·IM (above) and III·VIR·R·P·C (below/around).

coins_engraved.obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
coins_engraved.reverse: Three legionary standards (aquila between two signa); CHORTIVM PRAETORIARVM
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the cohors praetoria as Antony's praetorian guard, noting its Scipionic precedent. He reads CHORTIS PRAETORIAE with the three standards as the emblem of Antony's personal escort, connecting it to Scipio Africanus's use of a praetorian cohort.

coins_engraved.obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
coins_engraved.reverse: Three legionary standards; CHORTIS SPECULATORVM
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini reads CHORTIS SPECULATORVM as the reconnaissance and intelligence unit of Antony's army. He discusses the three legionary standards and the galley obverse as marking this special cohort's place within the legionary series.

coins_engraved.obverse: Galley right with rowers; ANT.AVG above, III.VIR.R.P.C below
coins_engraved.reverse: Aquila between two signa; LEG II
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes LEG II as the second legion in Antony's order of battle. He reads the galley obverse (ANT.AVG / III.VIR.R.P.C) as marking the fleet context and the aquila between two signa as the legion's standards.

completed.family_note: The Antonii were a plebeian gens claiming descent from Anton, a son of Hercules. This is by far the largest family section in the work, with 65 coins across 12 plates. L. Antonius, consul in 41 BC, struck denarii with portrait types and the stork (ciconia) as a symbol of his cognomen Pietas (Crawford 489). M. Antonius the triumvir dominates the section with portrait denarii, Armenian victory types (ARMENIA DEVICTA, Crawford 539), the famous joint issue with Cleopatra VII (Crawford 543/1), Dionysiac types, augural implements, and the complete series of legionary denarii (Crawford 544) naming Legions II through XXII plus special units including the Cohors Praetoria, Cohors Speculatorum, Legio XII Antiquae, XVII Classicae, and XVIII Lybicae. Provincial and allied commander issues by Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus, M. Silanus, L. Munatius Plancus, and L. Bibulus are also included. Q. Antonius Balbus (Crawford 364/1, 83 BC) represents the earliest Antonius on the plates.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini devotes extensive commentary to M. Antonius, drawing heavily on Plutarch, Dio, Appian, Velleius, and Cicero's Philippics. He discusses the stork as a symbol of Pietas for L. Antonius (citing Dio XLVIII). For M. Antonius he discusses his Dionysiac associations (Antony as Liber Pater, citing Velleius) and the Armenia Devicta types commemorating the capture of Artavasdes. For the Cleopatra denarius he records the legend 'reginam regum, ut in secundo denario inscriptum est' (CLEOPATRAE REGINAE REGVM FILIORVM REGVM). The caduceus coins are connected to the peace between Antony and Caesar in anno DCCXIII (citing Dio XLVIII). He discusses the cohors praetoria with reference to Scipio Africanus, the Lugdunum colony (citing the lion as colony emblem and Dio XLV), and attributes Legio XII Antiquae solely to the coin ('nullus, quod sciam, ueterum scriptorum facit mentionem'). Legio XVII Classica and Legio XVIII Lybicae are likewise known only from the coins, Orsini guessing Lybicae was named from the region ('à regione') as were Cyrenaicam and Macedonicam (citing Dio LV). For Bibulus, Fonteius, and Atratinus, Orsini explicitly defers: 'non est hic locus scribendi: sed in Calpurnia, Fonteia, & Sempronia gentibus...diligenter à nobis indicabuntur.'

coins_engraved.obverse: MESSALLA.APRONIVS / SISENNA.GALVS around; priestly implements

completed.family_note: The Apronii were a plebeian gens (Orsini: 'ut arbitror, plebeiae'). Orsini records L. Apronius who accused Sex. Clodius, and Cn. Apronius Cn.F. who accused M. Sauefeius. Apronius Galvs served as one of the IIIviri monetales (A.A.A.F.F.) under Augustus alongside Sisenna, striking bronzes; the two co-moneyers visible on the Orsini plate are SISENNA and GALVS (not Messalla). Orsini tentatively identifies Galvs as the consul who succeeded M. Camillo ex kal. Iul. in the Capitoline tables, anno DCCLX, citing Dio lib. LVIII, Velleius lib. II, and Tacitus lib. III. He notes that Galvs is also a cognomen of the Sulpicia family.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini notes the plebeian gens, citing Valerius Maximus lib. VII cap. VIII and Paedianum in Miloniana. The co-moneyers on the coin are Sisenna and Galvs (not Messalla). Orsini discusses Galvs's possible identity as the consul recorded in the Capitoline tables (anno DCCLX), citing Dio lib. LVIII, Velleius lib. II, and Tacitus lib. III on his Germanicus-related triumphal honours. He notes Galvs may be a Sulpiciae family cognomen as well, and that VIPSTANVS APRONIANVS was adopted by C. Vipstanus.

completed.family_note: The Aquillii were a gens with both patrician and plebeian branches. Two important Republican issues are known: Mn. Aquillius (Crawford 303/1, 109 BC) struck denarii with a radiate bust of Sol and Luna driving a biga of stags, while Mn. Aquillius Mn.f. Mn.n. (Crawford 401/1, 71 BC) produced the famous Virtus/Sicilia type commemorating his grandfather's suppression of the slave revolt in Sicily in 101 BC, showing a warrior raising a fallen female personification of Sicilia. Under Augustus, L. Aquillius Florus served as IIIvir monetalis (c. 19 BC), striking multiple denarius and aureus types with Augustus's portrait.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini identifies the Virtus/Sicilia type as commemorating Mn. Aquillius who suppressed the Sicilian slave revolt, correctly reading the SICIL legend. He discusses the Sol/Luna biga type as an earlier issue of the gens. For the Augustan issues by L. Aquillius Florus, he notes the IIIvir monetalis title and discusses the star/flower reverse type in connection with the cognomen Florus (relating to Flora). His commentary on the Aquillii draws on standard historical sources for the Sicilian slave wars without extended digression.

He quotes Catullus Carmen 84 on Q. Arrius's aspirated pronunciation as prosopographic context. He leaves the identity of M. Arrius Secundus explicitly open ('incertum mihi'): he may be the person in Pedianus's argument to Verr. IV, or the Suriae praefectus.

completed.family_note: The Arrii were a plebeian gens. M. Arrius Secundus struck denarii with his name on the obverse legend and military decorations (clathros/lattice-work, hasta pura, and corona) on the reverse — Orsini argues these were the dona with which Arrius was honoured for defending a camp gate against enemy assault. Orsini leaves his identity uncertain, noting he may be the person mentioned by Pedianus in relation to a speech by Cicero (Verr. IV), or the Arrius who served as praefectus Suriae (prefect of Syria). Q. Arrius, a prominent member known from Cicero's Brutus as a quasi-secundarius to Crassus, aspired to the consulship; Catullus (Carmen 84) mocks his aspirated pronunciation. The gens is not widely attested in Republican magistracies beyond these individuals.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini opens by quoting Cicero's Brutus on Q. Arrius as a quasi-secundarius to Crassus, and discusses Q. Arrius's consulship aspirations and his role as Suriae praefectus (as one of two candidates for the identity of M. Arrius Secundus). He quotes Catullus Carmen 84 in full, which ridicules Q. Arrius's aspirated pronunciation (hinsidias for insidias, chommoda for commoda). For the coin, he identifies the military decorations on the reverse as clathros (lattice-work for barricading camp gates), hasta pura, and corona, arguing from Horace and Columella that clathri were used to fortify camp gates. He explicitly leaves the identity of M. Arrius Secundus uncertain ('incertum mihi'), offering two possibilities: the person mentioned in Pedianus's argument to Cicero's In Verrem IV, or the Suriae praefectus — he does NOT identify him as praefectus classis.

completed.family_note: The Asinii were a plebeian gens originally from Teate in the territory of the Marrucini. C. Asinius Pollio, the famous orator, historian, and patron of Virgil, was consul in 40 BC and celebrated a triumph over the Parthini in Illyria. His son C. Asinius Gallus served as IIIvir monetalis under Augustus (c. 8 BC), striking bronze coins with Augustus's portrait and S C reverses. No Republican denarii are known for the gens; both coins in Orsini's plates are Augustan bronzes.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini identifies C. Asinius Gallus as 'orator & poeta' who struck (signavit) these bronze coins, and as the son of Asinius Pollio, who was consul with C. Marcius Censorinus in anno DCCXIX (= 35 BC). He summarises Pollio's fame, citing Seneca in Declamationes, Pliny in Epistolae, and Suetonius in De claris grammaticis. He notes that Cornelius Tacitus (Annals I) records Gallus being censured, and that Gallus suffered severely under Tiberius, being put to death (per Eusebius) before the death of Livy. Orsini does NOT mention the title 'IIIvir monetalis' anywhere; he simply says Gallus 'signavit' the coins.

Atilius consul (anno DCXLVII) — but explicitly states the identification is uncertain ('difficile est... affirmare'). He does not confidently assign the coins to M. Atilius Saranus.

completed.family_note: The Atilii were a gens with both patrician and plebeian branches, the most notable being the Reguli, Serani, and Bulbi. M. Atilius Saranus (Crawford 214/1a, 148 BC) struck denarii with the standard Roma/Dioscuri type bearing the legend M.ATILI. The cognomen Saranus (or Serranus) derives from serendo (sowing), as Pliny records that C. Atilius Regulus was found sowing his fields when summoned to his second consulship. M. Atilius Regulus is famous for his legendary captivity and death at Carthage during the First Punic War.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini establishes that the Atilii had both patrician and plebeian branches. For the Serani/Saranus family, he follows Pliny (Lib. XVIII cap. III) in deriving the cognomen from serendo (sowing), but immediately notes that in the silver denarii and in an ancient inscription the form Saranus (not Seranus) appears, and doubts whether this family's cognomen actually derived from serendo — suggesting instead a different origin. He quotes Virgil (Aen. VI, 'et te sulco Serane serentem') and notes Saranus also appears in Obsequens's book of prodigies. He identifies two possible moneyers: M. Atilii Serani triumviri coloniae deducendae (anno DLXVIII) and C. Atilius, consul with Q. Servilius Caepio (anno DCXLVII). He explicitly states it is DIFFICULT to affirm which specific member the denarii designate ('difficile est, qui praecipue his denariis designentur, affirmare'). He does NOT invoke M. Atilius Regulus of the First Punic War.

coins_engraved.reverse: Horseman in biga right; M.AVRELI / ROMA below

completed.family_note: The Aurelii were a plebeian gens with the Cottae and Scauri as their principal families. M. Aurelius Cotta (Crawford 229/1a, 139 BC) struck denarii with the Roma/horseman type bearing the cognomen COTT. L. Aurelius Cotta (Crawford 314/1b, 105 BC) produced the distinctive Vulcan/eagle type, featuring a draped bust of Vulcan wearing a pileus with tongs behind, and an eagle on thunderbolt within a laurel wreath on the reverse. M. Aurelius Scaurus (Crawford 282/1, 118 BC) struck a denarius serratus at Narbo (Roma / Gallic warrior in biga, M·AVRELI) as part of the Narbo colonial joint issue. The gens produced numerous consuls throughout the Republic.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini identifies the Cottae and Scauri as the main Aurelian families. For the first coin he identifies M. AVRELIVM COTTAM, consul with L. Licinius Lucullus in anno DCLXXIX, and brother of C. Aurelius praised by Cicero in the Brutus as 'disertus.' For the L. Cotta Vulcan coin, he argues the bearded, pileus-wearing bust represents Vulcan, citing Virgil ('Nam certè Vulcanus opus faciebat, & illi / Tristi, turpabatq. mala fuligine barbam') and Arnobius (lib. VI: 'cum pileo Vulcanus & malleo'). He does not describe the eagle reverse as connected to an augural tradition; the eagle is not discussed in his text. For the third (Scaurus) coin he identifies M. AVRELIVS SCAVRVS as perhaps the consul suffectus in anno DCXLV, father of L. Hortensius the orator.

coins_engraved.reverse: Diana in biga of stags right, holding spear; L.AXSIVS.L.F below, NASO in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini admits to great difficulty with this family, writing in tanta praesertim huius familiae ignoratione (given such ignorance about this family). He discusses the archaic spelling AXSIVS and its possible connection to MAXIMVS. For the Diana/stag reverse, he cites Apollonius Rhodius (book III) and Callimachus on the stag-drawn chariot.

completed.family_note: The Axsii were a rare plebeian gens known almost exclusively from numismatic evidence. L. Axsius L.f. Naso (Crawford 400/1, 71 BC) struck denarii with a helmeted head of Mars on the obverse and Diana driving a biga of stags on the reverse, with the legends L.AXSIVS.L.F and NASO in the exergue. The archaic spelling AXSIVS preserves the older Latin form. The gens is virtually unattested in literary sources, and no members are known to have held major magistracies.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini admits to great difficulty with this family, writing in tanta praesertim huius familiae ignoratione (given such ignorance about this family). He discusses the archaic spelling AXSIVS and its possible connection to MAXIMVS. For the reverse type, he cites Apollonius Rhodius (book III) and Callimachus on Diana's stag-drawn chariot. Despite his admitted ignorance, he provides characteristically learned mythological parallels for the coin types, even when the prosopographic evidence is essentially nil.

completed.family_note: The Baebii were a plebeian gens active from the third century BC. M. Baebius Q.f. Tampilus (Crawford 236/1, 137 BC) struck denarii with a helmeted head of Roma left on the obverse and Jupiter in a quadriga right on the reverse. Historically, M. Baebius Tampilus held the consulship in 181 BC and celebrated a triumph over the Ligurians. The coin legend reads TAMPIL without aspiration, contrasting with the form Tamphilus found in the Capitoline Fasti.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini identifies M. Baebius Tampilus as consul in 181 BC with P. Cornelius Cethegus, noting his triumph over the Ligurians. He discusses the spelling TAMPIL on the coin versus Tamphilus in the Capitoline tablets, observing the absence of aspiration in the coin legend. The annotation on the second entry is a later owner's note discussing the Tampilus cognomen variants. His treatment is brief, limited to a single engraved denarius with one later annotation.

completed.family_note: The Caecilii Metelli were one of Rome's most powerful plebeian families, ennobled through military success and prolific magistracies. Their coinage spans over a century: M. Caecilius Q.f. Q.n. Metellus (Crawford 263/1, 127 BC) struck the Macedonian shield denarius; C. Caecilius Metellus Caprarius (Crawford 269/1, 125 BC) produced Jupiter quadriga types; Q. Caecilius Metellus Pius (Crawford 374, 81 BC) struck the famous Diana/elephant denarii and Pietas/priestly implement types; and Q. Metellus Scipio (Crawford 459-461, 47-46 BC) issued coins during the African campaign against Caesar. The gens produced more consuls than almost any other plebeian family, including Macedonicus, Numidicus, and Pius among their most distinguished members.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Caecilia gens at length across two plates. He identifies the four sons of Q. Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus as Marcus, Caius (Caprarius), Quintus (Balearicus), and Lucius (Diadematus/Delmaticus). He attributes the first two denarii to Marcus, consul with M. Aemilius Scaurus (anno DCXVIII) who triumphed from Sardinia (anno DCXL); the third to Caius Caprarius, consul with Cn. Papirius Carbo (anno DCXL); the fifth to Quintus Balearicus, consul with T. Quintius Flamininus (anno DCXXX). He explains that the elephants on the first four denarii celebrate L. Metellus (cos. anno DII), who first led elephants in his Sicilian triumph (citing Pliny VIII.XLIII). Lucius Delmaticus, the fourth son, is placed on the second plate. For the Scipio coins, Orsini devotes extensive discussion to Q. Caecilius Metellus Pius Scipio (identified from Caesar's Bellum Civile III as imperator in Africa), the Isis/Genius Terrae Africae iconography, and the priestly implements (lituus, praefericulum). He also identifies P. Crassus Iunianus as Scipio's legate proquaestor on the joint coins. He does NOT specifically discuss Crawford 335/1 (the L. Metellus/A. Albinus/C. Malleolus joint issue) in the surviving text visible on these pages.

completed.family_note: The Caecinae were an Etruscan family from Volaterrae (modern Volterra). A. Caecina, a Roman knight and correspondent of Cicero (Fam. VI), is the most prominent Republican member. The family later produced consuls suffecti under Augustus. The single bronze coin attributed to the gens shows a bare head of Augustus on the obverse with A.CAECINA and a platform or tribunal scene on the reverse, placing it firmly in the Augustan period.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini opens by posing the question whether the bronze coin belongs to A. Caecina the Roman knight from Volaterrae (Cicero's correspondent in Fam. VI, who fought for Pompey against Caesar) or to his son, who he believes was consul suffectus under Augustus in the XIII consulship (anno DCCLI, with M. Plautius Silvanus as colleague). He draws on Hirtius's Bellum Africum for Caecina patris and Velleius (lib. II) for the son as 'consularis.' He argues from two grounds that the consul suffectus was in anno DCCLI. He does not give the year as '2 BC'; he expresses it as anno DCCLI = the XIII consulship of Augustus.

completed.family_note: The Caesii were a minor gens of uncertain social status. L. Caesius (Crawford 298/1, 112-111 BC) struck denarii with a distinctive youthful bust of Apollo (or Veiovis) on the obverse with flowing hair and sceptre, and two seated Lares Praestites with a dog between them on the reverse, with ROMA below and L.CAESI around. completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini notes that the status (patrician or plebeian) of the Caesii is uncertain. He identifies L. Caesius from Cicero's letter to his brother Quintus (ad Q. Fratrem, ep. II, lib. I). He discusses the obverse bust as Veiovis, citing Gellius (Agellius lib. V cap. XII), who says Veiovis holds arrows and stands between the arx and the Capitolium, associated with Apollo. For the reverse, Orsini says the Lares depicted have Vulcan's head superimposed ('Vulcani caput superpositum est') because Lares are worshipped at the hearth (in foco), and cites Plutarch's Problemata on why a dog attends the Lares. He notes that his final opinion is that L. Caesius struck this coin to honour both Lares and Vulcan (connecting the coin to an Augustan-era inscription), but this is his conclusion from the coin as a whole — not a claim that the legend LARIVS itself 'connects to Vulcan.'
