completed.family_note: The Calpurnii were a distinguished plebeian gens claiming descent from Numa Pompilius, with the Pisones and Bibuli as their principal branches. L. Calpurnius Piso Frugi (Crawford 340/1, 90 BC) produced the most prolific Republican denarius series, with the laureate head of Apollo and a desultor (horseman) on the reverse, in an extraordinary number of die variants. C. Calpurnius Piso L.f. Frugi (Crawford 408/1, 67 BC) continued the Apollo/horseman type. The Augustan period saw bronzes by Cn. Calpurnius Piso and L. Calpurnius Bibulus as IIIviri monetales, with Augustus portrait obverses and S C reverses. The gens also includes the grain-purchase type with Numa Pompilius (Crawford 330, attributed to Calpurnius Piso and Caepio). The family produced numerous consuls and provincial governors throughout the Republic.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Calpurnii at great length across three pages, covering the Pisonum and Bibulorum families. He identifies L. Calpurnius Piso Frugi as consul in 620 AUC and interprets the horseman (desultorius eques) on the reverse as relating to the Ludi Apollinares. The Terminus head on the obverse is connected to Numa Pompilius's cult, and the sacrificial instruments (simpulum, patera, culter) also reference Numa. For C. Calpurnius Piso L.f. Frugi, he notes the many die variants. The Augustan bronzes of Cn. Calpurnius Piso and L. Calpurnius Bibulus receive separate discussion, with Orsini noting the IIIvir monetalis title and the A.A.A.F.F. inscription. He conflates some Bibulus and Piso attributions in his treatment of the later coins.

He does not describe it as a tribunal or altar.

completed.family_note: The Caninii were a plebeian gens with four known branches: Rebili, Reguli, Galli, and Labones. L. Caninius Gallus served as consul in 37 BC and later as IIIvir monetalis under Augustus, striking bronzes with Augustus's portrait and altar/tribunal reverses. Orsini himself dates the consulship 'cum M. Agrippa anno DCCVI' (p. 49); the numeral reads clearly DCCVI in the print, an AUC figure that does not align with the standard Varronian 716/717 for 37 BC — indicating either a variant AUC base or a printing error in the 1577 text. The two coins in Orsini's plates are both Augustan issues, making this a gens represented only in the imperial period numismatically, though its members were politically active in the late Republic.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini enumerates four known families within the Caninia gens: Rebili (from Livy lib. XLII), Reguli (from Caesar lib. VII de bello Gallico), Galli (known from the coins on this plate), and Labones (who were enrolled in the Arniensian tribe, known from an inscription). He identifies L. Caninius Gallus as IIIvir under Augustus and discusses the kneeling figure with Parthian standards on the first coin reverse as 'signa pertinent de Parthis ab Augusto recuperata.' For the second coin he reads the reverse as a tabernaculum (military tent), designating the assault on a town under Augustus: 'oppidi alicuius oppugnatione sub eodem Augusto designat.'

completed.family_note: The Carisii are known primarily from two members. T. Carisius (Crawford 464, 46 BC) struck a diverse series of Republican denarii at Rome featuring Juno Moneta, a sphinx, Roma with anvil/tongs/hammer (minting implements), and Diana with a running hound. P. Carisius served as Augustus's legatus pro praetore in Lusitania (c. 25-23 BC), founding the colony of Augusta Emerita (modern Merida) and striking an extensive provincial series with Augustus portrait obverses and reverses showing the city gateway, crossed weapons, standing Victory, and military implements, commemorating the victory over the Cantabri and Astures.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini notes that no ancient writers mention the gens except Dio (lib. LIII and LIV) on T. Carisius. He discusses the coin types systematically: the first denarius shows Victoria, recording T. Carisius's Cantabrian victory; the second shows monetalibus instrumentis (anvil, hammer, tongs) for his minting office; the third shows the Sphinx, which Orsini connects to Augustus's own signet seal (citing Suetonius lib. II cap. V: 'initio Sphinge vsus est'), explaining that Carisius struck it in Augustus's honour; the fourth he interprets as indicating the 'imperium orbis terrarum Augusto delatum'; the sixth he connects to the Ludi Saeculares of Apollo and Diana. For P. Carisius in Lusitania, he discusses the magistrate titles and connects the colonial foundation of Emerita Augusta to Dio's account.

completed.family_note: The Cassii were a prominent gens with both patrician and plebeian branches. Q. Cassius Longinus (Crawford 428, 55 BC) struck denarii with Vesta and the temple of Vesta, referencing the lex Cassia tabellaria. C. Cassius Longinus (Crawford 266/1, 126 BC) produced earlier Roma/horseman types. The tyrannicide C. Cassius Longinus issued joint denarii with Brutus and Lentulus Spinther (Crawford 500-507, 43-42 BC) featuring Libertas and priestly implements. C. Cassius Celer served as IIIvir monetalis under Augustus, striking bronzes with S C types. The gens is one of the most extensively represented in Republican numismatics, with seventeen coins spanning from the mid-second century BC to the Augustan period.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini organises the Cassii into two families: patrician Bcellinorum and plebeian Longorum and Longinorum. He connects the ballot-law types (Libertas/voting urn) to L. Cassius Longinus's lex tabellaria on judicial voting, citing Cicero de legibus III, and discusses the voting tablets marked A (Absolvo), C (Condemno), and NL (Non Liquet). For Q. Cassius Longinus (Crawford 428), he notes the Vesta and temple types. He identifies the tyrannicide C. Cassius Longinus on the joint issues with Brutus and Lentulus Spinther (Crawford 500-507), connecting them to Cassius's fleet command against Dolabella and the joint command before Philippi. The Augustan bronzes of C. Cassius Celer as IIIvir monetalis complete his treatment.

completed.family_note: The Cestii were a plebeian gens. L. Cestius and C. Norbanus (Crawford 491/1, 43 BC) struck joint denarii as praetors, with a veiled bust wearing an elephant-skin headdress (representing Africa) on the obverse and a curule chair flanked by fasces on the reverse. L. Cestius is attested in Cicero's orations and in Appian's account of the civil wars. An inscription records a C. Cestius as L.F. POB. EPVLO PR. TR. PL. The gens is otherwise of limited prominence in Republican prosopography.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini identifies L. Cestius from Cicero (pro L. Flacco, Philippicae III) and Appian (Bella Civilia IV). He reads an inscription giving C. Cestius as L.F. POB. EPVLO PR. TR. PL. and discusses the curule chair on the reverse as indicating praetorship, citing Varro for the significance of the sella curulis. He connects the elephant-skin headdress on the obverse to Africa and Metellus Scipio. The two annotations record later scholarly cross-references to the Reimann catalogue and other numismatic works.

completed.family_note: The Cipii (or Cispii) were a minor plebeian gens. M. Cipius M.f. (Crawford 289/1, 115-114 BC) struck denarii with a helmeted head of Roma right on the obverse with X behind, and Victory driving a biga right on the reverse, with M.CIPI.M.F below and ROMA in exergue. The gens is virtually absent from literary sources. The spelling Cipius may represent the same family as Cispius without the S, though this identification is not universally accepted.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini notes that no ancient writers mention the gens Cipia ("Cipiae gentis nullus (quod sciam) ueterum scriptorum facit mentionem"). He believes Cipia is the same as Cispia without the S, citing the antiquo scribendi mos in inscriptions. He argues from Cicero's oratione pro P. Sextio and the oratione post reditum in senatu that M. Cipium = M. Cispius, and notes that a manuscript reading of Mospius was corrected to M. Cispius by Manutio ("emendatur a Manutio M. Cifpius"), not by Orsini himself. He concludes the gens was plebeian.

completed.family_note: The Claudii were one of Rome's oldest and most powerful patrician gentes, with the Pulchri, Marcelli, and Nerones as their principal branches. The coinage spans twelve coins across two pages: P. Cornelius Lentulus Marcellinus (Crawford 439, 50 BC) struck types honoring the great M. Claudius Marcellus with Apollo/Diana Lucifera in a temple; Ap. Claudius Pulcher, T. Manlius Mancinus, and Q. Urbinius (Crawford 299/1, 111 BC) produced Victory-in-triga types; Ti. Claudius Nero (Crawford 383/1, 79 BC) struck Jupiter quadriga denarii; C. Claudius Pulcher (Crawford 300/1, 110-109 BC) produced Roma/Victory biga types; and P. Clodius M.f. (Crawford 494/23-25, 42 BC) struck Apollo/crescent-stars types. An Augustan bronze by Regulus Pulcher completes the series.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini organises the Claudii into two families: patrician Pulchri and plebeian Marcellorum. He celebrates M. Claudius Marcellus, five-times consul, who took the spolia opima from the Gallic chieftain Virdumarus at Clastidium and dedicated them to Jupiter Feretrius. He attributes the Marcellinus coin to Cn. Lentulus Marcellinus ("sine dubio a Cn. Lentvlo Marcellino cusus est") and discusses the Sicilian symbol ("tria crura") on the reverse as referring to Marcellus's Sicilian connections. For coins 4 and 5 of the second plate he refers them to C. Claudivм C.F. Pvlchrvm (cos. DCXXIII). For the fifth coin of the first plate he identifies the Quaestor Vrbanus from the legend but cannot name him, noting it may pertain to Ap. Claudius Pulcher or his father. Ti. Claudius Nero's denarius (coin 6 of plate 1) is connected to Cn. Pompey's Mithridatic war. For P. Clodius M.F. (coins on plate 2), Orsini explicitly states he CANNOT determine the meaning of Sol, Luna, or Mars imagery ("nec Solis mihi, nec Lunae, Martisq. simulacra... diuinare licet"), and explains Diana by citing Callimachus and Sophocles on her twin torches. He cites Hirtius lib. VIII de bello Gallico on L. Lentulus and C. Marcellus.

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head of Caesar right; CAESAR DICT·TER around
coins_engraved.reverse: Standing Victory left; C·LOVIVS PRAEF around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies C. Cluvius as praefectus urbis under Caesar, citing Dio lib. XLIII (no chapter specified). He notes the gens's origins in Puteoli from Cicero's epistle to Thermum and in oratione pro Q. Roscio calls a Cluvius equitem Romanum ornatissimum.

completed.family_note: The Clovii (Cluvii, Clivii) were a minor gens originally from Puteoli in Campania. C. Cluvius served as praefectus urbis under Caesar, as recorded by Dio Cassius (XLIII.48). Cicero mentions a Cluvius as a distinguished Roman knight. The single bronze coin attributed to the gens shows a helmeted head of Minerva on the obverse with standing Victory on the reverse, dated to the Caesarian period (c. 45-44 BC).
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats Clovia, Cluvia, and Clvia as variant spellings of the same gens, noting all appear in ancient monuments ("utroque enim modo in antiquis monumentis scripta reperitur"). He identifies C. Cluvius as praefectus urbis under Caesar, citing Dio lib. XLIII (no chapter number given). He notes the family's origins in Puteoli inferred from Cicero's epistola to Thermum (lib. XIII, ep. LVI). In oratione pro Q. Roscio he describes a Cluvius as equitem Romanum ornatissimum.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory in biga right; T.CLOVL / ROMA below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini equates the Clovlia gens with the patrician Cloelia and cites Livy on the lex Canuleia and Dionysius lib. III on the family's Alban origin. He discusses T. Cloelius's connection to a Siculi cognomen and connects the spica symbol on the coin to possible Sicilian or frumentarian associations ("spica eius insulae peculiari symbolo T. Cloelium; qui denarium cudit, indicare uoluisse, credi potest"). He does NOT reference Dio or C. Cluvius as consul in 723 AUC — those belong to the Clovia section.

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head right; F behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Standing figure (Victory) crowning trophy; T.CLOVLI around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses only a single moneyer, T. Cloelius, in the Clovlia section and does not distinguish multiple coin types. He focusses on the question of which Cloelius struck the coin (the Tribunus militum consulari potestate of anno CCCIX who led the Ardea colony, or another Cloelius), and on the spica symbol as a possible indicator of Sicilian or frumentarian associations ('spica eius insulae peculiari symbolo T. Cloelium; qui denarium cudit, indicare uoluisse, credi potest'). He provides no description that would allow identification of a second distinct type. The Crawford number for this coin cannot be confirmed from Orsini's text.

completed.family_note: The Cloelii (also spelled Cloullii or Clovlii) were a patrician gens of legendary antiquity, famous for the heroine Cloelia who escaped Etruscan captivity by swimming the Tiber. T. Cloelius (Crawford 260/1, 128 BC) struck denarii with a helmeted head of Roma with quiver behind on the obverse and Victory driving a biga right on the reverse, with T.CLOVL below and ROMA in exergue. A second type shows Apollo/Victory with trophy. The gens is attested from the earliest period of Roman history but had limited political prominence in the later Republic.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini equates the Clovlia gens with the patrician Cloelia ("eadem enim est"), noting spelling variations. He references Livy on the lex Canuleia permitting plebeian consuls as evidence of the gens's patrician status, and Dionysius lib. III on the Cloelian family's origin from Alba. He cites Cicero (Philippics lib. IX) and Livy lib. IV and Pliny lib. III on Tullus Cluuium, Roscius, Nautius, and Fulcinius as Veientum legates, and discusses whether T. Cloelius should be read in Cicero's text. He does NOT cite Dio on a consul suffectus in 723 AUC with C. Furnius in this section — that reference belongs to the Clovia gens.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right (Mark Antony); M.ANT.IMP.III.VIR.R.P.C.M.NERVA.PROQ.P around
coins_engraved.reverse: Bare head right (Antony); ANTONIVS.COS around
coins_engraved.identification: Crawford 517/5a — M. Cocceius Nerva (proquaestor pro praetore under Mark Antony), AR denarius, 41 BC
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the coin's portrait as M. Cocceius Nerva, consul with L. Gellius Poplicola in 717 AUC (37 BC by his reckoning), and cites Appian (Bella Civilia V) on his mediation between Antony and Octavian at Brundisium, and Horace (Satires I.5). Separately, Orsini speculates the coin was actually struck by L. Cocceius (M. Nerva's brother) as Antony's legatus pro praetore ("Antonii Legatus Pro Praetore... denarium cufit"). He does not conflate the Republican figure with the Emperor Nerva.

completed.family_note: The Cocceii were a gens of uncertain status (patrician or plebeian: "non satis constat patricia ne fuerit an plebeia"). From them descended Emperor Nerva, who succeeded Domitian. The coin Orsini illustrates is a Republican silver denarius showing two facing portraits; Orsini identifies the figure as M. Cocceius Nerva, who he states was Consul with L. Gellius Poplicola in 717 AUC ("anno DCCXVII" = 37 BC by Orsini's reckoning). On the continuation page Orsini speculates that L. Cocceius (brother of M. Nerva) was Antony's legatus pro praetore who struck the denarius. He cites Appian (Bella Civilia V) on the mediation at Brundisium and Horace (Satires I.5) for the journey to Brundisium. The coin is NOT an imperial portrait issue of Emperor Nerva.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini states the Cocceii are of uncertain status ("non satis constat patricia ne fuerit an plebeia"). He identifies the coin's figure as M. Cocceius Nerva, consul with L. Gellius Poplicola in 717 AUC (37 BC by his reckoning). He cites Appian (Bella Civilia V) at length on M. Cocceius Nerva's role as peacemaker between Antony and Octavian, and Horace (Satires I.5) for the journey to Brundisium. He then cites Pomponius Porphyrio's commentary. On the continuation (p. 66) he speculates that L. Cocceius (M. Nerva's brother) was the actual striker of the denarius as Antony's legatus pro praetore. He does NOT conflate the Republican Nerva with Emperor Nerva — he simply notes Emperor Nerva descended from this gens.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right; C·COEL·CALDVS / COS around

He identifies the two bare heads as the consul and a family member and discusses the L.D. inscription as libero/damno (absolvo/condemno), relating it to the lex Cassia tabellaria.

He connects the joint naming to the Republican practice of honouring consular ancestors on moneyers' coins and reads the reverse in connection with the family's voting-law associations.

He does NOT connect this early type to the Epulonum imagery — that interpretation (Jupiter on a couch) applies specifically to the fifth coin (IMP.A.X type) in relation to L. Coelius Caldus's Septemuirum Epulonum membership.

coins_engraved.observed_obverse: Helmeted head right, female head (Roma) wearing a crested helmet, facing right. Similar to Coelia_4. Catalog says 'helmeted head of Roma right' — confirmed, direction RIGHT.

Legend L·COIL visible above and ROMA in the exergue below. Catalog says 'horseman galloping right; L.COIL / ROMA below' — confirmed. This differs from Coelia_4 which has a biga; this is a single horseman.

completed.family_note: The Coelii were a plebeian gens, with C. Coelius Caldus as their most notable member, rising from humble origins to become consul in 94 BC as a novus homo. C. Coelius Caldus (Crawford 318/1, 104 BC) struck denarii with Roma/warrior biga types bearing the C.COIL CALD legend. His grandson struck a later series (Crawford 437, 51 BC) as IIIvir monetalis with ancestral portraits and military trophy reverses. L. Coelius Caldus served as Septemvir Epulonum, one of the major priestly colleges. The five coins span the family across two generations of moneyers.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini identifies the Coelii as a plebeian gens. He discusses C. Coelius Caldus as consul in 659 AUC ("Consul fuit cum L. Domitio Ahenobarbo anno DCLIX") and the ballot tablet in the perduellionis iudicio with notae L.D. = libero & damno, relating it to the lex Cassia tabellaria. He believes this consul's son was L. Coelius Caldus (IIIvir monetalis), who struck coins in honour of his father and grandfather ("in patris, aniique memoriam"). L. Coelius Caldus's membership of the Septemuiri Epulonum is attested both from the denarius inscription and from the signum of Jupiter reclining on a couch ("Iouis signo in lectulo discumbentis") — Orsini says "lectulo," not "lectisternium." For a coin reading IMP. A. X., Orsini says he finds no ancient source ("non memini me apud scriptores quicquam legisse") and speculates the bearer was a brother of L. Caldus IIIviri Epulonum.

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head of Apollo right; A behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Curule chair (sella curulis); C·CONSIDI above, PAETI below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini classifies the Considii as plebeian, citing Liuius lib. II and Dionyfius lib. IX. He does NOT definitively identify C. Considius Paetus as quaestor — he says the coins suggest he was "Praetorem uel Aedilem" (praetor or aedile), and identifies the curule chair with quaestors for capital cases without assigning that role to Paetus himself.

coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Curule chair between two crossed fasces; C.CONSIDI / PAETI below

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory in galloping quadriga right, holding the reins; C·CONSIDI in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this Venus Erycina type as struck by C. Considius Nonianus and documents the temple from Liuius lib. XXX and XL, Ovid Fasti III, and Strabo lib. VI. He connects Nonianus to Gallia citerior (from Cicero ep. XI ad Tironem: "citeriorem Confidio Noniano"), NOT to an African command. The Africa passage in Orsini refers to C. Considius the proconsul (the Ligarius oration), not to Nonianus.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Laureate head of Venus right
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Victory flying right, carrying wreath and palm; C.CONSIDI below

He carefully distinguishes Paetus's multiple curule-chair types from the Nonianus Venus Erycina issue, treating the five denarii systematically as evidence of two separate moneyers within the same magistracy year.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Laureate head left; PAETI behind

completed.family_note: The Considii were a plebeian gens attested from the early Republic. C. Considius Paetus (Crawford 465/1-4, 46 BC) struck four denarius types with varied obverses (Apollo, Victory, Venus) and reverses (curule chair with cornucopiae, flying Victory). C. Considius Nonianus (Crawford 424/1, 57 BC) produced the distinctive denarius showing a laureate head of Venus Erycina on the obverse and a tetrastyle temple on a rocky outcrop on the reverse, representing the famous temple of Venus on Mt. Eryx in Sicily. The gens is attested in Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus from the early Republic.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini cites Liuius lib. II, Dionyfius lib. IX, Caesar lib. II de bello ciuili, Cicero lib. XII ep. XXVI ad Cornuficium, and Valerius Maximus lib. IV cap. VIII. He identifies two moneyers: C. Considius Paetus and C. Considius Nonianus. For Paetus, Orsini says he finds no ancient literary source but infers from the coins that he was "Praetorem uel Aedilem" ("cum tamen eum Praetorem uel Aedilem fuisse... coniiicere possumus") — NOT definitively a quaestor. He identifies the curule chair on the reverse as characteristic of Quaestores for capital cases, but infers Paetus's magistracy separately as praetor or aedile. He connects Nonianus to Cicero's letter ad Tironem (ep. XI), where Gallia citerior is assigned to Considio Noniano — not to an African command. The Africa reference in the text comes from the Ligarius oration about C. Considio (the proconsul), not about Nonianus. The temple of Venus Erycina on Nonianus's coin is documented by Liuius lib. XXX and XL, Ovid Fasti III, and Strabo lib. VI.

completed.family_note: The Coponii were a gens originally from Tibur, later admitted to Roman citizenship. C. Coponius served as praetor in 49 BC and commanded a fleet for Pompey during the Civil War. His denarius (Crawford 444/1, 49 BC), a joint issue with Q. Sicinius, shows a diademed bust of Diana on the obverse and a club within wreath with lion skin on the reverse, with the legend PR.S.C (Praetor Senatus Consulto) indicating his magistracy and senatorial authorisation.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini notes the gens's origin from Tibur and its admission to Roman citizenship (plebeian status uncertain). He identifies T. Coponius as the first of the gens to become a Roman citizen ("primus ex ea gente ciuis Romanus factus est"), not the first to hold a Roman magistracy. He discusses C. Coponius as praetor commanding the Rhodian fleet at Dyrrachium, citing Caesar lib. III de bello ciuili (noting that the praenomen Quintus in vulgate texts is an error for Caius), Cicero de Diuinatione lib. I, Velleius lib. II, and Appian in Parthico. He reads PR.S.C as Praetor Senatus Consulto and identifies the club and lion skin on the reverse as Herculean attributes tied to Tibur's Hercules temple ("erat enim Tiburi templum Herculis").

completed.family_note: The Cordii were a minor gens known primarily from numismatic evidence. Mn. Cordius Rufus (Crawford 463, 46 BC) struck three distinctive denarius types: jugate heads of the Dioscuri with Venus Verticordia holding scales on the reverse; a helmeted head of Minerva (or Mars) with Cupid riding a dolphin; and a Corinthian helmet with owl above and an aegis pattern on the reverse. The Venus and Cupid imagery may honour Caesar's Julian claim to descent from Venus. Cicero mentions an L. Cordius (in Verrem IV), but the gens is otherwise poorly attested in literary sources.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini notes the gens is known only from Cicero (book IV in Verrem) on L. Cordius. He suggests the Venus Verticordia with Cupid on the first type was struck in Caesaris gratiam, connecting the imagery to Caesar's Julian lineage claiming descent from Venus. For the Cupid on dolphin type, he admits difficulty explaining the connection (Amor on dolphin relates to Venus's maritime origins). The Corinthian helmet with owl on the third type is identified as Minerva's aegis and noctua (owl). He candidly acknowledges that some types remain unexplained by historical sources.

completed.family_note: The Cornelii were the most prolific of all Roman patrician gentes, with the Blasiones, Lentuli, Scipiones, Cinnae, Sisennae, and Sullae among their principal branches. The coinage is the most extensive in the B-C section with 33 coins across six pages. Cn. Cornelius Blasio (Crawford 296/1, 112-111 BC) struck the Jupiter/Capitoline triad type. The Lentuli produced multiple moneyers including Cn. Cornelius Lentulus (Crawford 345/1, 88 BC; Crawford 393/1, 76-75 BC) with Genius of the Roman People types, and P. Cornelius Lentulus Marcellinus (Crawford 439/1, 50 BC). L. Cornelius Sulla's extensive military coinage includes the triumph quadriga type jointly with L. Manlius Torquatus (Crawford 367/3, 82 BC) and various imperator issues. Faustus Cornelius Sulla (Crawford 426, 56 BC) struck types honouring both his father Sulla and Q. Pompeius Rufus. The Lentulus Spinther joint issues with Cassius and Brutus (Crawford 500, 43-42 BC) were struck during the civil wars. A Cornelius Cinna bronze prow type is also included.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini devotes six pages to the Cornelii, the longest treatment of any gens in the B-C section, covering the patrician branches of Blasiones, Lentuli, Scipiones, Cinnae, Sisennae, and Sullae. He identifies Cn. Cornelius Blasio as consul in anno CDXCVI AUC (with C. Atilio Regulo) and discusses the plate's first coin. For the Lentulus coins (second and third), he notes they must belong to some member of the Lentulorum family with the Cn. praenomen, who served as Quaestor and overseer of coin-striking before the institution of the IIIviri monetales; and he identifies the most plausible candidate as Cn. Lentulus, consul cum L. Mummio anno DCVII. For the Sulla types, the second coin designates Sulla Dictator's triumph de rege Mithridate (citing Cicero pro lege Manilia and Plutarch); the third coin he connects to the Sullae cognomen, which the family is said to have derived from the Sibylla (Sibylla ipsa impressa), and whose libri Sulla administered as one of the XVviri sacris faciundis. The fourth coin he reads as a monument struck by Faustus for his father, with four crowns on the reverse indicating quatuor Sullae triumphos ex Graecia, Asia, Ponto, et rege Mithridate (citing Plutarch and Dio XLII). The Spinther/Cassius/Brutus joint issues are connected to Spinther's pontificate (Caesar, de bello civili I) and auguratus (Dio XXXIX), and the cognomen Spinther is noted as derived from an actor to whom Lentulus bore resemblance (Valerius Max. and Pliny). The Flamen Martialis coins (coins 5–6 of the Spinther plate) are attributed to L. Cornelius P.F. Flamen Martialis, consul anno DCCIII with C. Marcellus. Cossus Cornelius Cn.f. Lentulus (first two coins of the final plate) is identified as consul cum L. Calpurnio Pisone anno DCCII, having received triumphal honours from the Isaurians in Cilicia. L. Cornelius Balbus is discussed as suffect consul cum P. Canidio Crasso anno DCCXIII, a Gaditanus whose city had a temple of Hercules (whence the deity on the reverse). The final bronze is attributed to P. Cornelius Blasio, praetor anno DLIX.

completed.family_note: The Cornuficii were a plebeian gens. Q. Cornuficius served as augur and as governor of Africa province, where he was acclaimed Imperator and struck coins: Jupiter Ammon (referencing Africa, where the god was worshipped) on the obverse of one coin, Ceres on the other ob provinciae fertilitatem. The Juno Sospita type with goatskin headdress, spear, and shield is not directly attributed to Cornuficius's coins by Orsini; it is discussed as appearing in the Augurem-crowning imagery on these denarii and noted to be discussed later under the Procilia gens. Q. Cornuficius was also Cicero's competitor in Consulatu and colleague in Auguratu. His brother may have been L. Cornuficius L.F., who was consul cum Sex. Pompeio Sex. filio anno DCCVIII.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini identifies Q. Cornuficius as augur and Cicero's competitor in Consulatu and colleague in Auguratu (citing Cicero's letters, books XVII, XVIII, XX, XXII). He interprets the head of Jupiter Ammon on the first coin as representing Africa (the province where Cornuficius served as imperator, citing Livy epitome XXIII, Dio XLVIII, and Appian). He reads Ceres on the second coin's reverse as representing Africa's fertility (ob provinciae fertilitatem). For the Juno Sospita figure with goatskin, Orsini does NOT connect it to Lanuvian origins as a firm identification; he explicitly states he could find no explanation ('nondum quicquam reperire potui') and offers the Lanuvium conjecture only tentatively ('nisi forte … velimus'). He notes this type will be discussed further under the Procilia gens.

completed.family_note: The Cosconii were a gens of uncertain social status (Orsini: 'incertum est, patricia ne, an plebeia fuerit'). L. Cosconius M.f. struck a denarius with a helmeted head on the obverse and a warrior driving a biga on the reverse with L.IC.CN.DON (as visible on the plate). Livy (book XXX) records M. Cosconius as tribune of soldiers, who may have been the father of L. Cosconius M.F. Cicero (pro Sulla) mentions C. Cosconius as praetor in the year of Caesar and Bibulus as consuls. Orsini cites no Narbo mint attribution; the Narbo connection is a modern numismatic identification not found in Orsini.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini is uncertain whether the Cosconii were patrician or plebeian. He identifies L. Cosconius M.F. from the denarius legend and cites Livius (book XXX) for M. Cosconius as tribune of soldiers, making L. Cosconius his son. He also references Cicero's oration pro Sulla for C. Cosconius as praetor. He additionally cites Appianus (Bellum civile I) for C. Cosconius being invited to take the place of a praetor who had died; Valerius Maximus (lib. III.cap.I) for a C. Cosconius Calidianus mentioned by Cicero in Brutus; and Livy epitome LXXVI for a Cosconius who defeated the Samnites. Orsini does NOT mention a Narbo mint or the serrated fabric of the coin. His note about the serrate (serrated-edge) denarius 'from Narbo' in the concordance is an unattested addition.

completed.family_note: The Cossutii were an equestrian family, notable primarily because Caesar's first wife Cossutia came from this gens (Suetonius, Caesar 1). C. Cossutius Maridianus (Crawford 480/19, 44 BC) served as IIIvir monetalis A.A.A.F.F. (Aere Argento Auro Flando Feriundo), striking denarii with Caesar's laureate portrait and seated Roma or Minerva on the reverse. L. Cossutius Sabula struck types with Cybele wearing a turreted crown (SABVLA legend) and Medusa/Bellerophon on Pegasus imagery. Three coins represent the gens in Orsini's plates.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini identifies the Cossutii as an equestrian gens and connects them to Caesar's first wife Cossutia, citing Suetonius (Caesar cap. I). He notes that C. Cossutius struck two silver denarii after Caesar gained power ('Caesare iam rerum potito, argenteos duos denarios signauit'), and that C. Cossutius's son may be L. Cossutius Sabula (third coin, C.F.). For L. Cossutius Sabula he notes no ancient writers mention him ('de quo nihil extat apud scriptores') and conjectures that the Medusa and Bellerophon on Pegasus may pertain to the Corinth colony founded by Caesar, to be discussed under the Petronia gens. Orsini does NOT expand or discuss the A.A.F.F. inscription anywhere in his Cossutia commentary.

completed.family_note: The Crepereii were an equestrian gens. Q. Crepereius M.f. struck denarii (c. 72 BC) with a helmeted head of Roma right and cornucopia behind on the obverse, and Dioscuri riding right with lances on the reverse and ROMA below. A second type by C. Creperius also features the Roma/Dioscuri scheme. Cicero (in Verrem I) mentions M. Crepereius as an eques, likely the moneyer's father. Tacitus (Annales XIV) records a Crepereius Gallus active under Nero, showing the family's continued presence in later periods.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini cites Cicero (book I in Verrem) for M. Crepereius from an equestrian family, identifying him as the likely father of the moneyer Q. Crepereius M.F. known from the denarius. He then mentions Crepereius Gallus under Nero cited by Tacitus in book XIII (not XIV). From the coin imagery (the plate shows a horseman or maritime-themed reverse), Orsini infers that some member of the Crepereii may have performed a successful maritime enterprise ('re mari prospere aliqñ gessisse'). He does not name a Neptune figure on the reverse; the inference of maritime activity is drawn from the imagery without identifying a specific deity.

completed.family_note: The Crepusii were a minor plebeian gens unattested in ancient literary sources. P. Crepusius (Crawford 361/1, 82 BC) struck a solo denarius — a helmeted Roma head with a horseman galloping right on the reverse, legend P·CREPVSI — in the same annual college as his colleagues C. Mamilius Limetanus (Crawford 362) and L. Marcius Censorinus (Crawford 363), each of whom struck his own separate issue. A second type shows Apollo with three horsemen, and a third features Venus with a galloping horseman. Three moneyers sharing a single annual college (each signing his own coins) is characteristic of the late second-century BC monetary system.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini notes that no ancient writers he has read mention the gens Crepusia ('nulla est mentio apud eos scriptores, quos ego quidem legerim'). He identifies P. Crepusius as described on the first and third coins of the plate, and notes he was IIIvir monetae cudendae with C. Mamilius Limetanus and L. Marcius Censorinus, who was consul cum C. Caluisio Sabino anno DCCXIV (not DCXIV). An equestrian statue had been granted to some Crepusius ('Equestri vero statua Crepusiorum aliquis, ut videtur, donatus fuerat'), and Orsini says Crepusius wished to indicate this honour by having it depicted on the coin ('quem honorem, ea in denario impressa indicare voluit Crepusius'). For the second coin, Orsini notes the control mark CRT (not CRV); if CRT stands for Crepusius, it shows the gens was plebeian since L. Crepusius served as Aedilis plebis.

Orsini does not cite Horace as a prose source; the information comes from Porphyrio.

completed.family_note: The Cupienii were a minor gens, with C. Cupiennius Libo from Cumae known as a friend of Augustus, mentioned by Horace in the Satires (book I). L. Cupiennius struck a denarius (c. 147 BC) with the standard Roma/Dioscuri type: helmeted head of Roma right with cornucopia behind on the obverse, and Dioscuri riding right with ROMA below on the reverse. The moneyer L. Cupiennius is otherwise unattested in ancient literary sources.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini notes the gens Cupiennia descended from C. Cupiennius, to whom a letter of Cicero (epistola XX, lib. XVI ad Atticum) is extant, whose son may have been C. Cupiennius Libo Cumanus, famous for Augustus's friendship, his obsessive care of his body, and his pursuit of married women — as described by Pomponius Porphyrio commenting on the Horatian verse from Satire II (book I of the Sermones). Orsini cites Porphyrio on Horace's verse, not Horace himself as a prose source. L. Cupiennius on the denarius is not mentioned by any ancient writer ('à nullo veterum scriptorum, quod sciam, nominatur').

completed.family_note: The Curiatii were a plebeian gens originally from Alba Longa, famous in legend for the combat of the three Horatii and three Curiatii under King Tullus Hostilius. C. Curiatius f. Trigeminus (Crawford 240/1, 135 BC) struck denarii with a helmeted head of Roma right with X behind on the obverse, and Juno in a quadriga right being crowned by Victory on the reverse, with C.CVR below and ROMA in exergue. The cognomen Trigeminus (triplet) recalls the legendary combat. A bronze quadrans variant also bears the C.CVR.F legend.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini classifies the Curiatii as a plebeian gens from Alba, adscribed to Rome by King Tullus, citing Dionysius lib. III. He identifies the Trigeminorum family as producing C. Curiatius, who struck the coins on this plate (citing Livy book I, Livy epitome book LV, and Valerius Maximus lib. III. cap. VII). He notes a C. Curiatius who was tribune of the plebs and mentions him at Valerius Maximus III.7. From the stone at Nola he identifies a C. Curiatius as flamen Divi Augusti, primipilus, tribunus militum, praefectus castrorum, and praefectus fabrum. Orsini does NOT mention a trident symbol on the coin or connect it to the cognomen Trigeminus; he does NOT identify the reverse biga as 'Juno Caprotina.' These are inventions not supported by the text.

completed.family_note: The Curtii were a gens of uncertain social status, linked to the legendary M. Curtius who leapt fully armed into a chasm in the Forum to save Rome, mentioned by Dionysius of Halicarnassus (lib. II), Livy (lib. VII), Valerius Maximus (lib. V, cap. VI), and Orosius (lib. III, cap. V). P. Curtius Salassus is mentioned by Cicero (ep. XVIII, lib. VI ad Leptam). Q. Curtius struck bronze and silver jointly with M. Iunius Silanus and Cn. Domitius as IIIviri monetales; Orsini could find nothing about Q. Curtius in ancient sources. A Dei Penates type with jugate laureate heads is not attested by Orsini on this plate.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini is uncertain whether the Curtii were patrician or plebeian ('patricia ne, an plebeia fuerit… non satis constat'). He cites the famous legend of M. Curtius and the lacus Curtius, drawing on Dionysius of Halicarnassus (lib. II), Livy (lib. VII), Valerius Maximus (lib. V, cap. VI), and Orosius (lib. III, cap. V). He also notes Cicero's mention of P. Curtius Salassus (ep. XVIII, lib. VI ad Leptam). For Q. Curtius, who struck bronze and silver jointly with M. Iunius Silanus and Cn. Domitius as IIIviri monetales, Orsini states explicitly that he could find nothing in the ancient sources: 'nihil potui apud scriptores reperire.' He makes no claim about identifying Q. Curtius from literary evidence, and discusses no Dei Penates or Lavinium cult type.

coins_engraved.reverse: Two gladiators fighting; T.DEIDI in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this as T. Didius, citing Sallust via Aulus Gellius (lib. II, cap. XXVII) for the IMP title and the triumphus. The extended passage interprets the vitis (vine rod) impressed on the soldier figure on the coin as a reference to military discipline — centurions beating soldiers out of order — citing Livy (epitoma lib. LVII), Pliny (lib. XIII), Tacitus (lib. I), and Plutarch in Galba. This is Orsini's interpretation of the combat/beating scene, not of gladiatorial venationes or military victories.

coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the Villa Publica ('De Villa Publica, quae à Didio fortasse restituta, uel ornata, in altera parte secundi denarii signata est'), citing Cicero (ad Att. li. III), Livy (Macedones deducti extra urbem in Villam Publicam), and Varro (de re rustica li. I, cap. II). The second coin shows the Villa Publica and Orsini attributes it to T. Didius's restoration or ornamentation of the building. He also notes (p. 86 bottom) that Livy (li. CXXVII) mentions a Didius Saxa as legate of M. Antonius in Syria, 'à quo fortasse in T. Didii memoriam argenteus denarius cusus fuit.' Orsini does NOT describe the obverse legend of coin 2 as PONTIF·CAPITO·III·VIR·CONCORDIA; that legend belongs to a Fonteian coin (C. Fonteius Capito, Crawford 429/1) which is visible in the same plate but receives no Didian text. The PONTIF·CAPITO·CONCORDIA coin is a Fonteian interloper in the Didia plate; Orsini's coin 2 discussion concerns only the Villa Publica reverse.

The coin properly belongs to the Cornelia gens, as the legend CN.LENTVL.MARC.F clearly indicates Cn. Cornelius Lentulus Marcellinus. Its placement here reflects Orsini's prosopographic method of grouping coins by historical association rather than by moneyer family.

completed.family_note: The Didii were a plebeian gens of relatively modest origins who rose to prominence in the late Republic. T. Didius, consul 98 BC, triumphed over the Thracians and the Spanish and sponsored the lex Didia sumptuaria against extravagant banqueting. The moneyer T. Didius struck denarii (Crawford 294/1) around 113-112 BC featuring Roma and a gladiatorial combat scene on the reverse. A second coin in Orsini's plate (Crawford 480/6) belongs to L. Aemilius Buca — a 44 BC denarius with the portrait of Julius Caesar — and may have been misplaced under this family.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Didia gens on one plate (p. 85), noting uncertainty about whether it was patrician or plebeian but suspecting plebeian status because the proposer of the lex Didia Sumptuaria was likely a tribunus plebis, citing Macrobius (lib. III Saturnalia). He identifies the coins as pertaining to T. Didius, consul with Q. Caecilius Metellus Nepos (anno DCLV), who triumphed twice: first as propraetor over the Scordisci from Thracia, then as proconsul over Celtiberians from Hispania. He states that Sallust (in historia, cited via Aulus Gellius lib. II, cap. XXVII) records that T. Didius was called Imperator, explaining the IMP inscription on the second coin. He also identifies T. Didius as a legate of L. Caesar during the Marsic War (anno DCLXIII), citing Appianus lib. I of the civil wars. The extended discussion of the vine rod (vitis) and centurions beating soldiers out of order is Orsini's interpretation of an image on the first coin (a figure struck with a vine rod). Orsini cites no Livy epitome or triumphal Fasti by name; his source for the triumph is Sallust via Gellius.

The man fighting a lion in the exergue directly references these spectacles, which Orsini connects to the family's later prominence through Suetonius's account of Nero's ancestry.

completed.family_note: The Domitii were a prominent plebeian gens with two main branches, the Calvini and the Ahenobarbi, both of which attained the consulship multiple times. Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus, moneyer c. 128 BC, struck denarii (Crawford 261/1) featuring a man fighting a lion on the reverse, alluding to venationes given during his curule aedileship. A joint issue with L. Licinius Crassus (Crawford 282/4) commemorated the founding of Narbo Martius in 118 BC. Later imperatorial issues include Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus's silver and bronze from 41 BC (Crawford 519/2) and Cn. Domitius Calvinus's denarii from Osca (Crawford 532/1) struck during his Spanish proconsulship in 39 BC.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini devotes two plates (pp. 86, 88) to the Domitia gens, carefully distinguishing the Calvini and Ahenobarbi branches. For coin 1, he identifies Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus as curule aedile (anno DCXCII, with M. Pupius Piso and M. Valerius Messalla as consuls), citing Pliny (lib. VIII, cap. XXXVI) for his staging of lions and Aethiopian beast-hunters in the Circus — Orsini notes (against Pliny's number of 100 bears/Numidians) that Pliny may have had unreliable annals and that a man fighting a lion on the coin shows Ahenobarbus gave lions, not bears, in the show. For coin 2, Orsini tentatively connects it to Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus's triumph ex Hispania (anno DCCXXI) or alternatively to the proconsul who triumphed over the Arverni (anno DCXXXV). For coin 3, Orsini attributes it to Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus who was Censor with L. Licinius Crassus (anno DCLXI) and had been Consul with C. Cassius Longinus (anno DLVII); his consulship is documented in an inscription from Interamna — Orsini does NOT connect coin 3 to Narbo Martius. For coins 4 and 5, Orsini attributes them to the Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus who was proavus of Nero, citing Suetonius (in Nerone, cap. III) and extended passages from Dio (lib. XLVIII) and Appianus (lib. V, bell. ciuil.) and Suetonius (cap. III in Nerone) on his joining Antony's faction. Orsini specifically notes that the prow and trophy appear on coin 4 ('quia uero classi praefuit, nauis prora, & trophaeum in altera quarti denarii parte impressum est'). For coin 7 (second plate, p. 88), Orsini is unambiguous: 'Non est dubium, quin huius tabellaе denarius ad Cn. Domitium Calvinum pertineat,' attributing it to the consul iterum of anno DCCXIII with C. Asinius Pollio, who triumphed from Hispania anno DCCXII, noting the Oscenses (people of Osca) were known to strike coins with the image of the Hispani Dei, and discussing the pontifical instruments (Instrumenta Pontificalia) or the lex Domitia on priesthoods.

completed.family_note: The Durmii were an obscure gens known primarily from M. Durmius, who served as IIIvir monetalis (triumvir auro argento aere flando feriundo) under Augustus. His coins are exclusively Augustan bronzes and possibly one silver issue, bearing the head of Augustus on the obverse and various animal types on the reverse including lion attacking boar, a stag, and a quadriga. The animal-combat scenes are generally interpreted as references to the ludi saeculares and the cult of Diana. These coins are catalogued in RIC I (nos. 394-396) and were struck at the Rome mint.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Durmia gens on one plate (p. 89), noting that neither the gens Durmia nor M. Durmius, who served under Augustus as triumvir monetae cudendae, is mentioned by any ancient writer he has seen ('mentio aliqua apud scriptores, quos ego uiderim, reperitur'). He says that the reverses of the first coin ('quae uero in altera parte primi denarii impressa sunt') pertain to Augustus without doubt and perhaps to his ludi saeculares, since boar and stag ('apri & cerui fignis') were noted for Diana in whose honor the games were celebrated. He defers discussion of the simulacrum Honoris (HONORI legend) to the entry on Lollius Palicanus: 'De Honoris simulacro in Lollii Palicani denario dicetur.' He cites no ancient literary sources beyond this deferral; there is no mention of Horace's Carmen Saeculare.

completed.family_note: The Egnatii were a plebeian gens of probable Samnite origin who became active in Roman politics during the late Republic. C. Egnatius Cn.f. Cn.n. Maxsumus served as moneyer c. 75 BC, striking a varied series of denarii (Crawford 391/1-3) with obverse heads of Apollo and reverses including Cupid on goat, Roma seated on shields, and Roma with horse. M. Egnatius Rufus gained notoriety for organizing private fire brigades as aedile and was later executed for conspiring against Augustus. The Egnatian denarii are notable for their multiple reverse types within a single issue, all bearing the full tria nomina with filiation.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini devotes one plate (p. 90) to the Egnatia gens, noting it is plebeian. He cites Cicero for C. Egnatius Maxsumus: lib. III ad Atticum, ep. XXXIV, and lib. XIII ad Memmium, epist. XLIII, XLV, and LXXIII. The lib. XIII citations are for L. Egnatius Rufus, whose son ('cuius fortasse filius fuit') was perhaps M. Egnatius noted on the fourth (aes) coin, and who conspired against Augustus according to Suetonius (cap. XIX) and Velleius (lib. II). Orsini does not conflate C. Egnatius Maxsumus with M. Egnatius Rufus as the same person; he proposes a filial relationship between L. Egnatius Rufus and M. Egnatius. He presents the denarii as belonging to C. Egnatius Maxsumus and mentions the fourth aes coin as M. Egnatius. He does not read 'EGNATMS' as a legend variant, does not discuss Venus figures, and does not interpret specific reverses beyond assigning coins to the moneyer.

completed.family_note: The Egnatuleii were an obscure plebeian gens known almost solely from two individuals: C. Egnatuleius C.f., who struck quinarii (Crawford 333/1) c. 97 BC with Victory erecting a trophy over Gallic arms, and L. Egnatuleius, a quaestor praised by Cicero in the Third Philippic for rallying a legion to Octavian's side against Antony in 44 BC. The quinarius type with carnyx and oval shield at the base of the trophy indicates a commemorative reference to victories over Gauls. The family name appears to be a diminutive form of Egnatius.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Egnatuleia gens on a single plate (p. 91–92). He states that Cicero (lib. III Philippics) is the only source he knows that mentions the family ('unus, quòd sciam, Cicero facit mentionem lib. III Philipp.'), naming L. Egnatuleius as perhaps the son of C. Egnatuleius who struck the Victoriatus coin ('filium fortaffe C. Egnatulei huius, qui Victoriatum nummum percuffit'). Orsini calls the denomination a Victoriatus (not a quinarius), marked with a Q. He then quotes extensively from Cicero's Third Philippic for L. Egnatuleius the Quaestor who led the fourth legion to Caesar with C. Caesar's authority, and from Cicero's Fifth Philippic ('in libro V') on L. Egnatuleius's loyalty. He also cites inscriptions from Corduba and from the base of a Vespasian statue mentioning C. Egnatuleia C.f. and C. Egnatuleius Laurus. Orsini does not describe the trophy or carnyx on the coin reverse.

completed.family_note: The Eppii were an obscure plebeian gens known primarily from M. Eppius, who served as a legate of Q. Metellus Scipio during the African campaign against Caesar in 46 BC. His denarii (Crawford 461/1) were struck as military issues in Africa, featuring a draped bust (probably Africa personified) on the obverse and Hercules standing with club and trophy on the reverse. The LEG legend confirms his status as legatus. The family is otherwise attested only in inscriptions, including one recording a P. Eppius P.f. Fabruvus.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Eppia gens briefly (p. 92), establishing it from inscriptions in the tribus Cornelia and Fabia. He cites Hirtius (lib. V de bello Africo) for M. Eppius as legate of Scipio in Africa, quoting the passage about events at Adrameto. He also cites Cicero (ep. XIII ad Att.) on M. Eppius as an equestrian ('fuit autem M. Eppius ex ordine Equestri'). The inscription cited is 'P. EPPIVS P.F.FAB.RVFVS / MIL. COHOR. II. PRABT / T.F.I. ARBITR.' (tribe Fabia, cognomen Rufus), not 'P. Eppius P.f. Fabruvus.' Orsini explains the Africa obverse head from the coin inscription and the Hercules reverse as depicting the Hercules cult worshipped in Africa ('Herculis simulacrum, quod in Africa colebatur'), citing Herodotus (lib. II).

completed.family_note: The Fabii were one of the most ancient and distinguished patrician gentes at Rome, with branches including the Maximi, Pictores, Labrones, and Buteones. Q. Fabius Maximus Cunctator famously delayed Hannibal during the Second Punic War, and the historian Q. Fabius Pictor wrote the earliest Roman history in prose. Republican denarii were struck by Q. Fabius Labeo (Crawford 273/1, 124 BC), Q. Fabius Maximus (Crawford 265/1, 127 BC), N. Fabius Pictor (Crawford 268/1a, 126 BC), and C. Fabius C.f. Hadrianus (Crawford 322/1a, 102 BC). The coins show standard Roma/Victory biga types with some notable variants including a possible Quirinus head and the EX A.PV (ex argento publico) mark.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini devotes two pages (pp. 93–94) to the Fabia gens, finding only the Labeo, Maximi, and Pictores branches on coins ('Labeontes tantum, Maximi, & Pictores in denariis… reperiuntur'). For coin 1 (Q. Fabius Labeo), Orsini cites Cicero (lib. I off. & ad Q. fratrem) for his role as arbitrator between the Nolani and Neapolitani, given by the Senate. He does not cite Livy for Labeo. For coin 2, Orsini states it cannot be determined with certainty who it belongs to ('diuinare non licet') but tentatively assigns it to Q. Fabius Maximus, consul anno DCCCVIII with C. Trebonius; he says nothing about the Cunctator, the Hannibalic War, Polybius, or Livy for this coin. For coin 3 (N. Fabius Pictor), Orsini says it probably pertains to the Flamen Quirinalis ('Flaminẽ Quirinalem'), suggesting the helmeted image is that of Quirinus Flaminis ('Quirini certè imago Flaminis apicem manu tenentis'), and draws the connection to N. Fabius Pictor. For coin 4 (C. Fabius C.f. Pictor), Orsini explains EX.A.P. as 'ex argento publico' (not Cybele); no Cybele is mentioned. For coin 5, Orsini identifies a C. Fabius with praenomine Caius who was triumvir with 'L. Roscio, uel L. Rubrio, & Q. Marcio,' noting uncertainty on the L.R. reading. For coin 6, Orsini identifies L. Fabius Hispaniensis, a Sertorian (Sertorianarum partium), citing a Sallust fragment from Servius on Aeneid I, and noting that a related coin is inscribed L. FABI. L.F. HISP.Q.

coins_engraved.reverse: Ship prow right; M·FABRI/NI above; ROMA below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini creates this entry explicitly noting the possibility that the gens name arises from a die-cutter's error ('nisi fit erratum ab eo, qui nummum aereum cufit'). He reads the full nomen as Fabrinius from the coin legend M·FABRI NI, and acknowledges he cannot find when M. Fabrinius lived or who he was. The possibility of a mint error is central to his brief discussion and is absent from the current comment.

completed.family_note: The gens Fabrinia is unattested in ancient literary sources and may result from a misreading of M. Fabius on coin legends. No moneyer named Fabrinius appears in Crawford's Roman Republican Coinage, and the single bronze coin Orsini attributes to this family shows a standard Janus/prow type with the legend M.FABRI, which is more plausibly read as an abbreviation of M. Fabius. The family's inclusion in Orsini's work illustrates his comprehensive approach of creating entries even for doubtful gentes.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Fabrinia gens in half a plate (p. 95 top). He says there is no mention of the gens Fabrinia in ancient writers unless it was an error by the person who struck the bronze coin ('nisi fit erratum ab eo, qui nummum aereum cufit'). He also states he has been unable to discover who this M. Fabrinius was or when he lived ('Neque uero M. hic Fabrinius quis fuerit, quoue tempore uixerit, inuenire adhuc potui'). The coin plate legend reads M·FABRI NI (i.e. Fabrini, genitive of Fabrinius), so Orsini reads the full nomen Fabrinius from the coin, not a truncated M.FABRI interpreted as an abbreviation of Fabius. He provides no citations from any ancient author.

Fannius as Tribunus Plebis) and Cicero in Catone (for the orators); not De Oratore or Brutus.

completed.family_note: The Fannii were a plebeian gens active from the 2nd century BC onward. C. Fannius Strabo, consul 161 BC, sponsored the lex Fannia sumptuaria against luxurious banquets, and the family produced several tribunes and orators mentioned by Cicero. M. Fannius C.f. struck denarii (Crawford 275/1) c. 123 BC with the standard Roma/Victory biga type. A later joint tresviral issue (Crawford 351/1, 86 BC) by M. Fannius with L. Critonius and M. Plaetorius features Apollo and three seated figures, possibly judges (iudices). The Fannius coinage spans both standard Republican types and more distinctive late Republican designs.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Fannia gens on a half-plate (p. 95 bottom and p. 96), establishing its plebeian status from a Cicero passage (ep. XIII, lib. XVI ad Att.) asking about the censorship year of C. Fannius M.F. Tribunus Plebis. Orsini identifies the first coin's moneyer as M. Fannius C.F., before whom Cicero defended Sex. Roscius parricidii reus anno DLXXIII (with L. Sulla, Q. Metellus as consuls), citing Cicero in Catone for the orator C. Fannius's prosopography. He also cites Velleius (lib. II) for the orators of the Scipio Aemilianus circle. For the second coin, Orsini says it may also pertain to M. Fannius, who appears from the coin inscription to have been an Aedilis Plebis, citing Dio for the institution of Aediles Cereales (Caefar V and M. Antonius as consuls, anno DCCIX). The legends visible in the plate read M·FN·CE (coin 2, obverse) and M·FAN·L·CRT (coin 2, reverse), not M.PAN. Orsini does not discuss a PAN/FAN confusion, does not call the reverse figures iudices, and does not cite Cicero's De Oratore or Brutus as primary sources for this entry.

completed.family_note: The Farsuleii were an obscure gens known primarily from L. Farsuleius Mensor, who struck denarii (Crawford 392/1b) c. 75 BC. His coins feature a diademed and draped bust of Libertas on the obverse with pileus (cap of freedom) and S.C., and Roma assisted by a warrior in a biga on the reverse. The cognomen Mensor (surveyor) is unusual for a Roman moneyer. The family is otherwise attested only in inscriptions, including one from Sutrina recording Farsuleii among pontifices. The S.C. mark on the obverse indicates senatorial authorization for the issue.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Farsuleia gens on one plate (p. 97) with a single denarius. His main evidence for the family is the Sutrina inscription, in which M. Valerius Ferox is listed in place of L. Farsuleius Rufus in a collegium. He also notes that a Q. Farsuleius Vesper is named on the base of a Vespasian statue among those who contributed money for its dedication (under consuls L. Annius Bassus and C. Caecina Paetus). Regarding L. Farsuleius Mensor, who struck the denarius, Orsini explicitly states that he could find no mention of him in any ancient literary or epigraphic sources: 'nullam in ueteribus nec scriptorum nec lapidum monumentis reperire mentionem potui.' He makes no interpretive claim about the coin's obverse (Libertas, pileus, S.C.) or reverse (biga scene) — no iconographic commentary whatever appears in his text.

completed.family_note: The Flaminii were a plebeian gens best known for C. Flaminius, consul 223 and 217 BC, who built the Via Flaminia and the Circus Flaminius before falling at the Battle of Lake Trasimene against Hannibal. L. Flaminius Chilo struck denarii (Crawford 302/1) c. 109-108 BC with the standard Roma/Victory biga type, and also struck bronze (Crawford 302/2). A later C. Flaminius may have served as one of Caesar's augmented IIIIviri monetales. The family name derives from flamen, suggesting an early connection to priesthoods, and the Via Flaminia linking Rome to the Adriatic remains their most lasting monument.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Flaminia gens on one plate (p. 98) with three coins. He identifies L. Flaminius Chilo (also spelled Cilo — he notes both forms appear on the coins and in manuscripts) as a IIIIvir (quattuorvir) auro, argento, aere feriundo under Caesar as Dictator, and possibly the first Flamen of Divus Iulius. He discusses Caesar's augmentation of the monetary college from three to four members, drawing on Suetonius (in Caesare) and Dio (lib. LIIII, who called them Triumviri monetales under Augustus). He cites Cicero (li. VI ad Torquatum, ep. XX) and Appian (li. III bel. ciuil.) as identifying Chilo as one who looked to Caesar, with the Venus head on the second coin's reverse referencing the Julian family's divine ancestry. Orsini does NOT describe a 'FLAMININVS III VIR' legend — he consistently calls the office IIII uir (quattuorvir). He cites Cicero (in Bruto, ad Att.) and Livy (li. XXI) for the family in general, not specifically for C. Flaminius and the Via Flaminia in connection with the coins.

completed.family_note: The Flavii were a plebeian gens of ancient origin, with the cognomen Flavus (blond) suggesting physical characteristics. In the Republic, Cn. Flavius (aedile 304 BC) famously published the calendar (Fasti) and legal formulae (legis actiones), breaking the patrician monopoly on legal knowledge. Dec. Flavus struck denarii (Crawford 207/1) c. 150 BC with a Diana in biga and crescent type. C. Flavius Hemicillus served as Brutus's legate propraetor and struck imperatorial denarii (Crawford 504/1) in 43-42 BC. The family later rose to imperial prominence when the Flavian dynasty (Vespasian, Titus, Domitian) ruled Rome from 69 to 96 AD.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Flavia gens on one plate (pp. 99–100) with two coins. For the first coin, he reads the letters FLAVS as indicating a cognomen FLAVVS (noting that ancients wrote FLAVOS and FLAVS without double vowel) rather than the nomen FLAVIVS, and compiles cognomina FLAVVS attested in other gentes from Dionysius, Livy, Suetonius, and inscriptions. He makes no specific iconographic comment on the first coin's type. For the second coin, he identifies C. FLAVIVS HEMIS (his form of the name) as Brutus's legatus propraetore, drawing on Cornelius Nepos (Vita Attici), Appian (lib. V), and Plutarch (Brutus), who calls him Praefectum Fabrûm Bruti. Orsini explicitly defers full discussion of this coin to the Iunia gens: 'Cetera, quae in hoc denario signata sunt, ad M. Brutum pertinent, & in gente Iunia explicabuntur.' He does NOT describe the reverse as a trophy or celebrate a military success in the Liberators' campaign.

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head right; MN.FONTEIVS behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Winged Cupid riding a goat right within a laurel wreath; two pilei (caps) above; thyrsus and filleted vase below.

He does NOT describe the imagery as Venus/Bacchic. The Veiouis simulacrum and Castors' caps on this coin he explicitly says he cannot explain ('mihi quidem obscurum est').

coins_engraved.reverse: Horseman spearing fallen enemy; two combatants below

CAPITO as triumuir, possibly the grandson of the consul and perhaps the same man who commanded Antony's fleet as propraetor (inferred from a damaged coin inscription). He cites Horace (li. I, Ser. completed.family_note: The Fonteii were a plebeian gens active from the 2nd century BC. C. Fonteius struck denarii (Crawford 290/1) c. 114-113 BC with a distinctive Janus/galley type. Mn. Fonteius struck denarii (Crawford 307/1b, 108-107 BC) with Dioscuri/galley types, and his descendant Mn. Fonteius C.f. issued the famous Cupid-on-goat denarii (Crawford 353/1a, 85 BC) and was later defended by Cicero in Pro Fonteio. P. Fonteius P.f. Capito served as tresvir monetalis c. 55 BC, striking denarii (Crawford 429/1-2) with Mars/equestrian combat and Concordia/Villa Publica types. C. Fonteius Capito held the consulship in 33 BC.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini devotes one plate (pp. 100–101) to the Fonteia gens with six coins. He establishes the gens as plebeian from P. Clodius's adoption by P. Fonteius. Coin 1 he assigns to C. FONTEIVS CAPITO, consul suffect from the Kalends of July in 720 AUC. Coins 2–3 he assigns to M'. FONTEIVS, son of the consul, the defendant in Cicero's Pro Fonteio (accused by M. Plaetorius of misgovernment as Praetor of Gallia for three years). He cites Horace (li. I, Carm.) for the galley with Castor and Pollux ('quòd hae stellae sint nauigantibus propitiae'). Coins 4–5 he assigns to P. FONTEIVS P.F. CAPITO, who could be the consul's grandson, possibly a Praetor of Sardinia (Livy lib. XLIII) and perhaps the same who commanded Antony's fleet as propraеtor (inferred from a damaged bronze inscription). Orsini cites Horace (li. I, Ser. Sat. V) for P. Fonteius Capito. For coin 5's reverse ('Veiouis uero simulacrum, & pilei Castorum stellis superimpositis'), Orsini explicitly states these are 'mihi quidem obscurum' — he cannot explain them. For the M'. Fonteius of coin 4 (the fourth denarius), Orsini discusses a possible Tribunus militum connection, noting this is 'nobis ignotum.' He does NOT describe a 'Janus/ship type as referencing naval associations' for coin 1, does NOT describe coin 3's Cupid as Venus/Bacchic (he says 'Cupidinem hirco insidentem, quòd id animal maxime fit procliue ad libidinem'), and does NOT mention T. Didius IMP in his text.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Honos right; HO / VIR on sides; KALENI below
coins_engraved.reverse: Two standing figures clasping hands, the left holding a cornucopia; IT / RO on sides; CORDI below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Q. Fufius Kalenus as moneyer and tribune of the plebs in year DCXCI, later consul with P. Vatinius (DCCVI). He cites Dio (lib. XLII) for Calenus's Caesarian allegiance and Cicero's Philippica VIII for Cicero's attack on him. He makes no iconographic comment on the obverse heads or the reverse handshake scene.

coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Two clasped hands; figure with cornucopia between; IT / RO on sides; CORDI below

coins_engraved.obverse: Very lightly engraved head of Roma, right (generic type)
coins_engraved.reverse: Very lightly engraved quadriga (generic type)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Printing anomaly (the 'ghost coin'): a faint, generic Roma-head / quadriga composition on the Fufia cancel plate, too lightly and incompletely engraved to identify; Orsini's text treats only the Q. Fufius Calenus coin.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Female head right wearing a helmet (Roma type) with a feather or plume crest. The portrait is clean and clearly helmeted. This is a standard Roma or Virtus type.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: The reverse appears to show a scene within the circular field — too faint/degraded to read detailed elements. A biga (two-horse chariot) seems to be present galloping right, but the detail is lost in the engraving style. No clear legend readable.

completed.family_note: The Fufii were a plebeian gens. Q. Fufius Calenus, tribune of the plebs 61 BC and consul 47 BC, was a committed Caesarian who opposed Cicero and later commanded Antony's forces in Cisalpine Gaul, where he died in 40 BC. His joint denarii with Mucius Cordus (Crawford 403/1, 70 BC) feature the jugate heads of Honos and Virtus on the obverse and the famous Italia/Roma handshake on the reverse, celebrating the restoration of citizenship rights after the Social War. These coins are struck in Rome and are notable for their political iconography commemorating national reconciliation.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Fufia gens on one plate (p. 101) with two coins. He identifies Q. Fufius Calenus (or Kalenus) as tribune of the plebs anno DCXCI — under the consuls D. Iunius Silanus and L. Licinius Murena, i.e. 62 BC by his reckoning — and consul 47 BC, citing Cicero's speeches against him and Caesar's Civil War commentaries. Orsini discusses the Honos and Virtus obverse types and interprets the Italia/Roma handshake reverse as celebrating the restoration of rights after the Social War, connecting the political imagery to the lex Plautia Papiria of 89 BC. He notes Calenus supported Caesar throughout the civil war and died governing Cisalpine Gaul. The second coin receives less detailed treatment as a possible variant or smaller denomination.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; star below chin
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory in biga right holding wreath; CN·FOL·M·CAL·Q·MET text below; ROMA in field
coins_engraved.moneyer: Cn. Fulvius, M. Calidius, Q. Caecilius Metellus
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies CN. FVLVIVS as striking jointly with Q. Metellus and M. Calidius, and explicitly says he cannot determine who this Fulvius was ('nihil certi afferre possum'). He makes no mention of Livy XXV.17, the temple of Honos et Virtus at Clastidium, M. Fulvius Nobilior, or Hercules Musarum. Those references belong to the Fufia section.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Helmeted female head right (Roma type) — wearing a distinctive winged helmet or crested helmet. Wing visible above the helmet. Clear profile facing right.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Victory in biga galloping right — two horses, Victory holding reins and wreath. Below the horses: CN·FOV (partially readable) or CN·FOL. Letters arranged below biga. This is a standard Roma/Victory-in-biga type.
coins_engraved.specimen_shared_reason: same catalogue type cross-listed under multiple gentes (joint-moneyer issue or sub-variant); one museum specimen serves all

completed.family_note: The Fulvii were a plebeian gens from Tusculum that rose to great prominence in the 3rd and 2nd centuries BC. Q. Fulvius Flaccus held four consulships during the Second Punic War, and M. Fulvius Nobilior, consul 189 BC, conquered Aetolia and built the temple of Hercules Musarum. The coin attributed to this family under Crawford 284/1 was struck by Cn. Fulvius as part of a tresviral issue c. 117-116 BC jointly with M. Calidius and Q. Metellus. However, the attribution of Republican coins to the Fulvia gens is not entirely secure, and the family is better known from literary sources than from numismatic evidence.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Fulvia gens on one plate (p. 102) with a single denarius. He notes that among all the many divided families of the plebeian Fulvii, only one CN. FVLVII is attested in silver denarii, and explicitly states he cannot say anything certain about who this Fulvius was or when he lived: 'nihil certi afferre possum.' He observes that because the moneyer struck coins jointly with Q. Metellus and M. Calidius, contemporaries of Cicero, he can be presumed to have flourished in Cicero's time ('Ciceronis ipsius temporibus floruisse possumus suspicari'). He adds a note on archaic spelling: FOVLVIVS (and FOVRIVS) are early forms imitating Greek orthography. Orsini says NOTHING about the temple of Honos et Virtus at Clastidium, M. Fulvius Nobilior's Aetolian triumph, or the temple of Hercules Musarum — those discussions appear in the FUFIA section (pp. 101–102) in connection with Marcellus, not in the Fulvia section.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bearded male head right (Jupiter?)
coins_engraved.reverse: Two standing figures (man and woman) clasping hands or performing ritual
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this coin to C. Fundanius (= Varro's father-in-law), the Tribune of the Plebs named in the Farnese bronze tablet, stating 'ad eum autem referendos esse opinor.' He makes no statement about being unable to identify the moneyer.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right
coins_engraved.reverse: Figure in chariot right; C.FVNDVS below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes the coins on the plate to C. Fundanius, Varro's father-in-law (the Tribune who 'primus plebi scivit'), preferring this over the attribution to the consul of year DX. The claim that the attribution rests on a 'FVNDAN legend reading' is not stated by Orsini — he bases it on the chronological fit with the Farnese inscription.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Horseman galloping right; star below
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Figure in chariot right; C.FVNDVS below

completed.family_note: The Fundanii were a minor plebeian gens of uncertain political standing. C. Fundanius was a friend of Varro who appears as an interlocutor in De Re Rustica, and M. Fundanius Fundulus served as aedile of the plebs. No securely identified Fundanius moneyer appears in Crawford's Roman Republican Coinage, and the coins Orsini attributes to this family likely result from misread legends on worn specimens. The gens is better attested in literary and epigraphic sources than in numismatic evidence.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Fundania gens on one plate (p. 103) with two (visible) denarii. He cites Livy (lib. XXV) for M. Fundanus as Aedilis plebis, and a bronze tablet in the collection of Cardinal Alessandro Farnese recording a plebiscite for the Thermenses Maiores Pisidis, where C. FVNDANIVS C.I. TR. PL. DES. QVI. FLEBEM. PREIMVS. SCIVIT. is mentioned. Orsini argues ('ad eum autem referendos esse opinor') that the coins on the plate belong to this C. Fundanius, whom Varro (lib. I, De Re Rustica) calls his father-in-law. He acknowledges that others ('licet alii') attribute the coins to a different C. Fundanius who was consul with C. Sulpicius in year DX. Orsini does NOT say he cannot find a Fundanius moneyer or that the attribution is highly uncertain — he positively favours the Varro father-in-law identification.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted; X behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Goddess in biga right, holding reins; two galloping horses drawing chariot; PVR below, ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the moneyer as L. FVRIVS PVRPREONVM and notes he triumphed over the Gauls as PRAETOR (not consul) in years DLIIII and DLVII. He makes no iconographic statement about a Diana biga with two stags.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head of Roma right, helmeted; X behind
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Diana in biga right, holding reins; two stags drawing chariot

coins_engraved.obverse: Turreted female head right (Cybele); AED.CVR around
coins_engraved.reverse: Curule chair; P.FOVRIVS / CRASSIPES below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini says the coin's foot image indicates the cognomen's origin from the GREEK name Oedipus ('ἀπὸ τοῦ οἰδήματος τῶν ποδῶν' = from the swelling of the feet), NOT from Latin 'crassus pes.' The curule chair indicates the curule aedileship. He notes Livy names M. Furius Crassipes as triumvir coloniae deducendae and Praetor, and perhaps the coin was struck by Cicero's son-in-law.

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate double-faced head (Janus); I above; M.F behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Roma standing right crowning a trophy; ROMA in right field; PHLI in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini states this coin was struck by M. IVRIVS L.F. PHILO 'in memoriam sine dubio eius triumphi, quem egit P. Furius Philus anno DXXX. de Galleis Liguribus.' He identifies M. Furius as probably the son of L. Furius Philus the Praetor (anno DLXXXII, citing Livy lib. XLII). He does not describe a Janus head or military trophies on this coin.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Laureate double-faced head (Janus); I above; M.F behind
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Roma crowning trophy; kneeling captive; ROMA / PHLI in exergue

coins_engraved.obverse: Female head right (Ceres per Orsini); III / VIR around; BROCCHI below; corn-ear behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Curule chair flanked by fasces; L.FVRI / CN.F above
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies CN. FVRIVS BROCCHVS (praenomen Cn., not L.) as curule aedile, inferred from the curule chair and Ceres image on the coin. He does not provide an etymology of 'brocchi' as protruding teeth. He cites only Valerius Maximus (li. VI, cap. I) and Cicero (pro Q. Ligario; in Verrem lib. III for Anneius Brocchus).

completed.family_note: The Furii were among the oldest Roman gentes, with both patrician and plebeian branches. M. Furius Camillus, the legendary second founder of Rome, liberated the city from the Gauls c. 390 BC. Republican moneyers include L. Furius Purpureo (Crawford 187/1, 169-158 BC) with standard Roma/Victory biga type, P. Furius Crassipes (Crawford 356/1a, 84 BC) with a distinctive turreted head and curule chair reverse, M. Furius Philus (possibly Crawford 281/1, 119 BC) with Janus and military scene, and L. Furius Cn.f. Brocchus (Crawford 414/1, 63 BC) with Ceres and curule chair types. The family produced consuls, praetors, and dictators over several centuries.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini devotes one plate (pp. 104–105) to the Furia gens with four coins. He establishes the gens had both patrician and plebeian branches (citing Livy lib. IX and XXXIX). Coin 1 belongs to L. FVRIVS PVRPREONVM, who as Praetor (not consul) triumphed over the Gauls (anno DLIIII and DLVII). Coin 2 belongs to P. FOVRIVS CRASSIPES, whose cognomen origin Orsini traces to the GREEK name Oedipus ('Graecum nomen οἰδίπους imitatus est; quem ἀπὸ τοῦ οἰδήματος τῶν ποδῶν... Oedipodem appellatum fuisse, Graeci Poetae tradunt') — NOT from Latin 'crassus pes.' He notes the curule chair on the coin indicates Crassipes's curule aedileship (AED.CVR.), that Livy names M. Furius Craffipedem as triumvir coloniae deducendae and Praetor, and that the coin may have been struck by Cicero's son-in-law. Coin 3 was struck by M. IVRIVS L.F. PHILO in memory of the triumph of P. Furius Philus over the Galli Ligures in year DXXX. Coin 4 belongs to CN. FVRIVS BROCCHVS (not L.): Orsini finds only Valerius Maximus's mention of a Cn. Furius caught in adultery by a man named Brocchus, which he uses to correct Valerius's corrupt text (he thinks 'Brocchus' there is a name, not a cognomen). Orsini concludes from the curule chair and the Ceres image on the coin that Brocchus was a Curule Aedile ('Aedilem Curulem fuisse Brocchum hunc... ex sella Curuli intelligere possumus, & imagine Cereris, quae rei frumentariae praeest').

coins_engraved.reverse: AVGVSTVS TRIBVNIC POTEST in three lines within oak-wreath (no portrait)

V) was perhaps his father. Q. Gallius is a separate person — the Praetor accused of ambitus. Orsini does not identify C. Gallius himself as Praetor.
