coins_engraved.reverse_ai: S C in centre; C GALLIVS C F LVPERCVS IIIVIR A A A F F around

completed.family_note: The Gallii were a minor plebeian gens of limited political prominence. C. Gallius Lupercus served as an Augustan IIIvir monetalis (triumvir auro argento aere flando feriundo), striking bronze coins at the Rome mint with the characteristic S.C. legend and Augustus's titulature on the reverse. His coins are catalogued in RIC I (no. 373) and dated to c. 16 BC. Q. Gallius, a praetor mentioned by Cicero, was accused of ambitus (electoral bribery), providing the main literary attestation for the family.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Gallia gens on one plate (p. 105) with a single bronze coin. He notes the gens cannot be classified as patrician or plebeian from the available sources. Cicero (in Verrem lib. V) calls C. Gallius a Senatorial eques — Orsini says C. Gallius the eques was perhaps ('fortasse') the father of C. GALLII who struck the bronze coin as triumvir under Augustus. He also mentions Q. Gallius as Praetor in year DCLXXXVIII (L. Cotta and L. Torquatus as consuls), accused of ambitus the following year and defended by Cicero in a lost speech. He further draws on Asconius (in Corneliana), Valerius Maximus (lib. VIII, cap. X), Quintilian (lib. II, cap. III), and Appian (lib. III), citing a passage about Q. Gallius as Urban Praetor and his brother M. Gallius, whose estate Tiberius inherited (Suetonius, Tiberio cap. VI). Orsini does NOT 'conflate' the praetor and the moneyer — he carefully distinguishes them with 'fortasse' (father/son hypothesis). C. Gallius is a Senatorial eques, NOT himself described by Cicero as a praetor.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted
coins_engraved.reverse: Mars (or warrior deity) in quadriga right, hurling spear; CN·GEL below; ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this denarius 'fortasse' (perhaps) to a legate of Cn. Pompeius in the maritime war against the pirates, citing Florus lib. III. The 'perhaps' must be retained.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head of Roma right, helmeted
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Roma seated left on shields, holding spear; wolf and twins below

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of male figure right, laureate; legend around border
coins_engraved.reverse: Head of male figure right, laureate; legend around border
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this coin with certainty ('sine dubio') as belonging to L. GELLIVS POPLICOLA, Antony's Quaestor Propraetore, later consul with M. Cocceius Nerva in year DCCXVII. He cites Dio (lib. XLVII) at length. He expresses no difficulty in the attribution.

completed.family_note: The Gellii were a plebeian gens active from the mid-Republic onward. Cn. Gellius struck denarii (Crawford 232/1) c. 138 BC with a Roma head obverse and Mars driving a quadriga on the reverse. The annalist Cn. Gellius wrote a multi-volume history of Rome, and the antiquarian A. Gellius (2nd century AD) later bore this name. A second coin in Orsini's plate appears to be a triumviral or provincial issue with portrait types, not securely catalogued in Crawford or RIC and possibly belonging to the Roman Provincial Coinage series.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Gellia gens on one plate (p. 106) with two denarii. The first coin he assigns 'fortasse' (perhaps) to a GELLIVM who was Cn. Pompeius's legate in the maritime war against the pirates, citing Florus lib. III. The second coin he assigns with certainty ('sine dubio') to L. GELLIVS POPLICOLA, who struck it as Antony's Quaestor Propraetore, then held the consulship with M. Cocceius Nerva in year DCCXVII. He cites Dio (lib. XLVII) at length for L. Gellius Poplicola. He also notes that L. Gellius Poplicola's father was consul with Cn. Lentulus Clodianus in year DCLXXXXI, citing Cicero (in Pisonem and the post-reditum speech). He does NOT express uncertainty about the second coin — he says 'sine dubio.'

coins_engraved.obverse: Diademed head of Pietas right; PIETAS behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Running figure (Amphinomus or Anapias) carrying parent on shoulders; M.HERENNI below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes the denarius to M. Herennius, consul in year DCCXX (possibly the son of the consul with C. Valerius Flaccus in DCLX). He notes the coin bears a signum Pietatis and compares the reverse to the Aeneas/Anchises motif as a traditional symbol of pietas on ancient monuments. He does NOT name the Catanaean brothers. The consul with C. Valerius Flaccus is the FATHER (anno DCLX), not the moneyer himself.

completed.family_note: The Herennii were a plebeian gens of Samnite origin who rose to prominence in the late Republic. M. Herennius struck denarii (Crawford 308/1) c. 108-107 BC featuring the diademed head of Pietas on the obverse and one of the Catanaean brothers (Amphinomus or Anapias) carrying his father on his shoulders on the reverse. This type celebrates filial devotion (pietas) and references the legendary brothers of Catana who rescued their parents from an eruption of Etna. M. Herennius held the consulship in 93 BC alongside C. Valerius Flaccus.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Herennia gens on one plate (p. 107) with a single denarius. He identifies M. HERENNIVS hic as the moneyer, noting he was consul ex Kal. Nou. in year DCCXX. He says M. Herennius was perhaps ('fortasse') the son of the M. Herennius who held the consulship with C. Valerius Flaccus in year DCLX — it is this FATHER's consulship that Orsini connects to C. Valerius Flaccus. He cites Cicero (in Bruto) for the father's reputation as a mediocre but distinguished orator. For the coin type, Orsini observes that 'Aeneas autem Anchisem humeris ferens, Pietatis symbolum antiquis fuit, quod in aliis etiam uetustatism monumentis reperitur' — he compares the coin's reverse to the Aeneas/Anchises motif as a symbol of pietas. He does NOT name the Catanaean brothers (Amphinomus or Anapias) — that identification is not in his text. He does not describe the obverse as Pietas by name; he says 'denarium cum signo Pietatis.'

coins_engraved.obverse: Veiled head right (Caesar as Pontifex Maximus); CAESAR COS.TER around
coins_engraved.reverse: Sacrificial implements: lituus and capis (jug); A.HIRTIVS.PR around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini infers from this aureus that A. Hirtius was Praetor in year DCCVII (not DCCVI) when Caesar held his third consulship. Hirtius later died fighting M. Antonius at Mutina alongside C. Vibius Pansa. Orsini cites Livy (epitoma lib. CXIX) for this. He makes no iconographic comment on the reverse implements.

completed.family_note: The Hirtii were a plebeian gens known primarily from A. Hirtius, one of Caesar's most trusted legates and the author of Bellum Gallicum VIII (completing Caesar's commentaries). Hirtius struck aurei (Crawford 466/1) c. 46 BC as praetor under Caesar's third consulship, featuring the veiled head of Caesar on the obverse and priestly implements (lituus, praefericulum, axe) on the reverse. He held the consulship in 43 BC alongside C. Vibius Pansa and died at the Battle of Mutina fighting against Mark Antony.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Hirtia gens on one plate (p. 108) with a single aureus. He is uncertain whether the gens was patrician or plebeian ('incertum patriciá ne, an plebeia fuerit'). He reproduces an inscription (A. HIRTIVS A.F. M. LOLLIVS M.F. FVNDAMENTA FORNICIS FACIVNDA COERAVERE EIDEMQVE PROBAVERE) to establish the gens's existence. From the gold coin struck by A. HIRTIVS when Caesar held his third consulship, Orsini infers that Hirtius was Praetor in year DCCVII. He explains that praetors and their quaestors and legates had the right to strike gold and silver in the provinces for military pay ('licebat enim Praetoribus & eorum Quaestoribus, Legatisue... aurum, argentumque in prouinciis signare'). He notes Hirtius was made consul three years after his praetorship, alongside C. Vibius Pansa, and died fighting M. Antonius at Mutina; his body was brought to Rome and buried publicly in the Campus Martius. He cites Livy (in epitoma lib. CXIX) and 'alii' — NOT Suetonius or the Bellum Africum. He makes no specific identification of the priestly implements on the reverse.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Roma right with winged helmet; X (value mark) behind; COCLES before
coins_engraved.reverse: Castor and Pollux (Dioscuri) riding right; IMP·CAES·TRAIAN·AVG·GER·DAC·P·P·REST·ROMA around
coins_engraved.moneyer: Trajan restitution (restoration of archaic Horatia type)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes this is a Trajanic restitution coin recalling Horatius Cocles's defense of the Pons Sublicius, citing Livy (lib. II) at length and also Dionysius (lib. IV), Valerius Maximus (lib. III, cap. I), and Plutarch (in Poplicola) for the bronze statue decreed in the Forum. He makes no mention of the Horatii and Curiatii, nor of M. Horatius Pulvillus or the Capitoline temple.

completed.family_note: The Horatii were one of Rome's oldest patrician gentes, famous for the legendary combat of the Horatii and Curiatii in the regal period and for P. Horatius Cocles's defense of the Pons Sublicius against Lars Porsena. M. Horatius Pulvillus dedicated the Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus in the first year of the Republic. The coin Orsini attributes to this family is uncertain and does not appear securely in Crawford; it may be a hybrid or misattributed specimen, as no confirmed Horatius moneyer is known from the standard Republican coinage catalogues.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Horatia gens on one plate (p. 109) with a single denarius, a Trajanic restitution ('primum signatus, deinde a Traiano Imp. restitutus'). His entire discussion concerns HORATIVS COCLES and his defense of the Pons Sublicius against the enemies, citing Livy (lib. II) at great length, and then Dionysius (lib. IV), Valerius Maximus (lib. III, cap. I), Livy (li. II), and Plutarch (in Poplicola) for the bronze statue decreed for Cocles in the Roman Forum. He does NOT discuss the Horatii and Curiatii combat, and does NOT mention M. Horatius Pulvillus or the dedication of the Capitoline temple — those topics are entirely absent from Orsini's Horatia page.

coins_engraved.obverse: III·VIR GETA: Bust of Diana right, draped, with bow and quiver over shoulder.
coins_engraved.reverse: C·HOSIDI·C·F: the Calydonian boar right, wounded by a spear and attacked by a hound.
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the moneyer as the son of Hosidius Geta the proscript (saved by his son), citing Appian and Dio (lib. XLVII). Notes the marble inscription C. HOSIDIVS MARCIANVS CVM SVIS PANTHEO SACRVM. He does NOT call the moneyer 'IIIvir monetalis' — that office is the AI's interpolation; Orsini simply says he struck the silver denarii ('qui argenteos denarios cusit'). Orsini makes no comment on the Diana/boar type.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Bust of Diana right, draped, with bow and quiver over shoulder
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: She-wolf right, suckling twins; CNOMIDI.F in exergue

coins_engraved.obverse: Bust of Diana right, draped, with bow and quiver over shoulder
coins_engraved.reverse: Wild boar (the Calydonian boar) attacked, walking/charging right; C.HOSIDI.C.F in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini includes this die variant as one of the two denarii he has seen ('duos tantum denarios... nobis uidere licuit'). He makes no separate iconographic comment on this coin beyond attributing it to the same moneyer, and does NOT discuss Diana devotion or a Calydonian boar myth. C. Hosidius Geta (Dio lib. LX) is the Claudian general who received triumphal honours — he is the moneyer's probable brother or cousin, not the moneyer himself described as 'tresvir monetalis.'
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Bust of Diana right, draped, with bow and quiver over shoulder
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Horseman galloping right with spear

completed.family_note: The Hosidii were a minor plebeian gens. C. Hosidius C.f. Geta served as tresvir monetalis c. 64 BC, striking denarii (Crawford 407/2) with a bust of Diana on the obverse and the Calydonian boar pierced by a spear and attacked by a hound on the reverse. The Diana/boar type references the mythological hunt of the Calydonian boar, in which Diana sent the monstrous boar to ravage Calydon. These denarii are well-engraved and relatively common in the Republican series. The family is also attested in marble inscriptions recording a C. Hosidius Marcianus.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Hosidia gens on one plate (p. 110) with two die variants. He cites Appian (lib. III, de bel. ciuil.) and Dio (lib. XLVII) for HOSIDIVS GETAE proscribed by the Triumvirs and saved by his son. He notes a scribal error in Dio's manuscripts ('ο'σ'ειδίον' for 'ο'σ'ίδιον'). He argues this proscribed Hosidius was perhaps ('fortasse') the father of the moneyer who struck the silver denarii. He then cites Dio (lib. LX) for C. Hosidius Geta who, though not consul, was awarded triumphal honours under Claudius for a near-defeat against enemies ('Donec C. Hosidius Geta cum propè in hostium potestatem uenisset, ita eos uicit, ut ei proptereà honores triumphales... dati fint'). He reproduces the marble inscription C. HOSIDIVS MAR / CIANVS CVM SVIS / PANTHEO / SACRVM. He makes NO iconographic comment on the Diana or Calydonian boar type whatsoever.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of bearded male right, hair flowing
coins_engraved.reverse: Naked warrior in fast biga (chariot) galloping right, holding spear and shield, driven by a charioteer; SASERN below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to the Sasernae (father and son) who wrote on agriculture. The obverse shows images of the gods that the Sasernae wished to illustrate on their denarii, relating to Gallic monuments.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head of bearded male right, hair flowing
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Pegasus flying right; SASERN below

coins_engraved.obverse: Draped female head, unhelmeted
coins_engraved.reverse: Diana standing facing/front, holding a stag by the antlers in one hand and a spear in the other; SASERNA at left, L.HOSTILIVS at right
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes the Diana of Ephesus on the reverse may reference Saserna's praetorship in the province of Asia. The obverse female head relates to Gallia or Victory.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head of Roma right, helmeted
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Minerva standing left, holding spear and shield

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted with plume
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory advancing, holding a caduceus and a trophy over the shoulder; SASERNA at left, L.HOSTILIVS at right
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini suggests the Victory on the reverse may refer to King Tullus Hostilius's triumphs over the Albans, from whom the Hostilii traced their descent.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head of Roma right, helmeted with plume
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Victory standing left, holding wreath and palm branch

completed.family_note: The Hostilii were an ancient gens claiming descent from King Tullus Hostilius, the third king of Rome. L. Hostilius Saserna struck a distinctive series of denarii (Crawford 448/1-3) c. 48 BC under Caesar's authority, featuring Gallic war types: a bearded Gallic captive (possibly Vercingetorix) on the obverse, a female Gallia with wild hair, and Diana of Ephesus on the reverse. These coins are among the most recognizable Caesarian imperatorial issues, with their vivid imagery of conquered Gaul. The Saserna cognomen is also associated with agricultural writers mentioned by Varro and Columella.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Hostilia gens on one plate (p. 111) with three denarii of L. Hostilius Saserna. He connects the family to King Tullus Hostilius, who gained Roman citizenship under Romulus ("ab Hosto quodam Hostilio Medullino... Romulo regnante Romanam Ciuitatem adeptus fuit"). For the Gallic types, Orsini identifies the Sasernae (father and son) as agricultural writers cited by Varro ("Sasernae, pater & filius; qui de agricultura scripserunt, nominantur a Varrone in libris de re rustica") — Columella is not mentioned. He identifies the SASERNA on the coin as the man Caesar left at Leptis with a garrison ("a Caesare Lepti cum praesidio relictus est, ut scribit Hirtius li.v. de bello Africo"). For the Diana of Ephesus, Orsini says it is an open question ("quaerendum est"), and only tentatively suggests it may relate to a Saserna praetorship in Asia ("fortasse autem Ephesia Diana ad eius Praeturam refertur, in qua prouinciam Asiam obtinuerit"). The Victory on the third coin he says may refer to Tullus Hostilius's triumphs over the Albans ("Victoria uero, ad Tulli regis de Albanis triumphos, quos egit Alba diruta, spectare poterit"). He cites Livy for the regal origins and Hirtius for the Caesarian context; Columella is not cited.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted
coins_engraved.reverse: The Dioscuri galloping right; ROMA below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this single coin to L. Iccium (the coin reads L.ITIO, but Orsini argues 'ut opinor' that ITIUM is an error for ICCIUM in the manuscripts of Hirtius — 'sic enim in uetuftiffimis codicibus pro ICCIUM, scriptum reperiri'). He identifies this L. Iccium as the addressee of Horace, Odes 1.29, and notes that Cicero in Philippics 3 also mentions a M. Iccium. Orsini says nothing about a turreted head, Cybele, or poor condition of the coin.

completed.family_note: The gens Itia is an extremely obscure family known only from a single coin of uncertain reading in Orsini's collection. No ancient literary source mentions the family by the name Itia, and Orsini himself believes the coin legend L.ITIO may correspond to L. Iccium — a figure addressed in Horace's Odes 1.29 and mentioned by Cicero in Philippics 3 as M. Iccium — the name Itium being an error for Iccium found in manuscripts of Hirtius's Bellum Gallicum. The family's inclusion in Orsini's work reflects his comprehensive approach to Roman numismatic prosopography.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Itia gens on one plate (p. 112) with a single coin signed L.ITIO. He argues ("ut opinor") that this should be read as L. Iccium, because in the oldest manuscripts of Hirtius the name appears as ICCIUM not ITIUM — a reading brought to his attention by Carolus Langius, who also sent him the coin example. Orsini quotes Horace, Odes 1.29 (the ode addressed to L.ITIVM / ICCIUM) in full. He also cites Cicero, Philippics 3, where a M. Iccium is mentioned ("Cicero in lib.III Philipp. nominat M. quendam Iccium"). The entry is brief and tentative, but Orsini does cite Horace and Cicero; it is not the case that he relies solely on the coin legend.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Mars right, wearing winged helmet; X (value mark) behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Two horsemen (Dioscuri) galloping right, each holding spear; L.IVLI below, ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this first denarius to L. Iulius Caesar, consul with P. Rutilius Lupus. Notes the XVI numeral refers to the value (denarius = 16 asses after the reduction).

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right, wearing winged helmet; corn-ear (spica) behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory in biga right, holding reins; L·IVLI below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini presents this as the second denarius, attributable to a son of the L. Iulius of coin 1, who was Consul with L. Marcius Figulus ('Secundus denarius ad L.IVLIVM huius filium potest pertinere, qui Consul fuit cum L. Marcio Figulo anno DCLXXXIX'). He infers this moneyer was an Aedile from the spica (grain ear) symbol ('ex symbolo spicae, quo Aediles utebantur, intelligere possumus'). The reverse bears a Cupid chariot ('Cupidinis currus'), used to indicate the Iulian family's origin from Iulus, son of Aeneas, who was born of Venus ('ad indicandam Iuliae gentis originem, quae a Iulo Aeneae, qui Venere genitus est, filio principium habuisse dicitur').

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Mars left (Mars or Roma); D to left and right of head; CAESAR behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Venus in biga of Cupids left, holding sceptre and reins; L·IVLI·L·F below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to L. Iulius, son of the preceding, who served in Africa under Cato as Pro Quaestor during the civil war. The Venus with Cupid references the Iulian family's divine descent.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right, wearing winged helmet; mark behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Cupid driving biga right; SEX.IVLI / CAESAR in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini (p. 113-114) identifies the fourth coin as Sex. Iulius Caesar, noting many of the Caesarum family used this praenomen ('difficile est, quis fuerit affirmare'), and suggests he may be the consul with L. Marcius Philippus anno DCXLII. Orsini makes no specific statement about the reverse type of this coin (the plate shows ROMA/biga). The Venus/Cupid framing belongs to coins 2-3 in the same table; it is not applied by Orsini to coin 4.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head of Venus right, wearing diadem; X (or star) behind
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Cupid driving biga right; SEX.IVLI / CAESAR in exergue

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head of Julius Caesar right, wreathed; CAESAR.DICT behind, PERPETVO before
coins_engraved.reverse: Venus standing left, holding Victory and sceptre; L.BVCA in field
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes this denarius was struck by L. Aemilius Buca as IIIIvir monetalis, with Caesar as Dictator in perpetuum. The Venus Genetrix or Victrix on the reverse is described by Orsini as **standing** ('Veneris Genetricis siue Victricis simulacrum **stans**'), not seated. The standing Venus Genetrix relates to Caesar's claim of divine Iulian ancestry from Venus through Aeneas.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Laureate head of Julius Caesar right, wreathed; CAESAR.DICT behind, PERPETVO before
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Venus seated left, holding Victory and sceptre; L.BVCA in field
coins_engraved.specimen_shared_reason: same catalogue type cross-listed under multiple gentes (joint-moneyer issue or sub-variant); one museum specimen serves all

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head of Julius Caesar right; CAESAR.DICT.PERPETVO around
coins_engraved.reverse: Globe, crossed fasces and caduceus, axe, and clasped hands; L.BVCA.L below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini interprets the reverse symbols: the globe represents Caesar's world dominion; fasces signify justice; the caduceus peace; clasped hands concordia; and the securis religion. These were virtues Caesar promised the Roman people.

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head of Julius Caesar right; CAESAR.IM around
coins_engraved.reverse: Standing draped female figure (Venus Genetrix) holding sceptre; BVCA / COSSERTIVS (or CREMITIVS) around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes the Venus Genetrix on the reverse, standing with trophy, references the Iulian family's divine origin from Venus through Aeneas.
coins_engraved.specimen_shared_reason: same catalogue type cross-listed under multiple gentes (joint-moneyer issue or sub-variant); one museum specimen serves all

coins_engraved.obverse: Wreathed head right; CAESAR·IMP text on left side
coins_engraved.reverse: Text arrangement: L·AEMI at top right, then LI·VS below, then BVCA at bottom; small objects visible between text (clasped hands, fasces)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini interprets the clasped hands as symbolizing concordia. Notes the Augural lituus is added to indicate Caesar's sacerdotal office.
coins_engraved.observed_obverse: Laureate head of Julius Caesar right; CAESAR.IMP around
coins_engraved.observed_reverse: Clasped hands; IIII.VIR / L.AEMI / LIVS / BVCA around

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate and veiled head of Julius Caesar right; DICT.PERPETVO.CAESAR around
coins_engraved.reverse: Standing female figure (Venus) holding sceptre and Victory on globe; L.BVCA at right
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses Caesar's golden laurel wreath decreed by the Senate on this L. Aemilius Buca issue showing Caesar as DICT PERPETVO, and notes the golden chair (sella aurea) placed in the theatre as another of Caesar's unprecedented honors. He cites Suetonius and Dio Cassius on these extraordinary distinctions.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head of Julius Caesar right; CAESAR.III.VIR.R.P.C around
coins_engraved.reverse: Inscribed tablet/plaque reading CAES.DIC.PER, surmounted by a small wreath, resting on supports above two crossed cornucopiae
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the two Cossutius Maridianus coins together: one bears CAESAR PARENS PATRIAE and the other CAESAR DICT. PERPETVO ('in eorum altero CAESAR PARENS PATRIAE, in altero CAESAR DICT. PERPETVO inscriptum est'). The PARENS PATRIAE coin prompts his extended discussion citing Cicero, Suetonius, and Livy on when this honor was conferred. He does not mention a curule chair for these coins, and does not connect them to Octavian as IIIvir.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Bare head of Julius Caesar right; CAESAR.III.VIR.R.P.C around
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Trophy on platform (suggestus) decorated with prows; CAES.DIC.PER below

coins_engraved.obverse: Diademed bust of Venus right; C·CAESAR IMP COS ITER
coins_engraved.reverse: Trinacrus standing facing, holding triskeles, right foot on prow; A·ALLIENVS PRO COS
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to Allienus, Praetor governing Sicily with proconsular authority, struck in Caesar's second consulship with P. Servilius Isauricus, year 705 AUC ('Quintus denarius ab ALLIENO Praetore, qui Siciliam proconsu lari potestate obtinebat, signatus est Caesare II Consule cum P. Seruilio Isaurico anno DCCV'). On the reverse, Orsini sees Minerva's image ('Simulacrum Mineruae in altera nummi parte'), holding Victory alongside a snake, which he connects to the tradition that Minerva was called παρεδρον of Victory, citing Phurnutus. He notes the coin was struck the same year Caesar went to Africa.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Bare head of Julius Caesar right, laureate; IMP.CAESAR / C.CAESAR around
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Seated female figure (Pax or Concordia) left, holding caduceus and cornucopia; S.NVMITIVS / PRO.CO around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment_ai: Orsini notes the Aeneas carrying Anchises references the Iulian family's Trojan ancestry. Caesar struck this during his African campaign.
coins_engraved.specimen_shared_reason: same catalogue type cross-listed under multiple gentes (joint-moneyer issue or sub-variant); one museum specimen serves all

coins_engraved.obverse: Bust of Victory right, draped; CAESAR·DIC·TER legend; border of dots.
coins_engraved.reverse: Minerva standing left, holding trophy over shoulder, spear and shield with gorgoneion, snake before; C·CLOVI PRAEF legend; border of dots.
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes the Victory image and African trophy reference Caesar's victory over Juba in Africa. The bronze likely a colonial or praefectural issue.
coins_engraved.observed_obverse: Head of Venus or Diva Iulia right, with star above head; CAESAR behind
coins_engraved.observed_reverse: Trophy with arms; figure (Victory or captive) at base; CAESAR around; PRAEF (or similar) in field

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head of Julius Caesar right; COS.TERT / DICT.ITER around
coins_engraved.reverse: Augural implements: lituus, capis (jug), and axe; AVGVR / PONT.MAX around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses Caesar's Pontificatus Maximus and augural implements. Notes the lituus and capis indicate Caesar's priestly offices as both Pontifex Maximus and Augur.

coins_engraved.obverse: Elephant walking right, trampling serpent or dragon; CAESAR below
coins_engraved.reverse: Priestly implements: simpulum, aspergillum, axe (securis), and apex (priest's cap)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini says the elephant in this coin's reverse may relate to a beast-hunt spectacle Caesar put on in the arena ('licet ad elephantum quoque spectaculum in harena a Caesare editum referri possit; de quo meminit Plinius lib.viii.cap.vii'). The priestly implements (Augurat and Pontificat insignia) are discussed separately in connection with the adjacent coin (coin 13), not this one: 'De Caesaris Auguratu & Pontificatu Maximo, quorum insignia in primo denario notata sunt.' Orsini does not describe the elephant as symbolizing 'triumph over evil or the barbarian world,' nor does he connect this type to the outbreak of the civil war.

coins_engraved.obverse: Female head right (Venus), with hair tied back
coins_engraved.reverse: Aeneas walking left, carrying Anchises on shoulder and holding palladium; CAESAR at right
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes the Venus head indicates the Iulian family's origin, and Aeneas carrying Anchises with the palladium is the central symbol of Iulian pietas and Trojan descent.

coins_engraved.obverse: Female head right (Venus), wearing diadem, hair in knot at back
coins_engraved.reverse: Trophy of Gallic arms with oval shield and carnyx; two seated captives at base; CAESAR below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini interprets the trophy with captives as referencing Caesar's victories over the Gauls and Germans. The trophies and bound captives symbolize his military triumphs.

coins_engraved.obverse: Female head left (Venus or Pietas), hair in bun
coins_engraved.reverse: Trophy of arms with shields; seated captive at base; CAESAR at right
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes the Gallic trophy type and connects the trophies erected by Caesar after defeating Pharnaces, citing Dio. He treats the female head on the obverse as Venus or Pietas and discusses the seated captive at the base of the trophy as a representation of Caesar's eastern victories.

coins_engraved.obverse: Female head right wearing oak-wreath and diadem
coins_engraved.reverse: Gallic trophy: standing armored figure with horned helmet, oval shield (with trident device), and axe; CAESAR text below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini (p. 117) identifies coins 4-6 of this table (coins 16-18 in the concordance) as referencing Caesar's victories and trophies over the Gauls, Germans, and other peoples: 'Quartus, quintus, & sextus huius tabellae denarii referunt, ut opinor, victorias ac trophaea de Galleis, & Germaneis, aliisque gentibus à Caesare deuictis.' No carnyx or specific Gallic shields are mentioned by Orsini. The Venus image in these coins references the Iulian family's divine origin.
coins_engraved.observed_obverse: Diademed female head right (Venus), with star above; wreath or crown in hair
coins_engraved.observed_reverse: Trophy of arms with shield and carnyx; figure (Victory or priest) standing beside it, holding staff; CAE / SAR in field

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head of Julius Caesar right
coins_engraved.reverse: Cult/sacrificial implements (cornucopia, caduceus, apex, rudder) above a globe; L·MVSSIDIVS·LONGVS around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to L. Mussidius Longus as IIIIvir monetae cudendae. On the reverse, he says, are the symbols of goddesses ('Dearum symbola') in whose honor the Senate had dedicated temples to Caesar: CLEMENTIA, AEQVITAS, LIBERTAS PVBLICA, CONCORDIA NOVA, and FELICITAS ('eae uero sunt: CLEMENTIA, AEQVITAS, LIBERTAS PVBLICA, CONCORDIA NOVA; & FELICITAS'). Concordia and Felicitas are symbolized by cornucopia and caduceus; a ship's rudder and globe refer to imperial rule; an apex (priest's cap) is added for Caesar's priestly office ('ad indicandum Caesaris sacerdotium... Flamen Dialis'). Orsini cites Plutarch (in Caesare) and Dio lib.xliii.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Bare head of Julius Caesar right
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Shield and crossed spears; L.MVSSIDIVS.LONGVS around

coins_engraved.obverse: Bust of Victory, right, draped. C.CAES / DIC.TER around
coins_engraved.reverse: Praefericulum (sacrificial jug) with handle; L.PLANC / PRAEF.VR around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to L. Munatius Plancus as Praefectus Urbi under Caesar. Notes the Maximi Pontificatus insignia and Victory image on the reverse.
coins_engraved.specimen_shared_reason: same catalogue type cross-listed under multiple gentes (joint-moneyer issue or sub-variant); one museum specimen serves all

coins_engraved.obverse: Veiled head right; C·CAESAR COS·TER around
coins_engraved.reverse: Capis (jug) and lituus (augural staff); A·HIRTIVS·PR around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini does not describe a coin struck by A. Hirtius as moneyer in his Iulia section. Hirtius appears in Orsini only as a cited author (Hirtius lib.v de bello Africo, Hirtius lib.v de bello Gallico). No coin of A. Hirtius as moneyer is discussed in any of Orsini's Iulia tables (pp. 113–124).
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Laureate head right; legend CAESAR COS TER around
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Sacrificial implements: capis (jug) and lituus (augural staff); legend AVGVR PONT MAX around, PR below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment_ai: [QA: this note may describe a different type — flagged for review] Orsini attributes to P. Sepullius Macer and notes the priestly implements (culullus, aspergillum, axe, apex) signify Caesar's office as Pontifex Maximus.

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head right, no visible legend
coins_engraved.reverse: Legionary eagle (aquila) between two military standards; legend Q DESIG around, TI SEMPRONIVS above / GRACCVS in exergue, S C in field
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to Ti. Sempronius Graccus as Quaestor designatus. The denarius pertains to the colony of Cassilinum, deduced anno DCXCIII by Caesar and Bibulus. coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini (p. 118) discusses the fifth and sixth coins of this table as both struck by P. Sepullius Macer: the fifth (quintus) with a comet added = struck after Caesar's death ('mortuo iam Caesare'); the sixth (sextum), in which Caesar's image appears in Pontifical dress = struck while Caesar was still alive ('uiuente adhuc Caesare'). Orsini's coin 23 (sixth of the table) = ante mortem, Venus sedens with standard inscriptions.

completed.family_note: The Iulii were an ancient patrician gens claiming descent from Iulus (Ascanius), son of Aeneas, and ultimately from Venus herself. In the Republic, L. Iulius Caesar and Sex. Iulius Caesar struck denarii (Crawford 224/1, 258/1, 320/1, 323/1), several with Venus and Cupid reverse types reflecting the family's divine genealogy. C. Julius Caesar's own extensive coinage includes the famous elephant/priestly implements type (Crawford 443/1), Venus/Aeneas (Crawford 458/1) and Venus/trophy (Crawford 468/1) types, and portrait denarii struck by his IIIIviri monetales (L. Aemilius Buca, M. Mettius, P. Sepullius Macer, C. Cossutius Maridianus) in 44 BC. Posthumous Divus Julius types (Crawford 494, 526) were struck by the triumvirs, and Augustan commemoratives include the famous sidus Iulium (comet) denarius (RIC I 37a).
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini devotes seven plates (pp. 113–124) to the Iulia gens, making it by far the most extensively treated family in his work. He traces the Iulian genealogy from Iulus/Aeneas and Venus through the Republic, citing Virgil (Aeneid, Eclogues), Suetonius, Dio, Appianus, Livy, Cicero, Plutarch, and Pliny extensively. For the Republican denarii, he discusses the Venus/Cupid reverse imagery as evidence of divine descent, quoting Caesar's own funeral oration for his aunt Julia ('Amitae meae Iuliae maternum genus ab Regibus ortum: paternum cum Diis immortalibus coniunctum est... a Venere Iulii, cuius gentis familia est nostra'). Caesar's dictatorial coinage receives detailed treatment: Orsini discusses the elephant type, the DICT PERPETVO title, the sella aurea (golden chair decreed to Caesar), the symbols on the sixth coin (globe=imperium, fasces=iustitia, manus=concordia, caduceus=pax, securis=religio), and the PARENS PATRIAE inscription; he cites Cicero (ep. ad Cassium), Suetonius, Livy, Dio, and Appianus. The posthumous issues prompt extensive discussions of Caesar's deification, the sidus Iulium (comet) that appeared after his death ('stella crinita per septem continuos dies fulsit'), citing Suetonius, Pliny, Dio, and Virgil's Eclogues. Orsini does not explicitly treat the EID MAR type within the Iulia section, nor does he specifically frame Octavian's DIVI FILIVS title as a political claim in this section.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right (generic Republican obverse)
coins_engraved.reverse: Globe, caduceus, and ship’s rudder; legend BRVTVS·IMP
coins_engraved.identification: Renaissance fantasy / pasticcio bearing BRVTVS·IMP — no genuine ancient prototype (Caesarian globe-reverse of L. Mussidius Longus, Crawford 494/39 = Babelon Mussidia 58)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini (Familiae Romanae, p. 132, “Quintus denarius”) attributes this denarius to M. Brutus, reading the globe, caduceus and ship’s rudder as “orbis terrarum pace.” No genuine coin of M. Brutus bears this type. The globe-rudder-caduceus reverse belongs to L. Mussidius Longus (Crawford 494/39 = Babelon, Mussidia 58: head of Caesar / rudder, globe, cornucopia, winged caduceus, apex), where the globe is a Caesarian symbol of the calendar reform; the coinage of Brutus contains no globe or comparable motif (verified against Babelon, gens Iunia). The engraving therefore records a Renaissance fantasy or pasticcio — the Caesarian/Mussidian globe-reverse (minus its cornucopia) paired with a generic Roma head and relabelled BRVTVS·IMP, internally incoherent in its symbolism and unrecorded in any catalogue. It is the one entry in the corpus with no genuine ancient prototype. Moreover, genuine BRVTVS·IMP issues always name the magistrate who struck them — Brutus’s lieutenants in the East before Philippi (Babelon: Lentulus Spinther, Flavius Hemicillus, Pedanius Costa, L. Plaetorius Cestianus, M. Servilius, C. Servilius Casca), all represented in this corpus under their own gentes (Cornelia 26, Flavia 2, Pedania 1, Plaetoria 7–8, Servilia 1/9) and among the genuine Brutus coins of this very plate (Iunia 11–22). The present piece names no magistrate at all — a further mark of fabrication. The mistake here is the forger’s, not Orsini’s: he recorded in good faith a fabrication already circulating in a sixteenth-century cabinet — so this piece stands apart from his own identification errors.

completed.family_note: The Iunii were one of Rome's most prominent plebeian gentes, with two major branches: the Bruti and the Silani. L. Junius Brutus traditionally founded the Republic by expelling Tarquinius Superbus in 509 BC, and the family maintained a powerful ideology of tyrannicide throughout its history. M. Junius Brutus struck iconic denarii (Crawford 433/1-2, 54 BC) featuring his ancestors L. Brutus and C. Servilius Ahala, and later the famous EID MAR type (Crawford 508/3, 43-42 BC). The Silanus branch produced multiple Republican moneyers (Crawford 220/1, 285/2, 337/1-3). D. Junius Brutus Albinus struck denarii (Crawford 450/1-3, 451/1) before joining Caesar's assassination conspiracy.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini devotes four plates (pp. 125–132) to the Iunia gens, treating it as one of the most important families. He carefully distinguishes the Bruti and Silani branches, tracing the tyrannicide ideology from L. Brutus's expulsion of the kings through C. Servilius Ahala's killing of Sp. Maelius (discussed under the Seruilia gens) to M. Brutus's assassination of Caesar. For the EID MAR denarius, Orsini discusses the pileus (cap of liberty) and two daggers as symbols of the Ides of March, citing Suetonius, Cicero (Philippics), and Appianus. He cites Virgil (Aen. VI) for the lictors coin. For the Ludi Apollinares he draws on Livy (lib. XXV, XXIX) and Plutarch. For the Silanus branch, he notes the adoption connection to the Manlii Torquati. D. Brutus Albinus receives separate treatment: Orsini notes his adoption by 'A. Postumio Bruti F.' (not 'A. Postumius Albinus') and cites Plutarch (Caesar) and Velleius for his career and betrayal.

coins_engraved.reverse: Horse standing right; A below or in field
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes Q. Labienus was son of T. Labienus, Caesar's legate. He was sent to Orodes (the Parthian king) before the battle of Philippi; after the Republican defeat he remained with the Parthians, invaded Syria and Asia Minor with Parthian support, and took the cognomen Parthicus in a manner entirely contrary to Roman custom ('ratione a more Romano diuersissima'). Orsini cites Dio (lib. XLVIII) and Appianus (in Parthico) for this account. He does not state that Q. Labienus was defeated and killed in this section.

completed.family_note: The Labieni were a plebeian gens. T. Labienus was first a Tribune of the People who prosecuted C. Rabirius (accused, at Caesar's instigation, of killing Q. Labienus alongside Saturninus); Cicero's Pro Rabirio, Orosius lib. V cap. XVII, and Dio lib. XXXVII are the sources. He then joined Caesar's side as a legate in Gaul (Caesar, Bellum Gallicum lib. I–III), before becoming Pompeian and rebuilding the town of Cingulum. He was defeated fighting against Caesar (Hirtius, Bellum Africum lib. V). His son Q. Labienus struck this plate's single denarius. Orsini notes that Q. Labienus's praenomen would have remained unknown had an ancient coin not supplied it, since confusion between T. the father and Q. the son had misled earlier writers. Q. Labienus was sent to Orodes before the battle of Philippi; after the defeat he remained with the Parthians and later invaded Syria and Asia Minor with Parthian support, taking the cognomen PARTHICVS in a manner Orsini calls entirely contrary to Roman custom. Orsini cites Dio (lib. XLVIII) and Appianus (in Parthico) for this account. Orsini does not name P. Ventidius Bassus or give a date for Q. Labienus's defeat in this section.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Labiena gens on one plate (p. 133) with a single denarius. He provides an account of both T. Labienus (Tribune, Caesar's legate, then Pompeian; sources: Cicero, Orosius, Dio, Caesar, Hirtius) and Q. Labienus his son. He notes that the coin's praenomen resolved a long-standing confusion between father and son. He describes Q. Labienus being sent to Orodes before Philippi, remaining with the Parthians after the Republican defeat, invading Syria and Asia Minor with Parthian cavalry, and adopting the cognomen PARTHICVS 'ratione a more Romano diuersissima.' He cites Dio (lib. XLVIII) and Appianus (in Parthico) for Q. Labienus's career. Plutarch is not cited in the Labiena section. Orsini focuses on the coin legend (PARTHICVS) rather than on the horse type on the reverse.

completed.family_note: The Licinii were one of the most prolific plebeian gentes at Rome, with numerous branches including the Murenae, Crassi, Nervae, and Stolones. C. Licinius Stolo co-authored the landmark Licinian-Sextian laws of 367 BC opening the consulship to plebeians. The Republican moneyers include L. Licinius Murena (consul with D. Iunius Silanus, anno DCXCI), P. Licinius Crassus M.f. (Caesar's cavalry commander in Gaul), P. Licinius Nerva (with the famous voting-scene reverse), and C. Licinius Macer (orator and historian, father of the poet Calvus). Augustan issues include A. Licinius Nerva Silianus (adopted by P. Silius, consul anno DCCLIX) and P. Licinius Stolo (IIIvir monetalis under Augustus). The African campaign denarii signed by P. Licinius Crassus Iunianus as Scipio's legate Propraetore are notable imperatorial issues.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini devotes three plates (pp. 134, 137, 139) to the Licinia gens, reflecting its extraordinary size and political importance. He opens by listing four numismatic branches: Murenae, Crassi, Nervae, and Stolones ('MVRENAE tantum, CRASSI, NERVAE, & STOLONES in numis'). For P. Licinius Nerva, Orsini discusses at length the voting scene on the reverse, identifying the Septa, Pontes (angustiores per the law of C. Marius, Tr.Pl. anno DCXXXIII), Cista, and Diribitor. He draws on Cicero (de leg.), Plutarch in Mario, Dionysius, and Servius for this civic-procedure excursus. C. Licinius Macer receives attention as the orator and historian ('Licinii Calui poetae pater') whom Plutarch records committed suicide after conviction de pecuniis repetundis; Valerius Maximus lib. IX cap. XII gives a variant account. The Augustan issues prompt discussions of the ancilia (Salii shields) cited from Lucanus lib. I and Sex. Pompeius, with Orsini speculating P. Licinius Stolo may have been one of the twelve Salii. For the African campaign coins, Orsini discusses P. Licinius Crassus Iunianus's adoption from the Iunia family and his role as Scipio's legate propraetore, calling him Crassus Iunianus after the adoption formula ('ex uistata illa adoptionum formula, Crassus Iunianus appellatus esse').

coins_engraved.obverse: Head right, bare
coins_engraved.reverse: Modius with wheat ears; REGVLVS below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies L. Livineius Regulus as IIIvir monetalis and son of L. Regulus. Notes he was also Aedilis Curulis, as indicated by the curule chair and modius types on several of his coins.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of man right, bare
coins_engraved.reverse: Hunt/venatio scene: animals and figures in combat (no single standing Diana, no bow); REGVLVS in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini infers from the animal-combat scene that Regulus staged venationes during his aedileship ('quem Aedilem Curulem fuisse, ex iis quae in altera parte... expressa sunt, intelligere possumus'). He does not cite Pliny, and does not connect the scene to spectacles given by Caesar.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head of man right, bare
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Diana standing right, holding bow; hound at feet right; GREGVLVS below

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of male figure right, bare; legend around
coins_engraved.reverse: Two curule chairs (bisellium) between standards/columns under a triangular roof element; REGVLVS·F above, PRAEF·VR below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes the PRAEF·VR inscription indicates Regulus also served as Praefectus Urbi. The curule chair and fasces denote his magistracy.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head of male figure right, bare; legend around
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Temple or shrine with two columns and triangular pediment; legend around with REGVLVS and PRAEF·VR visible

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare male head right; REGVLVS above, PR below
coins_engraved.reverse: Ceremonial curule seats with two upright torches; L·LIVINEIVS above, REGVLVS below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini reads this as another die variant of the L. Livineius Regulus aedilician series. He does not cite Pliny for the spectacle scenes; Pliny does not appear in the Livineia section.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head of male figure right, bare; legend around
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Sacrificial scene with altar or table, vertical lines above representing incense or flames; legend around

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare male head right (portrait)
coins_engraved.reverse: Bisellium on platform; L.LIVINEIVS / REGVLVS below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini reads the PRAEF·VR inscription as confirming the Praefectura Urbi ('Eundem autem Regulum Vrbis etiam Praefectum aliquando fuisse, ex tertii denarii inscriptione apparet'). The seat shown is a Curuli sella (curule chair), not a bisellium.

coins_engraved.obverse: Male head right with attributes (possibly laureate); caduceus behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Bull charging right; L.LIVINEIVS / REGVLVS below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini interprets the bull as referencing venationes (beast hunts) staged during L. Livineius Regulus's aedileship under Caesar.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head of Octavian (Caesar) right; C·CAESAR·III·VIR·R·P·C (IIII·VIR / CAESAR) around.
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory standing right, holding wreath and palm-branch; L·LIVINEIVS / REGVLVS around.
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes this denarius pertains to L. Livineius Regulus, son of L. Regulus, whom he considers the same person described by Cornelius Tacitus and Dio.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Bare male head right (portrait); CAESAR around; laureate
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Victory (holding cornucopiae or other attribute); REGVL[VS] / L.LIVINEIVS around

coins_engraved.obverse: Clasped right hands holding a caduceus; REGVLVS PVLCHER around
coins_engraved.reverse: Large S C; III·VIR·A·A·A·F·F around
coins_engraved.moneyer: L. Livineius Regulus / P. Sulpicius Plautius Hericlianus / C. Plotius Rufus
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this bronze to L. Livineius Regulus, noting the animal (lion or panther) may also commemorate arena spectacles. Tacitus lib. III mentions Livineium Regulum as accused in Germanicus's death.
coins_engraved.observed_obverse: Map or plan view of land/region; REGVLVS.PVLCHRA around border
coins_engraved.observed_reverse: Large S C in center; III.VIR around
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Radiate bust of Sol facing, draped
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Shrine of Venus Cloacina; CLOACIN L·MVSSIDIVS·LONGVS

completed.family_note: The Livineii were a minor plebeian gens known only from the Regulorum family, as Orsini notes ('una tantum REGVLORVM familia'). L. Livineius Regulus (the elder) served as Aedilis Curulis and Praefectus Urbi, identified from coin inscriptions and cited in Cicero (ep. LX, lib. XIII) and Hirtium (lib. V de bello Africo). His son L. Livineius Regulus served as IIIvir monetalis under Augustus with Sisenna and Pulcher, but was subsequently removed from the senate by Augustus (Dio lib. LIII). Tacitus lib. III records a Livineius Regulus accused in connection with the death of Germanicus; Tacitus lib. XIV records a gladiatorial spectacle under Nero. The family's varied coin types document the elder Regulus's multiple magistracies.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini devotes two plates (pp. 140–141) to the Livineia gens. He identifies L. Livineius Regulus (elder) as Aedilis Curulis — inferred from the curule chair, grain-ears (spicae), and modius on the coins — and as Praefectus Urbi, confirmed by the PRAEF·VR inscription on the third coin. For the Aedilis Curulis identification Orsini cites Cicero (ep. LX, lib. XIII naming L. Livineius Trypho, libertus of L. Regulus) and Hirtium in lib. V de bello Africo. He notes the Praetura of the elder Regulus from the third and fourth coin inscriptions. The younger Regulus struck coins as IIIvir monetalis under Augustus with Sisenna and Pulcher; Orsini cites Dio lib. LIII for his subsequent removal from the senate. Tacitus lib. III is cited for his role at Piso's trial in Germanicus's death; Tacitus lib. XIV for a gladiatorial spectacle under Nero. Orsini does not cite Pliny, and does not connect the animal-combat scenes to spectacles given by Caesar.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Janus left and right, bearded
coins_engraved.reverse: Prow of galley right; C·CASSI above, C·SALIN below
coins_engraved.moneyer: L. Cassius and L. Livius Salinator
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes only one coin of the Salinator family appears in this tabella, as a bronze (aereus nummus). The coin legend reads C·CASSI / L·SALIN (visible in plate). Livy lib. XXXIX mentions a Livius who invented the cognomen Salinator by imposing a salt tax during a censorship. Orsini cannot identify which L. Salinator struck this coin.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head of Janus left and right, bearded
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Prow of galley right; C·CASSI above, L·SALIN below

completed.family_note: The Livii were a plebeian gens, with only the Salinatorvm family attested in numismatic evidence. The identity of the specific L. Salinator who struck the coin is unknown to Orsini ('L. is SALINATOR quis fuerit, quóue tempore uixerit, non dum apud scriptores inuenire potui'). Livy lib. XXXIX records a Livius who earned the cognomen Salinator by imposing a salt tax (vectigal) during a censorship.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Livia gens on one plate (p. 142) with a single bronze coin. He acknowledges deep uncertainty: he cannot identify which L. Salinator this was or when he lived ('non dum apud scriptores inuenire potui'), and notes that no member of this family using the praenomen Lucius is recorded in ancient monuments. His sole literary citation is Livy lib. XXXIX, where a Livius who imposed a salt tax (vectigal) during a censorship received the cognomen Salinator. Orsini does not discuss M. Livius Salinator's victory at the Metaurus, nor does he cite Livy lib. XXIX.

coins_engraved.obverse: Male head right (portrait); HONORIS behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Bisellium or sella curulis on platform; PALIKanvs around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to M. Lollius Palicanus, tribune of the plebs whom Valerius Maximus calls a seditious man. The Rostra on the reverse reference the speaker's platform in the Forum where Palicanus agitated for restoration of tribunician power.

coins_engraved.obverse: Female head right (Libertas); LIBERTAS around
coins_engraved.reverse: Rostra (speaker's platform) with ship prow; PALIKANUS below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes the Libertas head and Rostra celebrate the restoration of tribunician power under Pompey. Livy and Varro describe the Rostra as a platform adorned with ship prows captured from enemies.

completed.family_note: The Lollii were a plebeian gens. M. Lollius Palicanus served as Tribune of the Plebs and vigorously championed the restoration of full tribunician power, which had been curtailed by Sulla; Valerius Maximus calls him a seditious man. His denarii feature the Rostra (speaker's platform) and Libertas or Honos head. Orsini connects the imagery to Pompey's eventual restoration of tribunician power, citing Livy, Varro, Asconius, and Dio (lib. XXXVI). Orsini also identifies a second denarius as belonging to M. Lollius Palicanus as Aedilis Curulis, inferred from the curule chair and grain-ears on the reverse. Orsini does not mention a consulship for any member of the gens.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Lollia gens on one plate (p. 143) with two denarii. He identifies M. Lollius Palicanus as tribune of the plebs, citing Valerius Maximus who calls him a seditious man. Orsini interprets the Rostra on the reverse as the speaker's platform in the Forum where Palicanus agitated for the restoration of tribunician power curtailed by Sulla. He also cites Livy and Varro for descriptions of the Rostra as a platform adorned with ship prows captured from enemies. The Libertas head on the second coin's obverse receives attention as a symbol of the political freedom Palicanus championed. Orsini connects the imagery to Pompey's eventual restoration of tribunician power in 70 BC.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory in biga right; M.LVCILI below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini tentatively identifies M. Lucilius Rufus as possibly the tribune of the plebs who proposed making Pompey dictator (Plutarch in Pompeio). He separately notes a different Lucilius ('alterius Lucilii') who at Philippi offered himself to the enemy in place of Brutus (Plutarch in Bruto and Antonio) — Orsini does not assert these are the same person. The marks A.PV. signify argento publico ('significant argento publico').

completed.family_note: The Lucilii were a gens from Suessa Aurunca in Campania, best known for the satirist C. Lucilius (c. 180-103 BC), who founded the genre of Roman verse satire. M. Lucilius Rufus struck denarii (Crawford 324/1) c. 101 BC with a helmeted Roma head and Victory driving a biga on the reverse. The coins bear the mark A.PV (argento publico), indicating they were struck from public silver. A later Lucilius is known from Plutarch's account of the Battle of Philippi, where he sacrificed himself for Brutus.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Lucilia gens on one plate (p. 144) with a single denarius. He notes that of Lucilius Ruforum there is no mention in the sources ('RVFORVM autem nulla, quod sciam, mentio extat'), then identifies M. Lucilius Rufus tentatively as the tribune of the plebs who proposed making Pompey dictator (citing Plutarch in Pompeio). He separately mentions a second, different Lucilius — 'alterius Lucilii' — whom Plutarch in Bruto and Antonio records as offering himself to the enemy at Philippi in place of Brutus. These are two distinct persons; Orsini does not identify the moneyer with the Philippi hero. He correctly reads A.PV. as argento publico ('significant argento publico'). He does not discuss the satirist C. Lucilius.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Roma left, helmeted
coins_engraved.reverse: The Dioscuri on horseback right; CN LVCR in exergue, ROMA below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to Cn. Lucretius Trio and suggests the cognomen Trio derives from the Triones (the seven stars of Ursa Major/the Plough), which appear on the later coins of this family.

coins_engraved.obverse: Radiate head of Sol right
coins_engraved.reverse: Crescent moon with stars around; TRIO above, L·LVCRETI below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini explains the seven stars represent the Triones (Septentriones/Ursa Major), a punning reference to the cognomen Trio. Varro in De Lingua Latina explains the etymology of Triones from ploughing oxen.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head of male figure right, laureate
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Crescent moon with stars around; TRIO above, LVCRBTI below

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate male head right
coins_engraved.reverse: Crescent moon above; stars around; TRIO in center
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the Triones (the seven stars of Ursa Major) imagery on this L. Lucretius Trio coin, citing Varro's De Lingua Latina for the etymology of Triones from ploughing oxen (tri + ones), and referencing Homer and Agellius (Aulus Gellius) for descriptions of the seven stars near the celestial pole. He derives the moneyer's cognomen Trio from this constellation.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head of Roma right, helmeted with plume
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Crescent moon above; stars around; TRIO in center

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head of Neptune right; trident behind; control numeral above
coins_engraved.reverse: Infant Genius (Cupid) seated on dolphin right; L·LVCRETI / TRIO
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes Neptune with trident and Cupid on dolphin on this coin but explicitly states he is uncertain what they signify ('mihi quidem incertum quò spectent'). He tentatively suggests, since the same types appear on M. Cordius Rufus's denarius and others, that they may indicate the Julian family's origin ('in Caesaris gratiam, ad indicandam Iuliae gentis originem'). He does not say 'from Venus through the sea.'

completed.family_note: The Lucretii were a patrician gens of great antiquity; Sp. Lucretius Tricipitinus was among the first consuls of the Republic, and the legendary Lucretia whose violation led to the expulsion of the kings bore this name. Cn. Lucretius Trio struck denarii (Crawford 237/1) c. 136 BC with varied types including Roma/Dioscuri, Sol/crescent with seven stars, and Neptune/river god. The seven stars on the crescent represent the Triones (Septentriones/Ursa Major), a punning reference to the cognomen Trio. The poet T. Lucretius Carus, author of De Rerum Natura, also belonged to this gens.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini devotes one plate (p. 145) to the Lucretia gens with four denarii. He identifies Cn. Lucretius Trio as the moneyer of the first coin and probable father of L. Lucretius Trio (second and fourth coins); the third coin was restored by the emperor Trajan many years later ('nam tertius ab Imp. Traiano, multis post annis restitutus est'). His most significant contribution is the etymology of the cognomen Trio from the seven stars of Ursa Major, citing Varro lib. VI de lingua Latina (ploughing oxen / triones as ground-workers) and Agellius (Aulus Gellius) lib. II cap. XXI for the grammarians' view that Septentrionem derives from the number of stars. For the fourth coin, Orsini notes Neptune and Cupid on dolphin but states explicitly he is uncertain what they signify ('mihi quidem incertum quò spectent'), and adds only that since the same types appear on M. Cordius Rufus's denarius and others, they may have been struck in Caesar's honour to indicate the Julian family's origin ('in Caesaris gratiam, ad indicandam Iuliae gentis originem').

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare male head right (imperial portrait); CAESAR.AVGVSTVS.PONT.MAX around
coins_engraved.reverse: Large S C in center; MVNIFICAG[...].III.VIR around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies M. Lurius as IIIvir monetalis under Augustus; Dio lib. XLVIII records him as governor of Sardinia. Tacitus lib. XII also mentions the gens. Marble inscriptions record M. LVRIVS TRIARIVS and M. LVRIVS TREPTVS.

completed.family_note: The Lurii were a minor gens attested by Tacitus (lib. XII) and Dio (lib. XLVIII). M. Lurius served as IIIvir monetalis under Augustus and, per Dio, as governor (praefectus) of Sardinia. Velleius lib. II mentions a M. Larius at Actium commanding the right wing of the Julians' fleet, whom Orsini tentatively identifies as M. Lurius ('pro M. enim Lario, M. Lurio reponendum opinor'). Marble inscriptions on an ancient base record M. LVRIVS TRIARIVS and M. LVRIVS TREPTUS among those who contributed to a statue dedicated to Vespasian by L. Annius Bassus and C. Caecina Paetus as consuls; a further L VRIVS MARTIALIS appears on a base for Caracalla.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Luria gens on one plate (p. 146) with a single bronze coin. He cites Tacitus lib. XII and Dio lib. XLVIII for the family, identifying M. Lurius from the coin as the triumvir sub Augusto who governed Sardinia (per Dio). He cites Velleius lib. II for a naval battle at Actium in which a M. Larius commanded the right wing of the Julians' fleet, tentatively emending 'M. Lario' to 'M. Lurio' ('pro M. enim Lario, M. Lurio reponendum opinor'). He adduces two marble inscriptions: a base dedicated to Vespasian recording M. LVRIVS TRIARIVS and M. LVRIVS TREPTUS, and an inscription on a Caracalla statue base naming LVRIVS MARTIALIS. He does not give the full coin legend text in the prose.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head right (Roma); ROMA behind; CERCO below
coins_engraved.reverse: Ship or galley; Q.LVTATI / Q below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini's friend ('amicus meus') proposed that the two sides of this coin refer to two brothers: Q. Lutatius Cerco (consul who triumphed at Falisceis anno DXII) and C. Lutatius Catulus (Procos. naval victory over the Carthaginians from Sicily, same year). Orsini presents this as his friend's view ('amicus meus existimabat'), not his own settled interpretation. He suggests the coin may have been struck by C. Lutatius Cerco (legatus to Alexandria anno DLXXX, Livy lib. XLII) to celebrate Caius's naval and Quintus's terrestrial victories at Falisceis.

completed.family_note: The Lutatii were a plebeian gens whose greatest achievement was C. Lutatius Catulus's decisive naval victory at the Battle of the Aegates Islands in 241 BC, which ended the First Punic War. Q. Lutatius Cerco struck denarii (Crawford 305/1) c. 109-108 BC with the distinctive feature of Roma's head within a laurel wreath on the obverse and a galley within a wreath on the reverse, both types being unusual for Republican coinage. The galley type clearly references the family's naval triumph. A later Q. Lutatius Catulus served as consul in 102 BC alongside C. Marius and helped defeat the Cimbri.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the Lutatia gens on one plate (p. 147) with a single denarius. He reports that a friend ('amicus meus') believed the coin referred to two Lutatius brothers: Q. Lutatius Cerco (consul who triumphed at Falisceis anno DXII) on one side and C. Lutatius Catulus (who that same year as Procos. conducted the naval campaign against the Carthaginians from Sicily) on the other. Orsini himself presents this as his friend's interpretation, not as his own established conclusion ('amicus meus existimabat'). He cites Livy lib. XLII for C. Lutatius Cerco, who anno DLXXX was sent as legatus to Alexandria to renew friendship with Ptolemy. Orsini does not cite Polybius.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head left; AVGVST PONT MAX TRIBVN around
coins_engraved.reverse: Large SC in centre; legend around including M MAECILI... IIII VIR
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this bronze coin to M. MAECILIVS TVL LVS, noting uncertainty whether this Maecilius traces origin from the patrician branch of the gens (admitted under Tullus Hostilius per Dionysius lib. III) or from the plebeian branch numbered by Livy.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory driving quadriga right; P.MAEN below, ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini is uncertain whether this silver denarius belongs to the Maecilia gens or should be read as MAENIVS and referred to the Maenia gens; he notes the reading of the monogram is ambiguous.

completed.family_note: Minor gens of Alban origin, admitted to the Roman patriciate under Tullus Hostilius. P. Maecilius Tullus served as Augustan IIIvir monetalis c. 7 BC, striking bronze coins with the standard S.C. types (RIC I 434). A Republican denarius (Crawford 249/1) with P.MAE ANT legend is tentatively attributed to the family, though the reading is debated between Maecilius and Maenius. The gens is otherwise poorly documented in literary sources.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents coins under Maecilia. He identifies the Alban origin of the gens, citing Dionysius lib. III on the admission under Tullus Hostilius. He notes uncertainty whether the gens claiming origin from M. MAECILIVS TVL LVS is the patrician branch (attested by Dionysius) or the plebeian branch numbered by Livy. The second silver coin and third bronze coin may belong to a member named P. MAECILIVS, unless one prefers to read the denarius mark as MAENIVS and refer those coins to the Maenia gens.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Roma right, helmeted
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory (or charioteer) driving biga of two horses right; C·MINI below, ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this silver denarius as belonging to the Maiania gens, which he equates with the Maenia found in the Capitoline Fasti; he cites an ancient Caeretan inscription as evidence for the family name.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head of Roma right, helmeted
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: The Dioscuri on horseback right; C·MINI below, ROMA in exergue

coins_engraved.obverse: Janiform head (double head) facing left and right, bare
coins_engraved.reverse: Prow of ship right; C M INI above
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this bronze coin to C. Maianius and tentatively connects him to C. Mainium P.f.P.n., who triumphed as consul in year CDXV over the Antiatians, Lavinians ('Lauinieis'), and Veliternaeans, and was later recorded as Dictator II in year CDXXXIX in the Capitoline monuments.

completed.family_note: Minor gens known primarily from Republican coinage. C. Maianius struck denarii (Crawford 203/1a) and bronze (Crawford 203/2) c. 153 BC with standard Roma/Victory in biga and Janus/prow types. The gens name appears variously as Maiania or Maenia in sources. An ancient Caeretan inscription provides epigraphic evidence for the family name. The consul of 415 AUC who triumphed over the Antiatians may belong to this gens.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents two coins under MAIANIA (Orsini's spelling). He opines the gens is the same as that called MAINIA or MAENIA in the Capitoline Fasti, and cites an ancient Caeretan inscription as evidence. He tentatively connects the moneyer C. Maianius to C. Mainium P.f.P.n., who triumphed as consul in year CDXV over the Antiatians, Lavinians ('Lauinieis'), and Veliternaeans ('Veliterneis') on the day before the Kalends of October, and who is recorded in the Capitoline monuments as Dictator II in year CDXXXIX with M. Foflius Flaccinator as Master of Horse.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Mars or Mercury right; caduceus behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Standing figure (Ulysses?) with staff beside column; C.MAMIL / LIMETA(N) around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this denarius to C. Mamilius Limetanus, explaining the Mamilia gens traced its origin from Mamilia, daughter of Telegonus (son of Ulysses and Circe), and identifies the reverse figure as Ulysses recognized by his dog after twenty years, following Homer.

coins_engraved.obverse: Wreathed/draped head right; ...CENSORIN behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Venus in biga right, holding reins and goad; XXVIII above, C·LIMETA / P·CREPVSI below
coins_engraved.moneyer: P. Crepusius, C. Mamilius Limetanus, L. Marcius Censorinus
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes this denarius shows Ulysses with a pileus (cap), citing Nicomachus as the first to add the pileus to Ulysses; he also mentions C. Mamilius as Tribune of the Plebs from Sallust's Jugurthine War, and corrects the moneyer's name to C. Mamilius Limetanus from older readings.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Bust of Mercury right, wearing winged petasus; caduceus behind
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Ulysses walking right, greeted by his dog; XXVIII above; C.LIMET / P.CREPVSI in exergue

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens claiming legendary descent from Mamilia, daughter of Telegonus (son of Ulysses and Circe). C. Mamilius Limetanus struck serrate denarii c. 82 BC (Crawford 362/1) with Mercury/Ulysses-and-Argos types referencing this mythical lineage. He also appears on joint issues with P. Crepusius and L. Marcius Censorinus (Crawford 360/1b). The family held the Tusculan dictatorship and was prominent in early Republic; a C. Mamilius served as Tribune of the Plebs during the Jugurthine War.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents two coins of the Mamilia gens. He explains the legendary descent from Ulysses and Circe through Mamilia, following Homer. He identifies the reverse figure as Ulysses recognized by his dog Argos after twenty years. He cites Nicomachus as the first to add the pileus to Ulysses and mentions C. Mamilius from Sallust's Jugurthine War. He corrects the moneyer's name to C. Mamilius Limetanus from older readings.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right (plume each side); SER, ROMA
coins_engraved.reverse: Sol in quadriga facing; star on either side, crescent at right, waves below; reverse legend A·MANLI·Q·F (NO TORQ); X (value mark)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this denarius to A. Manlius, identifying him as the son ('filius') of Q. Manlii Thurini (Livy lib. XXVIII; Quintilian lib. II), who was Praetor Peregrinus in year DXLV and Aedilis plebis in year DXLVI. He notes the SER mark on the reverse may indicate SERRATVS (serrated coinage), citing Tacitus on the Germans' esteem for serrate coins.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Helmeted head of Roma right; ROMA behind
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Horseman galloping right with spear; stars above; L.MN.TORQ in exergue

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory in triga right; T·MAL·AP·CL·Q·VR in exergue

coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes that the fourth and fifth denarii both belong to L. TORQVATVS, consul in year DCLXXXVIII with L. Cotta. He discusses the Torquatus cognomen's origin from T. Manlius, who took the golden torque from a Gaul in single combat at the River Anio in year CCCXCII (citing Livy, Plutarch in Mario, Cicero de officiis lib. III and de finibus). He notes that on both denarii the torque device refers to this cognomen.

Manlius Torquatus and notes the Sibyl's image on the obverse and the tripod on the reverse, connecting these to the XVviri sacris faciundis who guarded the Sibylline books, citing Cicero, Valerius Maximus, and others.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Sibyl right; SIBVLLI below
coins_engraved.reverse: Tripod with stars above; L.TORQVAT / III.VIR around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes that the Sibyl's image on one side and a tripod on the other of this fifth denarius allow the conjecture ('possumus suspicari') that L. Torquatus was an XVuir sacris faciundis, since the Sibylline books were guarded by the XVuiri and could not be consulted without senatorial decree, as attested by Cicero, Valerius Maximus, Lactantius, Suetonius in Caesare, and others. He also notes that Sibyls were accustomed to prophesy from a tripod sacred to Apollo.

completed.family_note: Distinguished patrician gens with both patrician and plebeian branches. T. Manlius Torquatus famously defeated a Gaul in single combat and took the torque (torques) as cognomen. L. Manlius Torquatus struck denarii c. 113-112 BC (Crawford 295/1) with Roma/horseman types within a torque border. T. Manlius Mancinus struck joint issues c. 111-110 BC (Crawford 299/1a) with Roma/Victory in triga. L. Manlius Torquatus also served as Sulla's proquaestor, striking military coinage (Crawford 367/5) with triumphal quadriga. L. Manlius Torquatus struck denarii c. 65 BC (Crawford 411/1a-b) with Sibyl/tripod types indicating his priesthood as XVvir sacris faciundis.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents five coins of the Manlia gens. He discusses both patrician and plebeian branches, citing Cicero's first Philippic. He identifies A. Manlius (coin 1) as the son of Q. Manlii Thurini (Livy lib. XXVIII; Quintilian lib. II), who was Praetor Peregrinus in year DXLV and Aedilis plebis in year DXLVI. He reads the SER mark on coin 1 as possibly indicating SERRATVS (serrated coinage), citing Tacitus. He identifies T. Manlius (coin 2) as possibly the T. Manlius who was Pontifex and Quaestor Vrbanus with Ap. Claudius, consul in year DLXXXVIII, or alternatively Cicero's contemporary described in the Brutus. He identifies L. Manlius (coin 3) as Sulla's ProQuaestor, citing Livy epitome lib. XL. He notes that coins 4 and 5 both belong to L. TORQVATVS, consul in year DCLXXXVIII with L. Cotta, who obtained the province of Macedonia and was hailed Imperator in absentia (citing Cicero in Pisonem). He connects the Sibyl and tripod on coin 5 to the possibility that L. Torquatus held the priestly office of XVuir sacris faciundis (citing Valerius Maximus, Lactantius, Suetonius in Caesare, and others).

The reverse shows Castor on horseback ('Castor equo insidens'), with Orsini citing Horace ('Castor gaudet equis') and Homer (Iliad lib. III; Odyssey lib. II) on Castor's association with horses.

coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this fifth denarius to L. Marcius Censorinus, consul in year DCCXIIII with C. Calvisius Sabinus, who triumphed from Macedonia on the Kalends of January. Orsini connects 'CONGIARVM populo ab Anco datum' (a grain distribution Ancus gave the people, Pliny lib. XXXI cap. VII) and the 'ACROSTIRIVM nauis' (a ship's ram) to L. Censorinus, who commanded the fleet against Carthage (Appian in Libyco). He also discusses the moneyer's role in publicizing Marcian family monuments.

coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes that the reverse of this sixth denarius shows a VICTORIA placed on a column ('VICTORIA columnae imposita'), representing Marcian family monuments, but he explicitly leaves open to which Marcius it pertains — whether to King Ancus or to another member of the gens ('quae ignoratur ad quem pertineat Marciorum, ad Ancum ne regem, an ad alium eius gentis'). Orsini attributes coins 5 and 6 together to L. Marcius Censorinus, consul DCCXIIII.

coins_engraved.reverse: Prow or galley right with stern ornament; C.CENSO / ROMA around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the two jugate heads as Kings Numa Pompilius and Ancus Marcius, from whom the Marcia gens claimed descent; the Marcii traced their lineage through Popilia, Numa's daughter, whose son was King Ancus.

coins_engraved.reverse: Prow right; C.MRCI / CENSO around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this bronze to C. Censorinus (triumuir sub Augusto), noting it shows the jugate heads of Kings Numa and Ancus. He explains that the first two bronze coins and sixth coin of the second plate also show the Ostia colony monument ('Ostiae quoque coloniae, quam anno CXXVII Ancus deduxit, monumentum expressit'), citing Livy lib. I and Strabo lib. V.

coins_engraved.obverse: Single bearded male head right
coins_engraved.reverse: Single horseman (desultor) galloping right; C·CENSOR below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this silver denarius to C. Censorinus (triumuir sub Augusto), noting that the third and fourth coins of this plate show circus victory types: equestrian ('equo singulari') and biga racing victories, which C. Censorinus placed on these coins to celebrate his progenitors' monuments. Orsini is uncertain which ancestor's victories are depicted and notes the Victoria column's referent is also unclear ('Victoriae columnae impositae... ignoratur ad quem pertineat'). Documented Orsini misattribution: these circus-victory reverses have no certain ancient source identifying the specific Marcius honored.

Cenforinus triumuir sub Augusto, ut progenitoris sui monumenta illustraret, in his nummis signauit.' Orsini does not describe the obverse type of this coin separately or name it as 'laureate Apollo.' The attribution is to C. Marcius Censorinus (triumuir sub Augusto) celebrating an ancestor's circus victories.

coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this coin to C. Marcius Censorinus (triumuir sub Augusto, consul DCCXLV with C. Asinius Gallus). Orsini confirms he was an Augur from the coin's own title and from a votive inscription found at Aquinum: 'C. MARCIO L.F. / CENSORINO. COS / AVGVRI. PATRONO. D.D.' He does not say Censorinus 'triumphed under Augustus'; no triumph is mentioned by Orsini for this Censorinus. Engraver metal note: Orsini's plate shows this coin in the bronze (AE) series consistent with an Augustan S.C. bronze.
