completed.family_note: Plebeian gens. Orsini records no patrician Marcii on coins ('patriciorum nulla in antiquis denariis extat memoria'). The plebeian branches represented are PHILIPPOS, CENSORINOS, and LIBONES. The Philippus branch: L. Marcius Philippus (coin 1) showed Ancus Marcius's image on his first denarius; a second Philippus denarius (coin 2) shows the equestrian statue voted to Q. Marcius and the image of L. Marcius with flame from his head (Spain); the third coin (coin 3, bronze) belongs to the L. Philippus who was Augustus's stepfather and consul with Cn. Lentulus Marcellinus in year DCXCVII; coin 4 belongs to Q. Philippus (consul twice: year DLXVII with Sp. Postumius Albinus, and year DLXXXIIII with Cn. Servilius Caepio, then Censor with L. Aemilius Paullus). The Censorinus branch: coins 5–6 belong to L. Marcius Censorinus, consul year DCCXIIII with C. Calvisius Sabinus, who triumphed from Macedonia. Coins 7–12 (second plate) belong to C. Marcius Censorinus, son of L. Censorinus, consul with C. Asinius Gallus year DCCXLV, triumuir sub Augusto. The Libo branch: Q. Marcii Libonis coins (plate 3) were struck as Triumuir with C. Fabius and L. Rubrius or L. Roscius.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents fifteen coins of the Marcia gens across three plates. He traces the descent from both Numa Marcius (first Pontifex Maximus, city prefect under Tullus Hostilius, from Popilia daughter of King Numa, who sired King Ancus Marcius) and Ancus Marcius, citing Plutarch, Livy, Ovid (Fasti lib. VI: 'Marcia sacrifico deductum nomen ab Anco'), Caesar's funeral oration for Julia, and Suetonius. For the Aqua Marcia he cites Strabo lib. V, Cornelius Tacitus lib. XIIII, Frontinus lib. I, and Pliny lib. XXXVI cap. III. He interprets the equestrian statue on coin 2 as honoring Q. Marcius, noting a possible identification with the statue Livy lib. IX says was placed before the temple of Castor by senatorial decree after Samnites and Anagnia were defeated. He discusses at length the flame from L. Marcius's head while haranguing troops in Spain (Livy lib. XXV, Valerius Maximus lib. I cap. VI, Pliny lib. II cap. CX). For coins 5–6 (L. Censorinus, consul DCCXIIII) the sixth denarius shows a VICTORIA column whose attribution to a specific Marcius Orsini leaves open ('quae ignoratur ad quem pertineat'). For coins 7–12 (second Censorinus plate) Orsini attributes the jugate Numa/Ancus heads and Ostia colony monument to C. Censorinus triumuir sub Augusto, and notes circus victory types (equo singulari & bigis). He provides two Flumentana inscriptions confirming C. Marcius L.f.L.n. Censorinus as consul and Augur. For the Libo coins Orsini finds no mention in ancient writers and notes the Libo cognomen belonged to multiple families including Julia.

coins_engraved.reverse: Ploughman with yoke of oxen left; legend C·MARI·C·F / S·C
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this denarius to C. Marius C.f. Capito, who served as Pro Triumuir apparently ('ut uidetur') under Augustus. He notes that the colony scene on the reverse may represent either one of the colonies Augustus founded or Eporedia, which C. Marius founded as consul (Pliny lib. III cap. VI; Velleius lib. I), Eporedia having been founded 23 years after Marius's sixth consulship ('Post tres & uiginti annos in Vagiennis Eporedia...'). Orsini leaves the identification open ('uel... uel').

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens from Arpinum. C. Marius, consul seven times (107-86 BC), reformed the Roman army and defeated the Cimbri and Teutones. C. Marius C.f. Capito struck serrate denarii c. 81 BC (Crawford 378/1c) with Ceres/ploughing types, possibly referencing the colony of Eporedia. C. Marius Tro. served as Augustan IIIvir monetalis c. 13 BC (RIC I 399-405), striking an extensive series with Augustus' portrait and dynastic types showing members of the imperial family.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents coins of the Maria gens. He establishes the plebeian status from C. Marius C.F. (no cognomen) and M. Marius Gratidianus both serving as Tribunes of the Plebs. He identifies C. MARIVS C. F. CAPITO as 'Pro Triumuiro (ut uidetur)' — apparently acting Pro Triumuir — under Augustus, and notes that in the first two denarii he impressed either one of the colonies Augustus founded or wished to indicate Eporedia, founded by C. Marius as consul (Pliny lib. III cap. VI; Velleius lib. I: 'Post tres & uiginti annos in Vagiennis Eporaedia Mario sexies, Valerioque Flacco Consulibus'), the year being 653 AUC. He explains that PRO III VIR in three of the denarii's inscriptions, misread by others as ProQuaestor Triumuir, in fact signifies one who performed the Triumuir's office while the Triumuir was dead or absent ('qui mortuo, aut absente Triumuiro, eius officio functus sit'). Orsini's text does not discuss the C. Marius Tro. Augustan denarii beyond the plate engraving.

coins_engraved.reverse: Ceres seated right on throne, holding torch and sceptre; C.MEMMI.C.F around; A.P.D.CERIA.MARVLLI.F behind
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this as C. Memmius C.f.'s denarius, noting that Memmius as Aedile was the first to celebrate the Cerealia games with horse races in the Circus; he cites Dio lib. XLVII on the games and identifies the bearded head as Quirinus.

coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this second denarius to C. Memmius C.F. (Consul suffectus year DCCXIX), son of C. Memmius L.F. The Imperator title in the inscription belongs to the father (L. Memmius's son C. Memmius L.F.), who obtained the Imperator title from Bithynia after serving as Praetor with L. Domitius. Orsini discusses at length whether this C. Memmius or a different one was the patron of Lucretius who sent him De Rerum Natura.

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens claiming Trojan descent. C. Memmius C.f. struck denarii c. 56 BC (Crawford 427/1-2) with Ceres/trophy types (427/1) and Quirinus/Ceres types (427/2) celebrating his role as first to hold Cerealia games with horse races; the Imperator title records his Bithynian praetorship. L. Memmius struck denarii c. 109-108 BC (Crawford 304/1) with Dioscuri standing types. L. Memmius Galeria struck serrate denarii c. 106 BC (Crawford 313/1) with Saturn/Venus in biga types. C. Memmius was the patron of Lucretius, who dedicated De Rerum Natura to him.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents six coins of the Memmia gens. He establishes the gens as plebeian from the first coin's evidence: a MEMMIVS was Aedilis plebeius who first held Cerealia games with horse races in the Circus, recorded by Dio lib. XLVII (noting this occurred before Brutus's death). He identifies the C. Memmius C.F. striking coins 1 and 2 as likely the Consul suffectus from the Kalends of July in year DCCXIX, son of C. Memmius L.F. whose Imperator title appears in the denarius inscriptions. He debates the identification of C. Memmius with the Aedile and the Praetor, concluding these were different persons but that the Triumuir moneyer combined both their titles. Coin 1 shows Quirinus or Romulus ('Quirini simulacrum siue Romuli') and a Ceres sign with colum (distaff), citing Porphyrius philosophus ex Orphei auctoritate. He discusses at length C. Memmius as Lucretius's patron — this patron is L. Memmius's son (the orator/father), who obtained Bithynia as Praetor with L. Domitius and was called Imperator thence; he later went to Greece in exile, adopted Lysonis Patrensis filius, and died there. The GAL abbreviation in coins 5–6 (L. Memmius cognomen) differs maximally from GEM (Gemellus in Cicero), suggesting copyist transposition: GALLVS or similar intended, not Gemellus.

completed.family_note: Minor plebeian gens. C. Mescinius (Tribunus Plebis in year DCXCVI) used his office to recall Cicero from exile (Cicero, pro P. Sextio; post reditum in Senatu). L. MESCINIVS RVFVS, who later served under Augustus as master of the mint ('monetae cudendae praefectus') and struck four denarii, had previously been Cicero's Quaestor in Cilicia (Cicero ep. XXVI lib. XIII; ep. VI lib. XVI; epistolae XX–XXI lib. V addressed to him). The four denarii record: (1) vows to Jupiter Optimus Maximus for Augustus's safety; (2) vows for Augustus's return from abroad; (3) a Mars statue dedicated with vows for Augustus's return and safety by senatorial decree; (4) the Ludi Saeculares (Secular Games) celebrated by Augustus (Dio lib. LIIII; Suetonius cap. XXXI), the columnar inscription noted by Politianus (Miscellaneis) as 'stelographia'.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents four coins of the Mescinia gens. He identifies C. Mescinius (Tr. Pl. year DCXCVI) as the means of Cicero's recall from exile. He identifies L. Mescinius Rufus as Cicero's Quaestor in Cilicia (pro Coss. = proconsul), succeeded by C. Coelius Caldus; cited from Cicero ep. XXVI lib. XIII and ep. VI lib. XVI. The first coin records the vows of the Senate and People to Iuppiter Optimus Maximus for Augustus's safety, its inscription interpreted as 'IMP. CAE. AVGV. COMM. CONS.' = 'Imperatori Caesari Augusto communi consensu.' The second coin records the vows for Augustus's return: 'S.P.Q.R. V.PR. R.ED. CAES.' The third coin shows a signum Martis at the base with inscription 'S.P.Q.R. V.S.PRO. S. LT. R.ED. AVG.' and Orsini interprets this as a statue of Mars dedicated by senatorial decree to record vows fulfilled for Augustus's safety and return. The fourth coin records the Ludi Saeculares in a columnar inscription, which Politianus called 'stelographia' (in Miscellaneis), with Dio lib. LIIII and Suetonius cap. XXXI cited on the Secular Games. Orsini also infers from the inscription 'X V. S. F.' that Augustus himself was a Quindecemuir sacris faciundis when he celebrated the Secular Games; and cites Vitellius as another example of an emperor identifiable as XV-man from coin titles. Orsini cites Dio lib. LV for vows after Augustus's return from Germany (Tiberius's campaign context) and for the Ludi Votivi.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head right, bare; legend around
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory driving a galloping biga (two-horse chariot); M·METTIVS in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this as the first of Mettius's denarii; he notes the obverse as Juno Sospita of Lanuvium ('Iunonem Sospitam, quae Lanuuii cum hasta, scutulo, calceolis repandis, & pelle caprina colebatur, signauit'). The Lanuvian serpent is not attributed to this coin but to the third.

coins_engraved.obverse: Wreathed head of Caesar right; CAESAR IMPER
coins_engraved.reverse: Venus standing left, holding Victory and sceptre, elbow on shield on globe; M·METTIVS
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini presents this as the second of Mettius's denarii ('in secundo'). He does not describe specific types for this coin beyond its being struck under Caesar as Dictator ('sub quo Dictatore quarto M. METTIVS hic (ut apparet) cudendae monetae praefuit'). No citation of Propertius is attached to this coin; the Propertius verses are cited for the third coin.

coins_engraved.reverse: Standing draped figure facing/turned, holding object (simpulum/patera); M·METTI in field at right
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this denarius to M. Mettius and notes Caesar mentions a Mettius in two places in De Bello Gallico lib. I, though the vulgate texts erroneously print M. Tittius; he corrects this from Vatican manuscript evidence.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head of male figure right, bare
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Standing female figure right, holding uncertain object; VIMETTI in exergue

completed.family_note: Minor gens connected to Lanuvium. M. Mettius served as moneyer under Caesar as Dictator, striking denarii (Crawford 480/2-3) with Lanuvian types. Crawford 480/2 has Juno Sospita of Lanuvium on the obverse and Lanuvian serpent types; Crawford 480/3 has the types Orsini connects to Caesar's Lanuuium colony. Orsini corrects the reading of Mettius from Tittius using two manuscript witnesses: one from the Biblioteca Vaticana and one from his own collection. Cicero also mentions a Mettius (ep. xxvi. lib. xv), and a M. Mettius Epaphroditus, Greek grammarian, is attested in an ancient inscription as a freedman of this same M. Mettius.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents three coins of the Mettia gens. He identifies the Lanuvian Juno Sospita with her goatskin headdress and spear on the first coin; on the third coin he notes the types relating to the Lanuvian serpent, citing Propertius (Elegies lib. IIII, the elegy inscribed 'de Cynthia & Dracone'). He states M. Mettius was in charge of the mint ('cudendae monetae praefuit') under Caesar as Dictator (fourth dictatorship). He corrects the reading of Mettius from Tittius using two manuscript witnesses: the Biblioteca Vaticana copy and his own copy of De Bello Gallico.

coins_engraved.reverse: Three standing figures (central figure flanked by two); PR.Q above, M·MINAT / SABIN below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to M. Minatius Sabinus, whom he identifies as Cn. Pompey's pro-quaestor in Hispania ('M. MINATI I huius, qui Cn. Pompeii, ut ego arbitror in Hispania Pro-Quaestore fuit'). He cites Valerius Maximus lib. III cap. IV on Minatius Rufus (M. Cato's companion in the Cypriaca expeditione) and an inscription from Bisenti (Etruria) mentioning the Sabatina tribe.

coins_engraved.reverse: Standing figures, three figures in robes with one central figure between two others

completed.family_note: Minor gens. M. Minatius Sabinus served as pro-quaestor for Cn. Pompeius Magnus in Spain during the Civil Wars. An inscription from Bisenti (Bisenti Etruriae oppido) mentioning the Sabatina tribe provides evidence for the family's connection to that tribe. Valerius Maximus lib. III cap. IV mentions Minatius Rufus, companion of M. Cato in the Cypriaca expeditione. The gens is otherwise poorly documented beyond the numismatic evidence and an ancient inscription recording a libertus M. Minatius.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents two coins of the Minatia gens. He cites Valerius Maximus lib. III cap. IV on Minatius Rufus as companion of M. Cato in the Cypriaca expeditione. He also notes Velleius' mention of Minatius Magius (Asculanensem), but explicitly states he has nothing to do with this Minatia gens. He cites an inscription from Bisenti (Etruria) mentioning M.MINATI.M.L.SAB. GALLI as evidence for the family's enrollment in the Sabatina tribe. He states he finds no mention of M. Minati I (the moneyer, Pompey's pro-quaestor) in ancient writers ('nullam apud ueteres scriptores reperio mentionem'), and suggests his libertus may be the M. Minatius recorded in an ancient inscription.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Column (Columna Minucia) flanked by two standing figures holding grain ears; RVF.MINVC.AVGVR / ROMA around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to Ti. Minucius C.f. Augurinus and identifies the lituus symbol as indicating the moneyer is to be identified with M. Minucius Festum, who became the first Augur from the plebs out of this family in year CDLIII AUC ('anno CDLIII, ut scribit [Liuius] plebi lib. XI'). He does not say this dates to 'around 454 AUC' but to year CDLIII = 453 AUC.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; ROMA below; X behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Column flanked by two standing figures; C.AVG around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to C. Augurinus, identifying the column as the Columna Minucia erected outside the Porta Trigemina for L. Minucius' grain distribution; he cites Livy and Pliny on the statue and column set up by popular subscription.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
coins_engraved.reverse: The Dioscuri (two horsemen) galloping right; Q.MINV below; ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini tentatively identifies this as Q. Minucius Rufus, noting he may be the consul who triumphed over the Ligurians and Boii, or possibly Q. Minucius who was dux in Asia against Mithridates, citing Appian.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Horseman galloping right; Q.MINV below; ROMA in exergue

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
coins_engraved.reverse: The Dioscuri galloping right; ROMA / C·MINVCI below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini is uncertain whether this is a separate moneyer or the same C. Augurinus as coin 2; he notes it lacks the Lucius cognomen and may represent a different family member who struck both the silver and the bronze (coin 6 of the Augurinus column type).
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Horseman galloping right attacking fallen enemy; ROMA / C.MINVCI below

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma(?) left
coins_engraved.reverse: Two warriors fighting; Q.THERM.M.F around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini states without doubt ('sine dubio') that this coin pertains to Q. Minucius M. Thermi filius, under whose praetorship in Asia C. Iulius Caesar (later Dictator) served his first military service and was awarded the civic crown at the siege of Mytilene ('in expugnatione Mytilenarum ciuica donatus est'). He cites Suetonius in Caesare cap. II. Orsini does NOT identify this coin's moneyer as the legatus of A. Manlius Vulsonis — that reference belongs to coin 4.

completed.family_note: Patrician gens. L. Minucius Augurinus received the Columna Minucia outside the Porta Trigemina for distributing grain during a famine, a monument celebrated on the family's coinage. Ti. Minucius C.f. Augurinus (Crawford 243/1, 134 BC) and C. Minucius Augurinus (Crawford 242/1, 135 BC) both struck denarii with the Columna Minucia type. Q. Minucius Rufus (Crawford 277/1, 122 BC) issued Roma/Dioscuri types. Q. Minucius Thermus M.f. (Crawford 319/1, 103 BC) struck the celebrated combat scene denarius. The Thermus branch is notable for connections to Caesar.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents five coins of the Minucia gens. He identifies the Columna Minucia erected outside the Porta Trigemina, citing Livy and Pliny on the statue set up by popular subscription. He discusses the first plebeian Augur, citing Livy lib. XI on M. Minucius Festus. He identifies Q. Minucius Thermus M.f. as the legatus of A. Manlius Vulsonis and possibly the same Thermus under whom Caesar served in Asia. His prosopographic connections are careful but sometimes speculative.

coins_engraved.obverse: Two heads jugate right (one with beard); HO...VIR / KALENI around
coins_engraved.reverse: Two standing figures (Italia and Roma clasping hands); CORDI below; RO(MA) behind
coins_engraved.moneyer: Q. Fufius Calenus & P. Mucius Scaevola Cordus
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the joint issue of Calenus (KALENVS) and Mucius Cordus, noting Cordus had 'monetam cum Honoris signo & Virtutis, ad illustranda gentilis sui monumenta signauit.' He cites Dionysius lib. IIII and Quintilian lib. I cap. VII on the Cordus cognomen, and Vitruvius lib. VII on C. Mucius who designed the aedes Honoris et Virtutis Marianae. He also notes (following Vitruvius) that any Mucia gens member 'ex Mucia gente ufi sint' might be connected to this Cordus. He cross-references to the Fufia gens (cognomen KALENVS) for the temple of Honos and Virtus.

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens (not patrician). Only one coin appears in Orsini's treatment: a joint issue of Q. Fufius Calenus (KALENVS) and Mucius Cordus (Crawford 403/1, 70 BC) with Honos and Virtus jugate heads on the obverse and clasped hands on the reverse. Orsini discusses the Cordorum cognomen, citing Dionysius lib. IIII and Quintilian lib. I cap. VII, and connects it to C. Mucius who used Vitruvius's architectural principles in designing the temple of Honos and Virtus for Marius.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents one coin of the Mucia gens. He discusses the Cordorum cognomen, citing Dionysius lib. IIII and Quintilian lib. I cap. VII on its etymology (cognomen arising from birth circumstances). He cites Vitruvius lib. VII on C. Mucius who designed the aedes Honoris et Virtutis Marianae ('magna scientia confisus aedes Honoris ac Virtutis Marianae... legitimis artis institutis perfecit'). He does not say C. Mucius 'built' the temple but that he completed it according to the proper rules of the art. The temple was associated with Marius (Marianae).

coins_engraved.obverse: Bust of Victory, right, draped. C.CAES / DIC.TER around
coins_engraved.reverse: Oenochoe (jug/capis); L·PLANC / PR·VRB around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this coin as struck by L. Munatius Plancus. He thinks the urceus (jug) on the reverse may indicate Plancus's role as VIIIvir Epulonum, but notes it could equally refer to Caesar as Pontifex Maximus ('quamuis ad C. quoque Caesarem, qui Pontifex Maximus fuit, referri urceolus possit'). He identifies Plancus as consul designatus with D. Brutus for year DCCXI AUC, and as Vrbis praefectus in the coin's inscription context.

coins_engraved.obverse: Capis (jug) and lituus; III.VIR.R.P.C.M.ANTON around
coins_engraved.reverse: Three implements: winged thunderbolt/sceptre at left, oenochoe (jug) at center, winged caduceus at right; C·PLANCVS·IMP·ITER around
coins_engraved.identification: Crawford 522/2 — L. Munatius Plancus (under Mark Antony), 32 BC
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to L. Munatius Plancus, citing Velleius lib. II ('Plancus, inquit, Antonianarum adiutor partium, spem magis ostendens auxilii, quam opem ferens Antonio') and Appian lib. III bell. ciuil. ('Plancus cum tribus legionibus transiuit ad Antonium'). The Greek passage from Appian shows Lepidus, Asinius Pollio, and Plancus as those who joined Antonius; Orsini does not say Plancus 'joined Lepidus' — Plancus joined Antonius.

coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Priestly implements (capis, aspergillum, securis, apex); L.PLANCVS.IMP.ITER around

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens. L. Munatius Plancus, consul designatus with D. Brutus for year DCCXI AUC, struck coins (as Orsini presents them) with a jug (urceolus) type that Orsini thinks may indicate his role as VIIIvir Epulonum, though he notes the jug could also refer to Caesar as Pontifex Maximus. Plancus founded the colonies of Lugdunum (Lyon) and Augusta Raurica (as stated in his Gaetan inscription). He followed Antony's faction (Velleius) and with three legions in Gallia Comata was among those joining Antonius (Appian lib. III bell. ciuil.). Cicero's letters to Plancus are in epistolae lib. XI.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents two coins of the Munatia gens. He identifies the urceus (jug) on the coin as possibly indicating Plancus was VIIIvir Epulonum, though he leaves open that it could refer to Caesar as Pontifex Maximus ('quamuis ad C. quoque Caesarem, qui Pontifex Maximus fuit, referri urceolus possit'). He cites Cicero ep. lib. XI and Pliny lib. XXXV on Plancus. He cites Velleius lib. II ('Plancus, inquit, Antonianarum adiutor partium') and Appian lib. III bell. ciuil. on Plancus joining Antonius with three legions in Gallia Comata. He notes Plancus as consul designatus with D. Brutus for year DCCXI and discusses the founding of Lugdunum from Eusebius and Dio.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Ceres right, wearing corn-ear wreath
coins_engraved.reverse: L.MVSSIDIVS / LONGVS within corn-ear wreath
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to L. Mussidius Longus, noting the aureus (gold) type with a spiked corona on one side and Ceres' image on the other; he suggests this coin may relate to the Mussidii's frumentary administration under Caesar as Dictator.

coins_engraved.obverse: Veiled head of Concordia right; CONCORDIA before
coins_engraved.reverse: Shrine of Venus Cloacina: raised circular platform bearing two statues; L.MVSSIDIVS.LONGVS above, CLOACIN on the platform
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the reverse as the shrine of Venus Cloacina, which stood in the Forum near the Cloaca Maxima; he cites Pliny, Plutarch, and Livy on the shrine's origin from the Sabine-Roman peace under Titus Tatius and Romulus, where arms were purified at the site.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Laureate head right; wreath border
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Ship or galley right; L.MVSSIDIVS.LONGVS / CLOACIN below

coins_engraved.obverse: Radiate bust right (Roma/Venus/Concordia per Orsini) (Sol); sun rays around head
coins_engraved.reverse: Shrine or altar on platform; L.MVSSIDIVS.LONGVS / CLOACIN around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes this is a second Cloacina type with the radiate Sol head on the obverse; he discusses the Concordia symbolism connecting the Roman-Sabine reconciliation to the shrine of Venus Cloacina, citing Ovid's Fasti.

coins_engraved.obverse: Female head right (Concordia); CONCORDIA around
coins_engraved.reverse: Clasped hands holding caduceus; L.MVSSIDIVS.LONGVS around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the Concordia head and clasped hands as symbolizing the Roman-Sabine peace; he connects the Concordia imagery across Mussidius' series to the coitio (union) of Romans and Sabines at the Comitium.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bust right (portrait); draped
coins_engraved.reverse: Biga or chariot right; L.MVSSIDIVS / LONGVS below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini connects this coin's spectacle types to C. Caesar's Dictatorial victories and cites Suetonius cap. XXXIX specifically ('Circensibus, inquit, spacio Circi ab utraque parte producto, & in gyrum euripo addito, quadrigas, bigasque & equos desultorios agitauerunt nobilissimi iuuenes').

coins_engraved.obverse: Head right; crescent behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Pontifical/sacrificial implements; L·MVSSIDIVS LONGVS around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Coinage of L. Mussidius Longus (Crawford 494/39). The obverse shows a head right with a crescent behind; the reverse displays pontifical and sacrificial implements with the legend L·MVSSIDIVS LONGVS around. The cult/sacrificial implements point to the moneyer's religious associations rather than to any games or spectacle.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head of male figure left, laureate
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Standing figure left holding globe and scepter; legend around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment_ai: [QA: this note may describe a different type — flagged for review] Orsini attributes this to L. Mussidius Longus, noting the combat or athletic scene on the reverse likely represents gladiatorial games or Caesar's spectacles; he considers this part of the same series celebrating public entertainments.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare male head left; M.LEPIDVS.III.VIR.R.P.C around
coins_engraved.reverse: Mars standing right, wearing Corinthian helmet, holding sword in left hand and spear in right hand and resting left foot on shield. Legend L·MVSSIDIVS·T·F·LONGVS·IIII·VIR·A·P·F
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this as showing the head of C. Caesar (later Augustus) with the triumviral title, noting the portrait of M. Antonius on the reverse; he considers it part of the concordia series indicating M. Antonii concordiam and connects it to Mussidius as IIIIvir A.P.F. Same type as Aemilia #13 (Crawford 494/7a) but with a different engraving: the coin appears under both gentes because it bears names from both families.
coins_engraved.observed_obverse: Head of male figure left, bare; legend around
coins_engraved.observed_reverse: Standing figure of Jupiter left, holding thunderbolt and scepter; legend around

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Octavian, right
coins_engraved.reverse: Mars standing right, wearing Corinthian helmet, holding sword in left hand and spear in right hand and resting left foot on shield
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this to Mussidius Longus as IIIIvir A.P.F. (quattuorvir for striking gold or silver by public authority); he notes the triumviral portrait of C. Caesar and reads the T.F. inscription as confirming the Quattuorviral monetary authority first instituted by Caesar.
coins_engraved.observed_obverse: Head of Caesar left, laureate
coins_engraved.observed_reverse: Venus standing left, holding Victory and scepter

completed.family_note: Minor gens. L. Mussidius Longus served as IIIvir monetalis c. 42 BC, striking an extensive denarius series (Crawford 494/39-43) that is one of the most varied in Republican coinage. Types include: Caesar portrait/cornucopiae (494/39), Victory bust/Victory in biga (494/40), Concordia head/clasped hands (494/41), Concordia head/Cloacina shrine (494/42), Sol bust/Cloacina shrine (494/43). He later served as IIIIvir A.P.F. (quattuorvir for striking gold/silver). Eight coins from this gens appear in Orsini's treatment, including triumviral portrait types.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents eight coins of the Mussidia gens. He identifies the shrine of Venus Cloacina in the Forum, citing Pliny, Plutarch, and Livy on its origin from the Sabine-Roman peace under Titus Tatius and Romulus. He connects the Concordia symbolism to the Roman-Sabine coitio (union) at the Comitium. He attributes the spectacle scenes to Caesar's Dictatorial games, citing Suetonius. He discusses the IIIIvir A.P.F. monetary authority first instituted by Caesar.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Venus right, wearing diadem
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory driving a triga (three-horse chariot) right; C.NAE.BALB in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the gens as plebeian and notes the S.C. behind the head indicates senatorial authorization on this C. Naevius Balbus denarius with Victory in triga. He connects the moneyer to the Balbus cognomen found in several gentes and discusses the family's limited literary attestation.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head of Venus right, wearing diadem
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Figure reclining right (Victory driving triga or cornucopia scene); C.NAE.BAB below

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare male head right (Augustus); legend around including CAESAR
coins_engraved.reverse: S C large in centre; L.SVRDNINVS III.VIR.A.A.A.F.F around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this as an Augustan bronze by L. Naevius Surdinus. He has no literary attestation for Surdinus ('nulla, quod sciam, extat mentio apud scriptores') and does not call him 'IIIvir A.A.A.F.F.' — this title is not in Orsini's text. He notes only that Surdinus 'sub Augusto nummum aereum signauit' and points to a Forum inscription about L. Naevius... Praetoris inter ciuis et peregrinos.

coins_engraved.obverse: Wreath enclosing legend AVGVSTVS TRIBVNIC POTEST; oak wreath border
coins_engraved.reverse: S C large in centre; L.NAEVIVS SVRDNINVS III.VIR.A.A.A.F.F around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini presents no specific textual discussion of this second Surdinus bronze on the Naevia page. He offers no description of the obverse legend (AVGVSTVS TRIBVNIC POTEST) and no dating formula discussion. The coin is visible in the plate but Orsini's text does not describe it separately.

coins_engraved.obverse: Partially visible; handwritten annotations over engraving; CLXV(?) and C.NAE.BA visible
coins_engraved.reverse: Partially visible with handwritten notes overlaid; details obscured
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Later collector's note (French) on a C. Naevius Balbus denarius: a control-number reading («CLXV»?) with «C·NAE·BA», and a diagnostic «S·C derrière la tête» (S·C behind the head).
coins_engraved.annotation_text: Left circle: «CLXV[?] … C·NAE·BA[LB]» (over erased text). Right circle: «Droit / S·C derrière la tête».

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens. C. Naevius Balbus struck denarii c. 79 BC (Crawford 382/1b) with the distinctive Victory in triga type and S.C. behind Roma's head. L. Naevius Surdinus served as Augustan IIIvir monetalis c. 15 BC (RIC I 385-386), striking standard bronze S.C. types. The poet Naevius may have belonged to this gens, though the connection is uncertain. The Balbus and Surdinus cognomina indicate two distinct branches.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents three coins plus an annotation for the Naevia gens. He identifies C. Naevius Balbus (the Republican denarius moneyer) via Livy lib. XLV, and L. Naevius Surdinus via the coin legend alone — he explicitly states Surdinus has NO literary attestation ('nulla, quod sciam, extat mentio apud scriptores'). He does NOT discuss an 'IIIvir A.A.A.F.F.' title; this title does not appear in his text. He does note a recently found Forum inscription referencing L. NAEVI L.F. SPVRINI PRAETORIS INTER CIVIS ET PEREGRINOS. The Valerius Maximus citation is lib. III cap. VII (for M. Naevius Tribunus who accused P. Scipio).

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head of Neptune right, trident behind; NEPTVNI legend
coins_engraved.reverse: Galley (warship) right with sail and ornamental stern; star above; Q.NASIDIV(S) below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the NEPTVNI legend as referring to Sextus Pompey's claim to be Neptune's son ('cuius se filium iactabat') and notes the galley type. He proposes the coin was struck either by Q. Nasidius to commemorate his father L. Nasidius's naval action (Caesar lib. II bell. ciuil.) or because Q. Nasidius himself at some point commanded Sex. Pompey's fleet ('nisi forte... aliquando praefuit'). He cites Dio lib. L and Appian lib. V bell. ciuil. and cross-references under the Pompeia gens.
coins_engraved.specimen_shared_reason: same catalogue type cross-listed under multiple gentes (joint-moneyer issue or sub-variant); one museum specimen serves all

completed.family_note: Minor gens of uncertain status (Orsini: 'incertum patriciae ne an plebeiae'). Orsini believes Q. Nasidius was the son of L. Nasidius, the latter mentioned by Cicero in Philippics lib. VII and by Caesar lib. II bell. ciuil. as commanding sixteen ships sent to aid L. Domitius and the Massilienses against Pompey. Orsini proposes two alternative explanations for the coin: either the coin commemorates L. Nasidius's exploit (struck by his son Q. Nasidius), or Q. Nasidius himself at some point commanded Sextus Pompey's fleet ('nisi forte, quia ipse quoque Q. NASIDIVS, Sex. Pompeii classi aliquando praefuit'). Both readings are presented as possibilities, not established facts.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents one coin of the Nasidia gens. He identifies the obverse with Sex. Pompeii imago and NEPTVNI legend ('cuius se filium iactabat'). He believes Q. Nasidius to be the son of L. Nasidius, citing Cicero in Philippicis lib. VII and Caesar lib. II bell. ciuil. He cites Verba Dionis ex lib. L on Q. Nasidius and the battle at Leucade (Agrippa took Leucas and ships), and Appian lib. V bell. ciuil. ('Meminit huius NASIDII Appianus lib. v. bell.ciuil.'). He cross-references the coin under the Pompeia gens for the Pompeian side of the imagery. Orsini does NOT definitively identify Q. Nasidius as praefectus classis; he presents two alternative explanations for the coin's existence.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Saturn right with harpa; legend NERI·Q·VRB
coins_engraved.reverse: Legionary eagle between two military standards (hastati and principes); legend L·LENT·C·MARC·COS
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini connects the coin's moneyer (NERI, Q. VRB.) with Cn. Nerius, mentioned in Cicero ep. III lib. II ad Q. Fratrem as accused by Sestius of electoral bribery in the Pupinia tribe ('Cn. Nerio Pupinia de ambitu est postulatus'). He reads the Q. VRB. as Quaestor Vrbanus. He notes the consular date L. Lentulo C. Marcello Coss. He does not describe the coin types (Saturn head; legionary eagle) — those descriptions are not in his text.

completed.family_note: Minor gens attested in Horatius (lib. II Serm. Satyra III, 'Scribe decem a Nerio &c.'), with Porphyrio commenting that Nerius Catienus was a legal scholar whom Horace treats as a miser. Orsini believes the coin's moneyer (NERI, Quaestor Vrbanus) is the same Cn. Nerius mentioned by Cicero in ep. III lib. II ad Q. Fratrem, accused of electoral bribery (de ambitu) by Sestius. Orsini gives the consular date as L. Lentulo C. Marcello Coss. The gens was enrolled in the Pupinia tribe (inter rusticas), named from ager Pupinus per Festus.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents one coin of the Neria gens. He cites Horatius lib. II Serm. Satyra III ('Scribe decem a Nerio') with Porphyrio's commentary identifying Nerius Catienus as a legal scholar (iuris studiosus) mocked as an miser. He believes the coin's moneyer (NERI, Q. VRB.) is the Cn. Nerius mentioned in Cicero ep. III lib. II ad Q. Fratrem, accused by Sestius of electoral bribery (de ambitu) in the Pupinia tribe. He does NOT say the individual has no mention in ancient sources — he in fact cites Cicero for Cn. Nerius. He notes the Neria gens was enrolled in the Pupinia tribe.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bearded head right (Saturnus); S C behind; SVFENAS around
coins_engraved.reverse: Seated female figure right (Roma or Victory) being crowned by standing figure; SEX.NONI below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini reads the PR L V P F abbreviation on this coin as 'Praetor Ludos Votiuos Publice Fecit' (the Praetor who publicly celebrated the Votive games). He tentatively identifies Sufenas with the person mentioned by Catullus ('Sufenas iste Vare, quem probe nosti') and corrects the vulgate spelling 'Suffenus' to 'Sufenas.' He cites Cicero ep. XIIII lib. III ad Att. and Valerius Maximus lib. VIII. He does not mention Sulla or 'Ludi Victoriae.'

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare male head left (Augustus or Tiberius); CAESAR AVGVST PONT MAX TRIBVNIC PO(T) around
coins_engraved.reverse: S C large in centre; SEX.NONIVS QVINCTILIAN(VS) III.VIR.A.A.A.F.F around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Sex. Nonius Quinctilianus as Consul anno DCCLX with M. Furius Camillo, citing Dio lib. LV ('SEX. NONIUS QVINCTILIANVS, qui in aereo huius tabellae nummo notatus est, Consul fuit anno DCCLX cum M. Furio Camillo, Dio lib. LV'). He makes no further comment on this coin's obverse portrait or on any dating formula. The plate (p.175) shows the coin with a bare head and legends including AVGVST·PONT·MAX around the obverse and S·C on the reverse, but Orsini does not describe or analyse these elements. Claims that Orsini 'describes the obverse as Augustus or Tiberius' or 'uses a PONT MAX TRIBVNIC dating formula' are not supported by his text.

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens. Sex. Nonius Sufenas, as Praetor, celebrated the Ludi Votiui publici (PR L V P F = Praetor Ludos Votiuos Publice Fecit), as Orsini interprets the coin legend. Orsini identifies him tentatively with the Sufenas mentioned by Catullus ('Sufenas iste Vare, quem probe nosti') and by Cicero (ep. XIIII lib. III ad Att.: Sufenas & Cato absoluti sunt, year Vrbis DCCIX). Sex. Nonius Quinctilianus served as Augustan IIIvir monetalis. The Sufenas cognomen is distinct.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents two coins of the Nonia gens. He interprets the PR L V P F abbreviation as 'Praetor Ludos Votiuos Publice Fecit' (Praetor who publicly celebrated the Votive games), not as 'Primus Ludos Victoriae' of any Sullan games. He tentatively identifies Sufenas with the person in Catullus and corrects the name's spelling in vulgate texts from 'Suffenus' to 'Sufenas'. He cites Cicero ep. XIIII lib. III ad Att. (Nonis Quinctilibus, year DCCIX AUC) to date Sufenas. He also cites Valerius Maximus lib. VIII on a 'Sufenatis cuiusdam.'

coins_engraved.obverse: Diademed female head right (Venus); IXXXI behind; C.NORBANVS below
coins_engraved.reverse: Fasces between caduceus (left) and corn-ear (right); axe attached to fasces
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes C. Norbanus was Tribune of the plebs (anno DCXLVIII) through whose initiative (rogatione) the proconsular imperium of Q. Seruilio Caepioni was abrogated. He identifies the fasces, corn-ear, and caduceus as symbols of justice, peace, and abundance ("Pacis enim, Iustitiae, & Abundantiae symbola sunt"). He reads C.NORBANVS on the obverse.

coins_engraved.obverse: Diademed female head right (Venus); C.NORBANVS below; control marks behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Fasces between caduceus (left) and corn-ear (right); prow or cornucopia at right
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes this second C. Norbanus denarius can be attributed to the man who was Consul with Ap. Claudius Pulchro anno DCCXV and had a triumph from Hispania noted anno DCCXIX, later serving as Antony's legate (Dio xlvii, Appian lib.III). He connects the fasces, corn-ear, and caduceus to the same programme of symbols as coin 1 ("Pacis enim, Iustitiae, & Abundantiae symbola sunt"). The 'B II' control mark attribution in the previous comment is not mentioned by Orsini.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare male head right; no legend
coins_engraved.reverse: Curule chair; L·CESTIVS above, S·C flanking, PR to right, C·NORBA below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this joint bronze of L. Cestius and C. Norbanus and notes that the Africa type and sella Praetorum on the reverse were already discussed under the Cestia gens ("De Africae imagine, & sella Praetorum, in gente Cestia dictum est"). He suggests the coin may belong either to the father of C. Norbanus (Antony's legate, Consul anno DCCXV) or to his grandfather, Consul with L. Scipio Asiatico anno DCLXX.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Two female/divine heads jugate right — or possibly two heads one behind the other. The heads are lightly drawn, with soft facial features suggesting female or youthful portraits. No clear legend visible in this crop.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: A pediment (triangular temple facade) or rectangular architectural structure — inscribed. Text clearly readable: L·CESTIVS (above pediment or within field), S·C (within pediment), PR (right of pediment), C·NORBA (below). Architectural structure with columns implied.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Bare male head right; L·CESTIVS text visible above
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Curule chair, front legs decorated with sculpted eagles, Corinthian helmet lying on seat; C·NORBA text
coins_engraved.specimen_shared_reason: same catalogue type cross-listed under multiple gentes (joint-moneyer issue or sub-variant); one museum specimen serves all

coins_engraved.obverse: Handwritten annotations covering engraving; text mentions 'Mai 1946' and other notes
coins_engraved.reverse: Handwritten annotations; mentions C. Norbanus; details obscured by manuscript notes
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Later manuscript note (French) recording a find at Mariana (Corsica) in May 1846: a C. Norbanus denarius (Crawford 357/1, 83 BC) — helmeted head right / fasces and caduceus.
coins_engraved.annotation_text: «En mai 1846, on a trouvé à Mariana un Denier, tête casquée à droite. Leg. L. VIII. C. Norbanus. Fasces, faisceau et caducée.»

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens. C. Norbanus struck denarii c. 83 BC (Crawford 357/1a-b) with Venus/fasces types during the civil war period; the corn-ear and caduceus flanking the fasces symbolize peace, justice, and abundance (Orsini: "Pacis enim, Iustitiae, & Abundantiae symbola sunt"). He served as tribune of the plebs and caused the imperium of Q. Servilius Caepio to be abrogated. The third coin (joint issue with L. Cestius) Orsini assigns either to C. Norbanus patris — later legate of Antony and Consul with Ap. Claudius Pulchro anno DCCXV — or to his grandfather, Consul with L. Scipio Asiatico anno DCLXX; for the Africa/curule chair types of this bronze issue Orsini defers to the Cestia gens ("De Africae imagine, & sella Praetorum, in gente Cestia dictum est"). The coin is bronze (Æ), not an aureus.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents three coins plus an annotation for the Norbana gens. He discusses C. Norbanus' tribunate and prosecution of Q. Caepio, citing Cicero's Brutus and de Oratore. He interprets the fasces, corn-ear, and caduceus as symbols of magistracy, abundance, and peace. His treatment of the Cestius-Norbanus joint issue is brief. The annotation records a 1946 find at Marina, added by a later hand.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare female head right with hair in bun
coins_engraved.reverse: Prow of galley right; L.NVMITORI above; ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the moneyer on this bronze as C. Numitorius (not L.), whom he believes to be the eques Romanus who testified against Verres and is cited by Cicero in the Verrine speeches (lib. VII): 'Numitorio equiti R. primario homini, testi meo.' He also notes Cicero's de Inventione (lib. II) mentions a Q. Numitorius cognominated Pullus. His treatment is brief, relying on the numismatic evidence and these two Ciceronian references.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Bare female head right with hair in bun
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Rectangular altar or architectural element with decorations; L.NVMITORI legend above; dolphin or serpent curving below

completed.family_note: Minor plebeian gens. Orsini draws on L. Numitorius, described as Tribune of the plebs by Livy (lib. II) and Dionysius (lib. XII), as the sole literary attestation of the family, but identifies the moneyer on the coin as C. Numitorius — the equestrian witness in Cicero's Verrine speeches (lib. VII in Verrem: 'Numitorio equiti R. primario homini, testi meo'). Orsini also notes a Q. Numitorius cognominated Pullus. The gens has no legendary connection to King Numitor in Orsini's text.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents one coin of the Numitoria gens. He establishes the gens is plebeian via L. Numitorius (Tribune of the plebs), cited from Livy lib. II and Dionysius lib. XII. He identifies the moneyer who struck this bronze as C. Numitorius — in his opinion the same equestrian witness cited by Cicero in the Verrine speeches (lib. VII in Verrem) — and notes a Q. Numitorius cognominated Pullus mentioned in Cicero's de Inventione (lib. II). There is no discussion of legendary connection to King Numitor.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare male head right; C.NVMONIVS around; VAALA below
coins_engraved.reverse: Scene of soldiers attacking a fortification (wall with rampart); soldier climbing wall; VAALA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the reverse figure as 'a man fighting at a rampart' ('uir quidam pugnans pro uallo') and connects it to the origin of the Vaala cognomen, which he derives from an ancestor who first gained distinction by defending a rampart ('uallo defenso id cognomen primus inuenit'). He believes this Numonius Vala is the same person to whom Horace addressed Epistle 1.15. He does not date the issue or mention the triumviral context.

completed.family_note: Minor gens known from a single moneyer. C. Numonius Vaala struck denarii c. 41 BC (Crawford 514/2) with one of the most dramatically military reverse types in Roman Republican coinage: a soldier attacking an enemy rampart defended by two figures. The cognomen Vaala may derive from the name of a fortification (vallum). This is among the last Republican denarius issues before the full establishment of triumviral coinage.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents one coin of the Numonia gens. His central concern is the correct form of the name: he establishes from Velleius (lib. II) that the correct form is VALA NUMONIUS (not Valnumonius, Volumnius, etc., as various scribal corruptions had it), and argues this is the Numonius Vala to whom Horace wrote Epistle 1.15. He connects the vallum imagery on the reverse to the cognomen Vaala, which he derives from a (hypothetical) ancestor who first gained fame by defending a rampart ('uallo defenso id cognomen primus inuenit'). He does not date the coin explicitly in this passage.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of male figure right, laureate
coins_engraved.reverse: Quadriga right with charioteer; VER above, CAR·OCV in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this coin to the Ogulnius he believes was Consul with C. Fabius Buteo anno CDLXXXIV ('Eū auté opinor esse, qui Consul in Fastis descriptus est anno CDLXXXIV cū C. Fabio Buteone') and also Dictator anno CDXCVI. He cites Livy (lib. X) and Valerius Maximus (lib. I, cap. VIII). The lex Ogulnia is mentioned in the broader family discussion, not as the primary identification for this coin.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head of male figure right, laureate
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Quadriga right with charioteer; CAR above, OCV below

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Janus left and right, laureate
coins_engraved.reverse: Prow of galley right; VEROCCVS above
coins_engraved.identification: Crawford 350A/3 — M. Vergilius, C. Gargonius, M. Ogulnius (joint issue), 86 BC (AE quadrans)
coins_engraved.moneyer: M. Vergilius, C. Gargonius, M. Ogulnius
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini explains that OCVLNIVS on the coin stands for OGVLNIVS because the ancients used C for G, citing the Duilii rostratae columnae inscription as confirmation ('Confirmat hoc antiquissima C. Duilii rostratae columnae inscriptio, in qua est, MAGISTRATOS, PVCNANDOD, CESSIT, CARTACINENSIS, proMAGISTRATOS, PVCNANDOD, GESSIT, CARTAGIN ENSIS'). The legend VROCU·CAR visible in the plate he reads as a form of OGVLNIVS. He does not use the reading 'VROCILAS'; the previous attribution of that word to Orsini is unfounded.
coins_engraved.specimen_shared_reason: same catalogue type cross-listed under multiple gentes (joint-moneyer issue or sub-variant); one museum specimen serves all

completed.family_note: Patrician gens known primarily from the lex Ogulnia of 300 BC, which opened the pontificate and augurate to plebeians, proposed by tribunes Cn. and Q. Ogulnius. The brothers also dedicated the famous she-wolf and twins statue at the Ficus Ruminalis. Orsini's attribution of these two coins to the gens is uncertain: coin 1 may be Crawford 350A/1 (anonymous issue of 86 BC jointly attributed to Gargonius, Ogulnius, and Vergilius), while coin 2 remains unidentified.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents two coins under Ogulnia. He identifies the moneyer as the Ogulnius who was Consul with C. Fabius Pictor anno CDLXXXIV and Dictator anno CDXCVI (citing Livy lib. X and Valerius Maximus lib. I, cap. VIII). He discusses the lex Ogulnia de Sacerdotiis (anno CDLIII), noting that Livy names Q. and Cn. Ogulnius as tribunes who proposed it. His key philological point is that OCVLNIVS on the coins stands for OGVLNIVS, because antiqui used C for G. He does not use the reading 'VROCILAS' anywhere; the coin legends show VER and VROCU·CAR. Modern scholarship is correct that his attributions are uncertain.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right with crest; X (value mark) behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Quadriga right driven by Victory; L.OPEIMI below, ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this moneyer as the future consul of anno DCXXXII who, with Q. Metellus, P. Lentulus, and others, pursued C. Gracchus and M. Fuluius Consularis to the Aventine, where Gracchus was killed. He cites Cicero (in Catilinam and de claris Oratoribus), Velleius (lib. I), Plinius (lib. XIII, cap. IV), and Plutarchus (in C. Graccho). He does not cite Appian. He does not describe the coin type as 'Apollo biga.'

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; crest with feathers; control mark behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Biga right driven by charioteer; Victory above; M.OPEIMI below, ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies M. Opimius (legend: M.OPEIM) as the brother ('fratrem fuisse arbitror') of L. Opimius the consul, and notes he can find no mention of M. Opimius in any author he has read ('de quo nullam inuenire potui mentionem apud eos scriptores, quos ipse legerim'). He does not resolve whether M. stands for Marcus or Manius.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Hercules right; three pellets behind (quadrans mark)
coins_engraved.reverse: Club within laurel-wreath; L·OPEIMI above, ROMA below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this bronze to L. Opimius (L.OPEIM in wreath visible in plate). He provides no description of the obverse head as Apollo, and does not discuss the laurel wreath as Apollo's attribute. His text groups all references to L. Opimius across coins 1 and 3 without distinguishing the type of coin 3 specifically.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Laureate head right (Janus or Apollo); wreath border
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Wreath enclosing L.OPEIM / ROMA legend

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens. L. Opimius and M. Opimius served as Republican moneyers c. 131 BC. L. Opimius struck denarii (Crawford 253/1) with Roma/Victory quadriga and bronze quadrantes (Crawford 253/3) with Hercules/club in wreath. M. Opimius issued a companion denarius (Crawford 254/1) with Roma/Apollo biga. L. Opimius later served as consul in 121 BC, famous for crushing C. Gracchus and his followers on the Aventine using the senatus consultum ultimum, the first time this emergency decree was employed.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents three coins of the Opeimia gens. He identifies L. Opimius (coins 1 and 3) as the future consul of anno DCXXXII who, according to Cicero and others, moved the Republic to persecute C. Gracchus and M. Fuluius on the Aventine. He cites Cicero (in Catilinam; de claris Oratoribus), Velleius (lib. I), Plinius (lib. XIII, cap. IV), and Plutarchus (in C. Graccho) — not Appian. He identifies M. Opimius (coin 2) as 'fratrem fuisse arbitror' of L. Opimius the consul, but finds no mention of M. Opimius in any author he has read.

coins_engraved.obverse: Female head right (Diana or Roma) with diadem; small and finely engraved
coins_engraved.reverse: Winged Victory standing, holding wreath/palm; Q·OPPIVS·PR
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the coin as struck by Q. Oppius, whom he believes ('ut opinor') to be the Praetor mentioned by Appian in the Mithridatico — captured at Laodicea and displayed by Mithridates. Livy's epitome (lib. LXXVII) further identifies him as Proconsul ('non Praetoria potestate') when Mithridates took Asia. The coin is a bronze (Æ). Orsini makes no mention of M. Oppius Capito, Antony, a praefectus classis, or Achaea.

coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Winged Victory standing right, holding wreath; M.OPPI(?) legend

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens. Orsini presents one bronze coin of Q. Oppius, who served as Praetor (or, per Livy's epitome, Proconsul) in Asia during the Mithridatic war, where he was captured and displayed in chains by Mithridates at Laodicea. Orsini cites Appian (Mithridatico) and Livy (epitome lib. LXXVII). He also notes C. Oppius Tribunus plebis (who proposed the lex Oppia de matronarum habitu, anno DXL) and L. Oppius Salinator (Aedilis plebis anno DLX). The gens is represented numismatically by Q. Oppius alone.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents one coin of the Oppia gens. He identifies the moneyer as Q. Oppius (Praetor or Proconsul) captured by Mithridates in Asia, citing Appian's Mithridatico (extensive Greek quotation) and Livy's epitome (lib. LXXVII). He notes the historical background of the Mithridatic capture at Laodicea. He also mentions C. Oppius Tr. Pl. (lex Oppia de matronarum habitu, anno DXL, Livy lib. XXXIII) and L. Oppius Salinator (Aedilis plebis anno DLX, Livy lib. XXXV). There is no mention of M. Oppius Capito, Antony, or a praefectus classis.

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate male head right; TRIVMPVS below
coins_engraved.reverse: She-wolf or dog walking right; CELSVS·III·VIR / L·PAPIVS in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes TRIVMPVS is written without aspiration on this L. Papius Celsus coin ('Trivмpvs sine aspiratione, ut Pilippvs & Pilvs, pro Philippvs & Philvs ab antiquis scriptum fit, ex denarii inscriptione & Quinctil.li.I. satis constat'). The obverse figure is the Triumph simulacrum (not a Juno Sospita headdress). Orsini identifies L. Papius Celsus as Triumvir monetalis.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head of Juno Sospita right, wearing goatskin headdress; TRIVMPVS behind
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: She-wolf or dog walking right; CELSVS.III.VIR / L.PAPIVS in exergue

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Juno Sospita right, wearing goatskin headdress
coins_engraved.reverse: CELSVS.III.VIR above; she-wolf or dog walking right; PAPIVS in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the Juno Sospita headdress and the she-wolf with twins on the reverse as indicating the Papia gens's Lanuvian connections, noting the bronze simulacra of the lupa displayed there. He discusses the lex Papia on foreign residents and the tribunate of C. Papius as establishing the family's political importance beyond the numismatic evidence.

coins_engraved.obverse: Female head right (Juno Sospita), wearing goatskin headdress; star above
coins_engraved.reverse: Griffin springing right; L.PAPI in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini connects this L. Papius denarius to Lanuvium through the Juno Sospita headdress and discusses the griffin type. He cites the lex Papia on peregrini and the tribunate of C. Papius as establishing the family's political importance beyond the numismatic evidence.

coins_engraved.reverse: Griffin springing right; L·PAPI in exergue

Papius denarius with a different control symbol in the exergue and the same Juno Sospita headdress identifying the coin's Lanuvian connections. He groups the two Papius variants together as evidence of the moneyer's prolific issue.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head right, laureate; CELSVS behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Lyre (cithara); L.PAPI to right
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes the chelys (lyre) was Mercury's invention but confesses uncertainty about its significance on this L. Papius Celsus denarius. He includes it in the Papia series as documentary evidence for the moneyer's range of types without providing a specific iconographic explanation.

coins_engraved.obverse: Female head right
coins_engraved.reverse: Standing figure (Ceres or Juno) holding patera, facing right; serpent before; L.PAPIVS / CELSVS around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this sixth coin to L. Papius Celsus but offers no specific explanation for the reverse type. The description of 'a standing figure (possibly Ceres or Juno) holding a patera' is not in Orsini's text.

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens associated with Lanuvium. L. Papius struck denarii c. 79 BC (Crawford 384/1) with Juno Sospita/griffin types reflecting the Lanuvian cult. L. Papius Celsus was triumvir monetalis in 45 BC (Crawford 472/1-4), issuing a varied series including Juno Sospita, she-wolf and twins, and lyre types. The gens is known historically for the lex Papia de peregrinis (65 BC) and C. Papius, tribune of the plebs. All coin types emphasize Lanuvian religious connections.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents six coins of the Papia gens, correctly identifying L. Papius and L. Papius Celsus as moneyers. He connects the Juno Sospita headdress and she-wolf types to Lanuvium, citing the bronze simulacra of the lupa displayed there. He discusses the lex Papia on foreign residents and the tribunate of C. Papius. His treatment of the lyre (chelys) on coin 5 is uncertain, noting Mercury's invention but confessing ignorance of its numismatic significance.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Jupiter in quadriga right; M.CARBO below, ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies only the Carbones branch in his numismatic record of the Papiria gens and cites Livy, Cicero, and Appian for the turbulent history of the three Cn. Carbones. He notes M. Carbo obtained Sicily as praetor and was accused by P. Flaccus, and reads the M.CARBO legend as confirming the moneyer's identity.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Jupiter in quadriga right, hurling thunderbolt; CARB below, ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this denarius (legend CARB) to Cn. Papirius Carbo, who was consul three times (anno DCLXVIII, DCLXI, & DCLXXI) and was killed by Pompey at Lilybaeum anno DCLXXI ('quique à Pompeio Lilybaei anno DCLXXI in magistratu occisus est'). He cites Cicero (epistola ad Paetum) and Velleius (lib. II for C. Carbo).

coins_engraved.obverse: Greek legend EΠIΓAIOY / ΠAΠIPIOY / KAPBΩNOΣ vertically in wreath
coins_engraved.reverse: Greek legend NIKAIEΩN; monogram below; triangular tent or trophy shape with two staffs
coins_engraved.orsini_error: Orsini does not recognize this as a provincial issue from Nicaea in Bithynia; misattributes the coin's origin.
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini places this bronze under the Papiria gens because some attribute it to C. Papirius Carbo, brother of Cn. Carbo ter Consul (cited from Velleius lib. II as Praetorius). He explicitly reads the Greek inscription NIKAIEON ('ut ex inscriptione NikaieΩN apparet') and recognizes the coin was struck by the Nicaeans. He suggests it might better be attributed to C. Carbo as Praetor of Sardinia (anno DLXXXV) who could have governed Corsica simultaneously, or possibly to C. Cicereius (Praetor anno DLXXX) who triumphed over Sardinians and Corsicans (Livy lib. XLII).

completed.family_note: Patrician gens of great antiquity, with patrician and plebeian branches (Orsini cites Cicero's letter to Paetus). Republican coinage comprises the denarii of M. Papirius Carbo (legend M.CARBO, Crawford 276/1) and Cn. Papirius Carbo (legend CARB, Crawford 279/1). A third bronze coin carries the Greek inscription NIKAIEON and was struck by the Nicaeans; Orsini reads this inscription correctly and debates whether it should be assigned to C. Papirius Carbo (Praetor of Sardinia anno DLXXXV) or to C. Cicereius (Praetor of Sardinia anno DLXXX, who triumphed over Sardinians and Corsicans). Orsini does not identify the province as Bithynia nor mention Nicomedia.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents three coins under Papiria, focusing on the Carbo branch. He cites Cicero (epistola ad Paetum, de claris Oratoribus) and Velleius (lib. II) for the Carbones. He correctly reads M.CARBO and CARB on the first two denarii. For coin 3, he explicitly reads the Greek inscription NIKAIEON ('ut ex inscriptione NikaieΩN apparet') and recognizes it as struck by the Nicaeans; he debates the attribution between C. Papirius Carbo (Praetor of Sardinia) and C. Cicereius. He does not fail to read the Greek inscription; he does not identify the province as Bithynia. Appian is not cited for this gens.

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head right; COSTA to left
coins_engraved.reverse: IMP / BRVTV[S] or similar legend visible around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Pedanius Costa as Brutus's legate from the coin legend (LEG·COSTA on the obverse, IMP·BRVTVS on the reverse). He cites Livy (lib. XXV), Valerius Maximus (lib. III, cap. II), Tacitus (lib. XIV and XVII) for the Pedanii, and Plutarch (in Cicerone) for P. Costa. He concludes: 'nulla extat, quòd sciam, mentio apud ueteres scriptores' for Pedanius Costa specifically. He also corrects scribal error: 'Male autem P. Cotta, pro P. Costa interpretes uerterunt.'

completed.family_note: Minor plebeian gens whose cognomen is Costa. Orsini identifies Pedanius Costa as Brutus's legate from the coin inscription (LEG·COSTA / IMP·BRVTVS visible on the plate). He cites Livy (lib. XXV), Valerius Maximus (lib. III, cap. II), Tacitus (lib. XIV and XVII) for members of the Pedania gens, and Plutarch (in Cicerone) for a P. Costa who wished to appear a jurist. He notes there is no mention of Pedanius Costa (Bruti legatus) in any ancient writer he has read.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents one coin for Pedania. He cites Livy (lib. XXV), Valerius Maximus (lib. III, cap. II), Tacitus (lib. XIV and XVII), and Plutarch (in Cicerone) for the gens, then notes that Pedanius Costa as Brutus's legate ('Bruti legatum fuisse') is known only from the coin — 'nulla extat, quòd sciam, mentio apud ueteres scriptores.' He corrects those who render the cognomen as P. Costa: 'Male autem P. Cotta, pro P. Costa interpretes uerterunt.'

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Jupiter right, laureate; CAPITOLINVS behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Hexastyle temple (Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus); PETILLIVS in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Petillius Capitolinus as the moneyer, named by Horace (Sat. I.4: 'De Capitolini furtis iniecta Petilli'). Porphyrio explains he had charge of the Capitol ('Capitolii curam ageret') and faced accusations about a crown taken from it ('coronae subreptae de Capitolio'), acquitted by Caesar/Augustus. Orsini does not call him sacerdos, does not describe the crown as golden, and says the temple was vowed by Tarquinius Superbus and dedicated by M. Horatius Poplicolae's colleague — not 'rebuilt after Tarquinius Superbus.'

coins_engraved.obverse: Eagle on thunderbolt; PETILLIVS / CAPITOLINVS around
coins_engraved.reverse: Hexastyle temple (Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus); S F in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini groups both Petillia coins together under the same moneyer (Petillius Capitolinus) and the same Horatian/Porphyrian context. He again cites the temple as vowed by Tarquinius Superbus and dedicated by M. Horatius Poplicolae's colleague — not rebuilt. He does not describe the crown as golden.

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens. Petillius Capitolinus struck denarii (Crawford 487/1-2) celebrating the Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus. Horace (Sat. I.4) alludes to Petillius Capitolinus in connection with a theft ('Capitolini furtis iniecta Petilli'); Pomponius Porphyrio explains he had charge of the Capitol ('Capitolii curam ageret') and faced accusations about a crown taken from the Capitol ('coronae subreptae de Capitolio'), being acquitted by Augustus. Orsini does not call him sacerdos, and neither Orsini nor Porphyrio specifies that the crown was golden.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents two coins of the Petillia gens. He cites Livy (lib. VII) for C. Petillius Balbus Tr. Pl. and Livy (lib. XXXVIII) for Q. Petillius Spurinus (who proposed the lex Petillia de peculatu anno DLXVI). He identifies the moneyer as Petillius Capitolinus, named by Horace (Sat. I.4) in connection with a theft at the Capitol. He quotes Pomponius Porphyrio and Helenius Acro explaining that Petillius had charge of the Capitol ('Capitolii curam ageret/gereret') and was accused over a crown taken from it ('coronae subreptae/sublatae'), and was acquitted by Augustus/Caesar. Orsini does not call him sacerdos Iovis Capitolini. He then discusses the Temple of Jupiter Capitolinus, citing Plutarchus (in Poplicola), Dionysius (lib. II, IIII, V), Livy (lib. II), Tacitus, Valerius Maximus, Suetonius, Plinius.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head of Augustus left; CAESAR·AVGVSTVS text around
coins_engraved.reverse: Winged Victory standing, holding wreath in raised hand and palm; P·PETRON·TVRPILIAN·III·VIR around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini traces the Petronia gens to the Sabines, citing Valerius Maximus on the Petronius Sabinus cognomen, and identifies this as P. Petronius Turpilianus as triumvir monetalis under Augustus. He discusses the Sabine origins as the unifying theme of the entire Petronia coinage series.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: The crop is very small and shows only a partial portrait — a laureate head right with the text SAR (or CAES·AR) on one side and AVGVS (Augustus) visible. This is clearly Augustus's portrait.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Also a very small crop showing a partial scene — PET visible (PETRONIVS?) and what looks like a figure or animal. Cannot clearly resolve the reverse scene from this crop size.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Bare head of Augustus left; CAESAR·AVGVSTVS text around
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Winged siren standing left, holding flute in raised right hand; P·PETRON·TVRPILIAN·III·VIR text

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Liber right, ivy-wreathed; P·PETRONIVS·TVRPILIAN·III·VIR text
coins_engraved.reverse: Armenian kneeling right, wearing tiara and robe, extending hands; CAESAR·DIVI·F·ARME·CAPT text
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this coin as pertaining to Augustus's Armenian victory through Caius (son of Agrippa and Julia), citing Velleius lib. II, Suetonius in Augusto cap. XXI and LXIV, Florus lib. IV, and Dio lib. LV ('ex Augusti spectat uictoriam de Armeniis, contra quos Caius ex Agrippa & Iulia Augusto filius, missus fuerat'). Orsini also notes the reverse shows Caius and Lucius Caesar with clipei and hastae ('in altera Cai ipsius & Lucii fratris imagines cum clypeis & hastis impressae sunt').
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Partial crop of a laureate head right — the coin is cut off at edges. TRON visible on right border, possibly PETRON (Petronius). The head appears young and laureate.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Partial crop — CAP visible at top right, TVRP visible at bottom. This spells out TVRPILIANVS (Turpilianus). The scene within is cut off but shows partial figural elements.
coins_engraved.orsini_comment_ai: [QA: this note may describe a different type — flagged for review] Orsini connects the Tarpeia image on this P. Petronius Turpilianus coin (conjecta in eam scutis a Sabinis necata) to the Sabine origins of the Petronia gens, citing Virgil and Propertius for the Tarpeia legend. He treats this as part of the series illustrating Sabine-Roman historical themes.

coins_engraved.obverse: CAESAR AVGVSTVS: Bare head of Augustus right.
coins_engraved.reverse: PETRON·TVRPILIAN·III·VIR: Pegasus springing right.
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this coin with the Corinthian colony (re-)founded by Caesar and restored by Augustus, citing the Pegasus type on Corinthian bronze coins as a parallel ('nam in aereis quoque Corinthiorum nummis, Pegasi signo coloniam hanc notari animadvertimus'). He is confident in the attribution: 'nullo modo dubitari potest.' No confusion or misinterpretation of the engraving is mentioned by Orsini.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Caesar left, laureate; legend around
coins_engraved.reverse: Crescent and star; legend around border
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini connects the star and crescent reverse to the broader Augustan coinage program and identifies this as part of Turpilianus's varied reverse types as triumvir monetalis. He treats the celestial imagery as reflecting Augustan religious themes.

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head of Augustus right; imperial titulature
coins_engraved.reverse: Tarpeia being crushed by shields; PETRONIVS TVRPILIANVS around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies coin 5 as the Tarpeia type, connecting it to the Sabine origin of the gens: 'Quòd igitur è Sabinis gens Petronia uenisset, Tarpeiae signum, coniectis in eam scutis à Sabinis necatae, in quinto denario Petronius expressit.' He discusses Tarpeia's story at length citing Varro and Virgil/Servius. The moneyer is the same P. Petronius of the series.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head right (Turpilianus); III·VIR / TVRPILIANVS around
coins_engraved.reverse: Kneeling figure presenting a military standard; CAESAR AVGVSTVS / SIGN·RECE around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the SIGNIS RECEPTIS type as celebrating Augustus's recovery of the Parthian standards lost at Carrhae, citing Dio and Suetonius on the temple of Mars Ultor built to house the returned signa. He correctly identifies P. Petronius Turpilianus as the moneyer.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Head right (Petronius Turpilianus); IIIVIR / TVRPILIANVS around
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Warrior (Mars or soldier) striding right, carrying trophy; CAESAR AVGVSTVS / SIGN.RECE around

coins_engraved.obverse: Head right; IIIVIR / TVRPILIAN[VS] around; ERS below
coins_engraved.reverse: Elephant walking right; AVGVSTVS above, altar or base below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses the Feronia simulacrum on this coin as indicating the Sabine deity Feronia, whose sanctuary at Soracte was famous for its market, cited by Strabo. He uses this to confirm the Petronia gens's Sabine origins, citing Dionysius of Halicarnassus for the Feronia cult's antiquity.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Feronia right, diademed; TVRPILIANVS III VIR FERON
coins_engraved.reverse: Parthian kneeling, extending a military standard (aquila); CAESAR AVGVSTVS SIGN(IS) RECE(PTIS) around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses a second Feronia type denarius and elaborates on the Feronia sanctuary at Soracte, its famous market, and the deity's Sabine character. He cites Strabo and Dionysius of Halicarnassus to establish the religious-geographical connection between the Petronia gens and the Sabine cult.

coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Caesar seated left on curule chair; legend around

completed.family_note: In Orsini's prose (p.193) the name is spelled TVRPILIANVS: 'cum esset Turpilia natus familia, in Petroniam iure adoptionis insertus, P.PETRONIVS TVRPILIANVS dictus est.' The form 'Tvtpilianvs' appears only in the coin-plate engraving legend (second plate, third coin, p.192), where the engraver rendered the name as TVTPILIANVS (T for R in the second syllable — an engraver error or optical confusion). Orsini himself consistently uses TVRPILIANVS in his text. The flag's suggestion that Orsini spells it 'Tvtpilianvs' is incorrect; any such claim in the concordance commentary should be corrected to distinguish the plate legend (TVTPILIANVS, engraver error) from Orsini's prose (TVRPILIANVS, standard).
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents eight denarii of Petronius Turpilianus across two plates. He traces the Sabine origin through Valerius Maximus (lib. I, cap. I) and two Sabine inscriptions (the Anconitan inscription for L. Petronius Sabinus, and the Trebula/Mutuesca fragment). He discusses the fifth coin's Tarpeia scene citing Varro and Virgil (via Servius on Aeneid VIII); he does not cite Propertius for Tarpeia. The SIGNIS RECEPTIS type (sixth coin) is discussed with citations of Velleius lib. II, Livy in epitome lib. CXXXIX, Suetonius in Augusto cap. XXI, and Dio lib. LIIII; Orsini also mentions the temple of Mars Ultor ('templum Martis Vltoris in Capitolio'). The Feronia cult at Soracte is documented via Dionysius of Halicarnassus lib. III and Strabo lib. V.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory in biga right; NAT behind; X below; ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this coin (and coin 2) to L. Natta, known from Cicero's pro Murena as a young man of high birth, and from Suetonius as co-heir with Q. Pedius of Caesar's estate ex quadrante. He also cites Tacitus lib. IV as noting a Pinarius Natta as a client of Sejanus under Tiberius. He cites Virgil lib. VIII ('Et domus Herculei custos Pinaria sacri') for the Pinarii's hereditary role.

coins_engraved.reverse: Victory in biga right, holding reins and whip; NAT in field; ROMA in exergue

He treats this second Natta denarius as confirming the family's late Republican prominence alongside the inherited priestly functions.

coins_engraved.reverse: Winged Victory advancing right, holding wreath and palm; SCARPVS to left, ANT(ONIO) AVG to right
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this coin to Pinarius Scarpus as Antony's praefectus in Africa, citing Dio lib. LI. He infers the coin was struck in Africa because Scarpus was called 'Imp.' there. He also connects the Jove Ammon obverse (visible on the denarius) to the African cult of Jove Ammon, citing Herodotus lib. II, Hyginus in fabulis, Ovid Metam. lib. V, Lucan lib. IX, Servius in Aeneid lib. IV. He does not cite the specific legend 'M.ANTO.COS.III' in his text.

completed.family_note: Patrician gens of great antiquity, traditionally sharing the hereditary priesthood of Hercules. Orsini cites Plutarch (in Numa) for the origin from Pinus, son of Numa Pompilius, while Livy lib. II and Dionysius lib. VIII prefer to derive the gens from the Pinarii who performed Hercules's anniversary rites at the Ara Maxima. Two branches are represented in the coins: Pinarius Natta (Republican denarii, coins 1–2, attributed by Orsini to the L. Natta of Cicero's time, known from pro Murena) and Pinarius Scarpus (coin 3), who was Antony's praefectus in Africa.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents three coins of the Pinaria gens. He derives the gens from Pinus son of Numa (Plutarch), with the alternative Livian/Dionysian derivation from the Hercules priests. He identifies coins 1–2 as pertaining to L. Natta, known from Cicero pro L. Murena ('natum loco summo adolescentem') and from Suetonius cap. LXXXIII as Caesar's heir ex quadrante together with Q. Pedius. He explicitly rules out the earlier Natta who was Magister Equitum under L. Manlius Dict. in year 390, as silver coinage did not yet exist then. He identifies coin 3 as Pinarius Scarpus, Antony's African prefect, citing Dio lib. LI. He derives the cognomen Scarpus from Greek κaρπός (meaning the hollow of the hand / palm), and connects the hand imagery on the reverse to this etymology. The characterization of Orsini's dating as 'imprecise' is a modern judgment not grounded in his text.

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens. M. Plaetorius Cestianus struck an extensive series as curule aedile c. 69 BC (Crawford 405/1-5) with Cybele, Sors, she-wolf, eagle, and caduceus types reflecting aedilician responsibilities. L. Plaetorius Cestianus served as Brutus' proquaestor, striking the famous EID MAR denarius (Crawford 508/3) commemorating Caesar's assassination, as well as military denarii (Crawford 508/2). The lex Plaetoria on minors' contracts gave the family historical prominence.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents nine coins across two plates for the Plaetoria gens. He discusses the Plaetorian/Laetoria name equivalence citing Varro lib. V de Ling. Lat. and Livy lib. XXX. He infers Sabine origin from inscriptions, noting 'Trebulam siue Mutuescam Sabinorum oppidum fuisse' and citing Pliny lib. III cap. XII and Virgil for this location. He identifies M. Plaetorius as aedilis curulis from Cicero's pro A. Cluentio and pro M. Fonteio (not from the lex Plaetoria, which is cited from Censorinus de die natali cap. XIX). On L. Plaetorius (coins 7–8), Orsini says he was perhaps the BROTHER ('frater fortasse') of the aedile and was Brutus's quaestor ('Bruti Procos. qui coniurationis princeps fuit, Quaestorem') — 'princeps coniurationis' applies to BRUTUS, not L. Plaetorius. The Moneta imago (coin 8) is explained as the treasury goddess associated with quaestors going to the provinces ('Quaestores Prouinciales... pecuniam sibi ex aerario a Senatu attributam'), not as a symbol of liberty from Caesar. Coin 9 of the second plate Orsini identifies as belonging to M. Plaetorius Cestianus (the aedile), not L. Plaetorius.

coins_engraved.reverse: Cretan goat (Amalthea) standing right
