He connects the coin's reverse to Plancius's Aedilitas ('monumenta quoque Aedilitatis expressa sunt'), citing Cicero lib. III de legibus on aediles as curatores of games. He does not connect the reverse type to Crete or to 'family associations.'

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens. Cn. Plancius served as Tribunus Plebis in year 696 AUC (under consuls P. Lentulus and Q. Metellus), as Quaestor in Macedonia (where he hosted Cicero in exile at Thessalonica for seven months), and sought the Aedileship in year 699 AUC under consuls L. Domitius Ahenobarbus and Ap. Claudius Pulcher, whereupon he was accused of ambitus by M. Iuuentius Laterensis and defended by Cicero (pro Plancio). He struck a single denarius. Orsini does not connect the reverse type to Crete or a 'Cretan quaestorship'; the quaestorship was in Macedonia.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents one coin of the Plancia gens. He identifies Cn. Plancius from the denarius inscription as Tribunus Plebis. He cites Cicero lib. II ad Q. Fratrem, lib. I ad P. Lentulum, and Dio lib. XXXIX for his Macedonian quaestorship and hosting of Cicero. He cites Cicero pro Plancio and ep. VIII lib. III ad Att. for the aedileship contest and ambitus accusation. He notes that the aediles were curatores of solemn games, citing Cicero lib. III de legibus ('curatores erant ludorum solemnium, in quibus praeter alia, uenationes & gladiatorum munera exhibebantur'). He connects the coin's reverse monument imagery to the Aedilitas ('eius Aedilitatis memoria, ipsa denarii inscriptione celebratur, in cuius altera parte monumenta quoque Aedilitatis expressa sunt'). Orsini does not connect the reverse type to Crete. The note that 'His attribution and prosopographic discussion are correct' is a modern editorial judgment absent from Orsini.

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens (Orsini explicitly says 'PLAUTIAM gentem plebeiam fuisse'). Orsini derives the name from the cognomen Plautus, as Augustine derives Iulia from Iulus and Varia from Varro. The gens appears also as Plotia and Plutia in ancient monuments. Coin 1 shows L. Plautus Plancus, identified as the brother of L. Munatius Plancus, proscribed by the Triumvirs (Velleius lib. II, Appian lib. IV). Coins 2–4 were struck by P. Plautius Hypsaeus in memory of C. Plautius Hupfaeus (consul who captured Privernum, cognominated Decianus in the Fasti). Coin 5 shows A. Plautius as curule aedile; Orsini debates whether the camel refers to Bacchius 'Iudaeus' (an Arab king) submitted to Plautius while serving under Pompey, ultimately preferring ('magis placeret') this Arabian reading. Coin 6 (C. Plutius) may be the same as C. Plotius Rufus on the next plate. Orsini says nothing about 'C. Plutius striking Roma/Dioscuri denarii c. 121 BC.'
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents six coins of the Plautia gens. He discusses the Plautius/Plotius/Plutius name variants (citing Augustine, Velleius, Appian, Pliny, Solinus). For coin 1 he identifies L. Plautus Plancus as proscribed brother of the triumvir L. Munatius Plancus. For coins 2–4 he identifies P. Plautius Hypsaeus and reads the legend 'C. HVPSAEO CONSULE PREIVERNVM CAPTV' (not 'PRIV' = privatus; PRIV = PREIVERNVM). He notes Hypsaeus was Pompey's quaestor and later curule aedile with M. Scaurus. For coin 5 he identifies A. Plautius as curule aedile (year 696 AUC, per Cicero lib. I ad Lentulum, lib. II ad Q. Fratrem, and Dio lib. XXXIX). He debates BACCHIVS IVDAEVS for coin 5, preferring the reading of an Arab king Bacchius submitted to Plautius. For coin 6 he tentatively identifies C. Plutius with C. Plotius Rufus (next plate). He confirms C. Plutius held the name 'Romanae familiae nomen non... unius Horatii testimonio' (Horace Sat. VII lib. I) but provides no prosopographic detail beyond a Sabine family connection.

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens, considered identical with the Plautia gens by ancient and modern scholars. C. Plotius Rufus served as triumvir monetalis under Augustus c. 15 BC (RIC I 389), striking bronze coins with the standard Augustan oak-wreath/S.C. type. Orsini explicitly states the Plotia and Plautia gentes were the same family.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents one bronze coin of C. Plotius Rufus, triumvir monetalis under Augustus. He immediately identifies the Plotia as the same gens as Plautia/Plutia ('PLOTIAM gentem eandem fuisse cum Plautia siue Plutia supra diximus'). He notes that C. Plotius Rufus may be the same person as C. Plutius mentioned on coin 6 of the Plautia plate ('fortasse is est, qui in sexto superioris tabellae denario C. Plutius nominatur'). He explicitly states that no mention of C. Plotius Rufus exists in ancient writers ('de eo, quicunq. sit (nulla, quòd sciam) extat mentio apud ueteres scriptores').

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens (also spelled Publicia). C. Poblicius Malleolus struck denarii c. 118 BC (Crawford 282/3) as part of the Narbo colonial founding series with L. Licinius and Cn. Domitius. C. Poblicius Q.f. issued Hercules/Nemean lion denarii c. 80 BC (Crawford 380/1). M. Poblicius served as Cn. Pompey's legatus pro praetore in Spain (Crawford 469/1a), striking military denarii during the Pompeian campaign of 46-45 BC.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents six coins of the Poblicia/Publicia gens (he uses both forms, treating them as the same name: 'siue Pvbliciam... utroque enim modò in ueteribus monumentis reperitur'). He attributes the first three denarii to C. POBLICIVM MALLEOLVM, identified as Cn. Dolobellae in Asia Quaestor, citing Cicero lib. ii in Verrem ('C. Maleolo occifo, Cn. Dolobellae Proquaeftore'). He derives the Malleolos cognomen from the malleus (hammer), inferring the family's ancestor was the first to discover the mallet. The fourth coin is assigned to C. Poblicius Q. f., identified from Cicero's pro Cluentio as possibly the son of Q. Poblicius who was Praetor Urbanus under M. Iunius. For the fifth coin, Orsini explicitly states M. Poblicius was Pompey's legatus Propraetore in HISPANIA — not in the Piratic war: 'M. autem Poblicium Cn. Pompei Legatum Propraetore, in Hispania, non in bello Piratico fuiffe, ex Hifpaniae ipfius imagine, quae in altera denarii parte fignata eft, facilè conftat.' The sixth coin is part of the joint Narbo colonial issue with L. Licinius and Cn. Domitius (legend L.LIC.CN.DOM visible on the coin). Orsini makes no claim connecting the Hercules types to any 'family tradition' or 'Sabine origins.'

coins_engraved.obverse: Single bare male head (Pompey); MAGNVS / PIVS·IMP·ITER around.
coins_engraved.reverse: PRAEF / CLAS.ET.ORAE / MARIT.EX.S.C around; two male heads facing each other
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the first coin as a gold aureus of Sex. Pompeius Magnus filius, struck when he held the praefecture of the fleet and maritime coast by senatorial decree ('claffis, & orae maritimae ex s.c. praefectus'). He argues at length that the obverse portrait is Cn. Pompey the Great (not a jugate portrait of father and son): 'facilè adducor ut credam hanc effe ueram Cn. Pompeii imaginem (non autem eam, quae uulgò creditur, quae cum Sexti fit, malè Cn. patri tributa eft).' On the reverse, besides his father's portrait, there is 'corona quaedam impressa est, quae licet è quercu sit, eam tamen esse arbitramur, quam Pompeio Senatum concessisse... tradit Dio li.xxxvii.' He draws on Dio lib. xxxvii for the oak crown and on Velleius for Alexander's likeness to Pompey.

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens of enormous political importance. Cn. Pompeius Magnus (Pompey the Great) dominates the family's numismatic record through coins struck by his legates and officers: Cn. Piso (Crawford 446/1), M. Terentius Varro (Crawford 447/1a), M. Poblicius (Crawford 469/1a), and M. Minatius Sabinus (Crawford 470/1c). Sextus Pompeius Magnus Pius struck naval-themed coinage in Sicily (Crawford 511/1-3) including the Scylla type. Q. Pompeius Rufus issued the famous grandfather portrait denarius (Crawford 434/1-2). Sex. Pompeius Fostlus struck the early she-wolf denarius (Crawford 235/1c, 137 BC).
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) devotes fifteen coins to the Pompeia gens, the most extensive P-family treatment. He discusses Pompey's naval triumphs over the pirates and the CLAS ET ORAE MARIT praefecture. He identifies Sextus Pompey's adoption of Neptune as patron, citing Dio and Appian. He connects Q. Pompeius Rufus to Sulla through the double-curule-chair type. His PIVS cognomen discussion notes it appears only on coins, not in literary sources. His prosopographic web linking Pompey's legates is extensive.

coins_engraved.orsini_comment: The substance of the coin 9 comment IS verifiable from the scan. The text continues on the following page: 'Barbiton quod Polyhymniae, ut diximus, Musae tribuit Horatius, cuiusmodi fuerit, ex eo, quod in denario impressum est, cognosci potest.' Orsini cites Horace Carm. I.1 for the barbiton ('si neque tibias / Euterpe cohibet: nec Polyhymnia / Lesboum refugit tendere barbiton') and identifies the Muse on the coin as Polyhymnia from this instrument. The comment is broadly correct; the flag's claim that it 'cannot be fully verified' is incorrect — both pages (the 'Barbi-' page and its continuation) fall within the readable range.

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens claiming descent from Pompo, son of King Numa Pompilius. L. Pomponius Molo struck denarii c. 97 BC (Crawford 334/1) with Numa sacrificing at altar. Q. Pomponius Musa issued the celebrated series of nine Muses plus Hercules Musarum c. 66 BC (Crawford 410/1-10), one of the most artistically ambitious Roman Republican coin series. The temple of Hercules Musarum, restored by L. Marcius Philippus, provided the iconographic program for the series.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents fourteen coins of the Pomponia gens. He derives the family from Pompo, son of Numa Pompilius, citing Plutarch (Numa). For the first coin he identifies L. POMPONIVS who 'indicare primo denario voluit' the Numa Pompilius connection (NVM.POMPIL on the coin). The second coin's moneyer (CN. F.) Orsini cannot identify: 'quis fuerit, quia nulla de eo apud fcriptores mentio reperitur, mihi diuinare non licet.' For the third coin he reads Q. POMPONI. MVSA and associates it with Q. Pomponius Musa. The fourth coin onwards (Q. POMPONIVS MVSA) he associates with the Muses series. He describes the Hercules Musarum temple as built by Fulvius Nobilior ('ex pecunia cenforia fecit') from booty in Greece, and later restored by L. Marcius Philippus (citing Suetonius in Augusto). He debates at length whether the MVSA and RVFVS coins belong to one person or two Pomponii families, ultimately concluding there were two families ('ad duas Pomponiae gentis familias pertinere hos denarios puto'). He cites Valerius Maximus (lib. iiii, cap. i v) and a bronze tablet inscription for Q. Pomponius Rufus. He does NOT mention a 'Gemellus cognomen' anywhere in his Pomponia text, and does not cite Cicero's Brutus for any cognomen in this context.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; LLIC[A] behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Naked bearded warrior (Bituitus) in biga right, hurling spear; L.PORCI around; L·LIC·CN·DOM in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the moneyer of the first Porcia coin as L. Porcius Licinus (not a member of the Cato branch), citing Livy lib. XXXIX for his praetorship (an. DLX) and consulship with P. Claudius Pulcher (an. DLXIX). The reverse legend ELIC·CN·DON identifies this as the Narbo colonial joint issue.
coins_engraved.specimen_shared_reason: same catalogue type cross-listed under multiple gentes (joint-moneyer issue or sub-variant); one museum specimen serves all

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory in biga right, holding reins and whip; C.CATO below; ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes C. Porcius Cato was consul with M. Acilius Balbus and treats this standard Roma/Victory biga type as the Cato moneyer's documentary coin. He cites Livy for the consular chronology and connects the coin to the Catones' Republican prominence.

coins_engraved.obverse: Female head right (Roma); ROM[A] behind; M.CATO.PRO.PR around
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory seated right, holding wreath; VICTRIX in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini connects the VICTRIX type on coin 3 primarily to M. Cato SENIOR's dedication of a Victoria virginis aedicula, citing Livy lib. XXXV: 'Victoriae simulacrum, quod in altera denariorum parte expressum est, pertinet, vt arbitror, ad ea, quae de M. Catone seniore tradit Livius lib. xxxv. iisdem diebus, aeculam Victoriae virginis prope aedem Victoriae M. Porcius Cato dedicauit, biennio postquam vouerat, P. Victor in VIII. regione Fori Romani.' He uses Velleius and Plutarch separately for Cato Uticensis's biography and propraetura, but the VICTRIX iconographic interpretation is anchored in the Livy passage on M. Cato Senior. The comment's attribution of 'anti-Caesarian stand' as Orsini's stated interpretive frame for the VICTRIX type is an editorial overstatement.

coins_engraved.obverse: Female head right; M.CATO around
coins_engraved.reverse: Seated Victory right, holding wreath; VICTRIX in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini connects this variant of the M. Cato pro praetore type to M. Cato Censori proavo, citing Cato's unparalleled virtue and Tusculan heritage. He treats the repeated VICTRIX type as the Porcia gens's most distinctive numismatic monument.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; LAECA behind; X below
coins_engraved.reverse: Libertas in quadriga right, crowned by flying Victory, holding rod and pileus; M.PORC / ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the moneyer of the fifth coin as M. Porcius Laeca, connecting him to Sallust's account of the Catilinarian conspiracy: 'is est quem cum Catilina coniurasse scribit Sallustuius in coniuratione Catilinae, in cuiusque domum coniuratos conuenisse D. Silano L. Murena Coss. anno DCXCI, tradit Cicero pro P. Sulla.' He notes Laeca was subsequently condemned under the lex Lutatia.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma or Libertas right; P.LAECA behind; X below
coins_engraved.reverse: Three standing figures (provocatio scene): a togate citizen at left, a magistrate raising his hand in the centre, and a lictor at right; PROVOCO in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini states explicitly that P. Laeca, moneyer of the sixth coin, is unknown in ancient literary sources ('De P. autem LAECA, qui sextum denarium cusit, nullam reperio apud scriptores mentionem'). He then connects the PROVOCO legend to the lex Porcia protecting citizens from arbitrary corporal punishment, citing Cicero pro Rabirio and Sallust's Catilina on the Porcia lex.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Helmeted head of Roma or Libertas right; P.LAECA behind; X below
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Scene with two standing figures (provocatio scene: citizen appealing to magistrate); PROVOCO in exergue

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens of Tusculan origin, famous for the Cato branch. C. Porcius Cato struck denarii c. 123 BC (Crawford 274/1) with standard Roma/Victory types. M. Porcius Cato Uticensis issued denarii as propraetor in Africa c. 47-46 BC (Crawford 462/1) with Victory/VICTRIX types celebrating his anti-Caesarian stand. M. Porcius Laeca (Crawford 270/1, 125 BC) and P. Porcius Laeca (Crawford 301/1, 110 BC) represent the Laeca branch; P. Laeca's PROVOCO type celebrates the lex Porcia protecting citizens from arbitrary punishment.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents six coins of the Porcia gens. He opens by identifying M. Cato Censorius as Tusculan by origin (p.215-216), citing Cicero de Legibus, Plutarch (Greek passage quoted), and Velleius. For the first coin he identifies the moneyer as L. Porcius Licinus (not a Cato), citing Livy lib. XXXIX for his praetorship and consulship with P. Claudius Pulcher. The second coin is attributed to C. Porcius Cato, consul with M'. Acilius Balbus (in Fastis). The third and fourth coins he assigns to M. Cato Uticensis (M. Catonis Censorii pronepos), drawing on Plutarch, Appianus, and Dio; the VICTRIX type he connects primarily to a tradition traceable to M. Cato Senior's dedication of an aedicula Victoriae virginis near the aedes Victoriae (citing Livy lib. XXXV), rather than to Cato's anti-Caesarian stand as such. For the fifth coin he identifies M. Porcius Laeca — the Catilinarian conspirator — citing Sallust's Coniuratio Catilinae. For the sixth coin (P. Laeca, PROVOCO) Orsini explicitly states he finds no mention of P. Laeca in ancient sources ('nullam reperio apud scriptores mentionem'), then discusses the lex Porcia on provocatio, citing Cicero pro Rabirio and Sallust's Catilina passage.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bust of Diana right, draped, with bow and quiver over shoulder
coins_engraved.reverse: Three horsemen charging left; before, two standards and fallen warrior; A·ALBINVS·S·F legend.
coins_engraved.moneyer: A. Postumius Albinus (with L. Caecilius Metellus and C. Publicius Malleolus)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini traces the Postumia gens as patrician, flourishing post reges exactos, and identifies A. Postumius Albinus from Sallust's Bellum Iugurthinum as the one who lost in Africa. He provides an extensive discussion of the Battle of Lake Regillus as the family's founding moment of glory, citing Dionysius and Livy.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Clear female or helmeted head right. Text: ROMA visible below the portrait. The head appears to be Roma or Diana — with hair tied back or helmeted.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: The reverse shows two coins side by side (the SAM extraction has grabbed a double coin). Left coin shows a horseman or battle scene — A·ALBINVS text visible below. Right coin shows a partial circle with a star and the beginning of ROMA text.

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head right (Apollo); ROMA behind; star before
coins_engraved.reverse: Horsemen (cavalry) galloping right; A.ALBINVS in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini connects the three horsemen on this A. Postumius Albinus type to A. Postumius Dictator's victory at Lake Regillus, where Castor and Pollux appeared to aid the Romans against the Latins, citing Dionysius and Livy. He treats this as the primary commemoration of the Regillus victory in Republican coinage.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Laureate head right (Apollo); ROMA behind; star before
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Figure in cart or chariot drawn by oxen; A.ALBINVS below

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate (bare, not helmeted) head right; A.ALBINVS / METELLI legend around
coins_engraved.reverse: Single winged Victory standing right; C.MAL above, ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: The obverse and reverse descriptions sometimes given for this coin ('bare head right with A·ALBINVS / METELLI', 'winged Victory with C·MAL above') do not appear in Orsini's text and is not confirmed by the plate. Orsini's discussion of coins 1-3 on the first Postumia plate concerns the Lake Regillus victory and the Albinus family's Jugurthine-war connection. The specific legend 'METELLI' is not mentioned by Orsini for any Postumia coin.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Helmeted head of Roma or Mars right; A.ALBINVS below; METE[LLI] around
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Seated Roma right; Victory crowning Roma; ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment_ai: [QA: this note may describe a different type — flagged for review] Orsini identifies the seated Roma crowned by Victory reverse as recalling A. Postumius Dictator's triumph over the Latins at Regillus, the first Roman triumph over a Latin people, citing Dionysius. He connects the three standing warriors on the obverse to the Roman forces at the battle.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Mars in quadriga, right, holding spear, shield and reins in left hand and trophy in right hand. L·POST·ALB ROMA
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini cites Livy on the Flamen Martialis inauguration and identifies the apex Flaminis insigne on this L. Postumius Albinus denarius. He connects the Mars quadriga type to L. Postumius Albinus's Flamenship and discusses the family's religious offices alongside their military commands.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Small helmeted Roma head facing right; X (denarius mark) before; plain field.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Galloping horse or horseman right; ROMA in exergue.

coins_engraved.obverse: Female head right (Diana), with hair tied back
coins_engraved.reverse: Hound running right; C.POSTVMI / A below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies C. Postumius (Diana head / dog type) as unknown in literary sources ('licet à nullo, quòd sciam, veterum scriptorum nominetur') and connects the Diana image and dog to the Ludi Saeculares. He does NOT mention an ox at the altar ('bos ad aram stans') for this coin — that detail appears for the third coin of the second plate (the Ludi Saeculares imagery discussed on p.220).
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Female head (Diana?) facing right; hair pulled back with headband; graceful profile.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Hound running right; hunting spear below; C·POSTUMI below; A in exergue.

coins_engraved.obverse: Draped head right (no beard), anchor control-symbol below; A.POST.A.F / S.N.ALBIN around
coins_engraved.reverse: Sacrifice scene: an ox standing left, a lighted altar/cippus in the centre, and a togate (priest) figure standing right; A.POST.A.F / S.N.ALBIN around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this coin to A. Postumius A.f.Sp.n. Albinus as the MONEYER commemorating L. Postumius Albini Propr.'s triumph over Vaccaei and Lusitani in Hispania (anno DLXXV), citing Livy lib. XLI. The moneyer (A. Postumius) and the honorand (L. Postumius) are distinct; Orsini's A.F.S.N. filiation identifies the moneyer as son of A. Postumius, grandson of Spurius.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Male portrait head facing right; laureate or with fillet; legend A·POST·A·F·RABIN(?) around.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Animal (ox or bull?) and second animal at altar or cippus; A·POST·A·F legend.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Bearded head right (Bacchus or Silenus), wreathed with ivy
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: A.POST.A.F / S.N.ALBIN around; figure with trophy or seated captive

coins_engraved.obverse: Veiled female head right (Hispania); HISPA[NIA] around
coins_engraved.reverse: Single togate figure standing right, raising hand, flanked by a legionary eagle (aquila) at left and a fasces at right; A[LBIN]VS / POST.A.F around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Same attribution context as coin 6: Orsini assigns the HISPANIA type to the moneyer A. Postumius A.f.Sp.n. Albinus, commemorating L. Postumius Albini's Hispania triumph. The Bacchus/Silenus obverse identification and the moneyer/honorand distinction should be maintained as in coin 6.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Male or female head facing right; legend around with POST or similar.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Standing figure (Roma or deity) right or left; POST·A in field.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Veiled female head right (Hispania); HISPA[NIA] around
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Standing togate figure at altar or column; A[LBIN]VS around; figure with spear to right

completed.family_note: Patrician gens of great distinction. The Albinus branch dominates the coinage: A. Postumius Albinus struck the Battle of Lake Regillus type c. 96 BC (Crawford 335/1, 335/10) commemorating the dictator A. Postumius' victory over the Latins with Castor and Pollux's aid. L. Postumius Albinus (Crawford 252/1, 131 BC) struck Roma/Mars quadriga types. C. Postumius issued Diana/hunting dog denarii c. 74 BC (Crawford 394/1a). A. Postumius A.f. Sp.n. Albinus (Crawford 372/1-2, 81 BC) struck types referencing the family's Spanish campaigns.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents coins of the Postumia gens across two separate plate-tables. He opens by identifying the gens as patrician ('gens patricia, Romae floruit post exactos reges') with the Albinus branch as the most distinguished in the coinage. For the first plate: coin 1 identifies A. Albinus (S.F. = Spurii Filius) as the brother and legate of Sp. Postumius, consul with Q. Minucius Rufus for the Numidian province (anno DCXLIII), citing Sallust Bellum Iugurthinum. The reverse of coin 1 he connects to A. Postumius Dictator's victory at Lake Regillus (anno CCLVII), citing Dionysius lib. VI and Livy lib. I, where Castor and Pollux appeared to aid the Romans. For the second plate: the first coin (concordance n.4) pertains to L. Postumius Albinus Flamen Martialis, citing Livy lib. XLV verbatim for his inauguration (anno DLXXXVI). The apex Flaminis insigne identifies the Flamenship. C. Postumius (concordance n.5, Diana/dog type) is connected to the Ludi Saeculares — Orsini notes Diana's image and the dog as indicators, but says C. Postumius is otherwise unattested in literary sources. The ox at the altar ('bos ad aram stans') appears on the THIRD coin of the second plate (concordance n.6 or similar), not on the C. Postumius Diana/dog coin. The HISPANIA type (concordance nn.6-7) is attributed by Orsini to A. Postumius A.f.Sp.n. Albinus (the moneyer) striking to commemorate L. Postumius Albini Propr.'s triumph over the Vaccaei and Lusitani ex Hispania (anno DLXXV), citing Livy lib. XLI.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Jupiter right, laureate; S.C behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Standing Juno Sospita right, holding spear and shield; serpent at feet; L.PROCILI / F around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies L. Procilius as from Lanuvium and connects the coin to the Juno Sospita cult, citing Cicero pro L. Murena and de Legibus lib. I. Livy is cited in the general Lanuvian discussion (ciuitas data) but not as the primary source for coin 1's identification. De Natura Deorum is not cited for this gens.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Juno Sospita right, wearing goatskin headdress
coins_engraved.reverse: Juno Sospita in biga right, hurling spear; serpent below horses; L.PROCILI.F around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini describes the Juno Sospita cult iconography, quoting the 'pelle caprina, cum hasta, cum scutulo, cum calceis repandis' passage from Cicero pro L. Murena and de Legibus lib. I. The source is NOT de Natura Deorum (AI hallucination). He also cites Livy (Lanuuinis ciuitas data) and Festus (Sispita = Sospita etymology) in the extended discussion.

completed.family_note: Plebeian gens of Lanuvian origin. L. Procilius struck two denarius types (Crawford 379/1-2) featuring Juno Sospita, the cult image of Lanuvium. Both types emphasize the Lanuvian cult of Juno Sospita, shared with the Roscia gens (cf. Orsini's cross-reference). The detailed rendering of the goatskin headdress (pelle caprina, cum hasta, cum scutulo, cum calceis repandis) is quoted by Orsini from Cicero's oratio pro L. Murena and de Legibus lib. I — not from de Natura Deorum.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents two coins of the Procilia gens. He identifies L. Procilius as from the Lanuvium municipality and provides a detailed description of the Juno Sospita cult, quoting Cicero's pro L. Murena and de Legibus lib. I (not de Natura Deorum) on the goddess's distinctive dress. He also cites Livy lib. VIII (ciuitas data Lanuuinis) and Cicero ad Q. Fratrem lib. II on L. Procilius's Lanuvine origin. He cross-references the Roscia gens for the same type. He does not cite de Natura Deorum for this gens.

coins_engraved.obverse: Large S C in centre of field; T.CRISPINVS around outside border; legend partially visible around edge including SVLPICIANVS
coins_engraved.reverse: AVGVSTVS TRIBVNIC POTEST in three lines within oak wreath
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this Augustan bronze to T. Quinctius Crispinus Sulpicianus, identified as consul anno DCCLIII with Nero Claudius Drusus. The S.C within oak wreath type is confirmed on the plate.

coins_engraved.obverse: Large S C in centre; T.CRISPINVS around outside
coins_engraved.reverse: AVGVSTVS TRIBVNIC POTEST in three lines within oak wreath
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this Augustan bronze (AVGVSTVS TRIBVNIC POTEST in wreath) to T. Quinctius Crispinus Sulpicianus. He connects Crispinus negatively to Velleius's characterization ('singularem nequitiam supercilio truci protegens') and to Horace's Ode XI lib. I (Cantaber/Scythes). The prosopographic link to Flamininus is part of the general family discussion, not presented by Orsini as a genealogical demonstration.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
coins_engraved.reverse: The Dioscuri galloping right; T.Q below, ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini includes the Republican T.Q denarius on the same plate as the Augustan bronzes, and the plate header assigns all to Crispinus Sulpicianus ('qui huius tabellae nummos signauit'). Orsini does NOT attribute this coin to T. Quinctius Flamininus; that attribution is an AI error.

completed.family_note: The Quinctii were a patrician gens of great antiquity, transferred from Alba to Rome under king Tullus (Livy lib. I). Orsini illustrates four Augustan bronzes and one Republican denarius, all attributed on the plate to T. Quinctius Crispinus Sulpicianus — identified as consul in anno DCCLIII with Nero Claudius Drusus, and adopted by insertion from the Sulpicia family into the Quinctia. Under Augustus, T. Quinctius Crispinus Sulpicianus served as coin-issuing magistrate, striking S.C bronze types. The Republican denarius with T.Q and standard Roma/Dioscuri reverse is included on the same plate and attributed by Orsini to Crispinus Sulpicianus, not to T. Quinctius Flamininus. Orsini does mention T. Quinctius Flamininus in the family discussion (citing Livy and Plutarch on the liberation of Greece) but does not attribute any coin specifically to him.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents five coins of the Quinctia gens. He attributes ALL coins on the plate to T. Quinctius Crispinus Sulpicianus, identified as consul anno DCCLIII with Nero Claudius Drusus, and adopted into the Quinctia from the Sulpicia family. Orsini discusses T. Quinctius Flamininus in the family history section (citing Livy and Plutarch on the Macedonian war and liberation of Greece) but makes no attribution of any coin to Flamininus. He identifies Crispinus with the figure mocked in Velleius lib. II for 'singularem nequitiam supercilio truci protegens.' He also connects the ode 'Quid bellicosus Cantaber et Scythes / Hirpine Quinctii' (Horace lib. I) to Crispinus Sulpicianus. He does NOT describe Crispinus as IIIvir monetalis (tresvir) — the role Orsini gives is consul. The gens is described as patrician in origin (transferred from Alba by king Tullus), with a separate plebeian Quinctia branch mentioned citing Cicero pro A. Cluentio and Livy lib. XXIII.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Juno Caprotina in biga of goats right; C.RENI below, ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini notes this is the only coin of the gens Renia and that neither the gens nor the moneyer appears in any ancient literary source. He explicitly declines to identify the deity in the biga and leaves open whether the biga animals are hirci (goats) or reni, noting others take them for reni. He does NOT describe the reverse as 'an attribute of Juno Caprotina.'

completed.family_note: The Renii were a minor gens known almost exclusively from the coinage of C. Renius, moneyer c. 138 BC. His denarius (Crawford 231/1) features on the reverse two animals drawing a biga. Orsini explicitly leaves open whether the animals are hirci (goats) or reni (reindeer-like animals), citing unnamed earlier authorities for the latter identification. He does not identify any deity in the biga; there is no reference in Orsini to Juno Caprotina or the Nonae Caprotinae festival. He suggests the moneyer Renius may have taken the family name from the animal (hirci or reni), citing Varro de re rustica lib. II cap. I for animal-derived Roman family names (Porcios, Ouilios, Caprilios, Equitios).
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) devotes a brief entry to the gens Renia, illustrating the single denarius of C. Renius. He states that the gens Renia has no mention in any ancient author he has read ('nulla apud scriptores, quos ipse legerim, mentio reperitur'), and C. Renius himself is likewise unattested. He explicitly leaves open the identification of the biga animals: some say hirci (goats), others say reni (an animal similar to a goat). He does NOT identify the reverse figure as Juno Caprotina, does NOT mention the Nonae Caprotinae festival, and does NOT cite Macrobius. He cites Varro de re rustica lib. II cap. I only for the etymology of family names from animals, not for a Juno cult.

coins_engraved.obverse: Female head right (Juno Sospita) wearing goat-skin headdress
coins_engraved.reverse: Standing draped figure on a base, feeding/offering to a serpent rearing up before it; ivy-leaf or small symbol in upper left field; FABATI in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates the Juno Sospita / girl-and-serpent type, connecting it to the cult at Lanuvium and noting the distinctive goatskin headdress of the goddess.
coins_engraved.obverse_ai: Female head right (Juno Sospita) wearing goat-skin headdress
coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Standing female figure right with spear and shield; FABATI in exergue

coins_engraved.obverse: Manuscript annotation by later collector: 'Alya 42 famil...' — not a coin image
coins_engraved.reverse: Blank circle (placeholder for coin that was never engraved)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Later collector's note (French): «42 variétés» for the gens Roscia (cf. Mionnet, who lists 43); the two circles were left blank.
coins_engraved.annotation_text: Left circle: «il y a 42 variétés». Right circle: blank (no coin engraved).

completed.family_note: The Roscii were a plebeian gens from Lanuvium. L. Roscius Fabatus struck serrate denarii (Crawford 412/1) with Juno Sospita types (obverse) and a girl feeding a sacred serpent (reverse), connected to the Lanuvian ritual described by Propertius (elegiae lib. IV). Orsini distinguishes the moneyer L. Roscius FABATUS from L. Roscius OTHO, who was the tribune (Tr. Pl.) responsible for the lex theatralis; Orsini uses Otho's law only to establish the family's plebeian status, not to connect Fabatus to the law. Crawford records numerous control symbols for this issue.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) treats the Roscii briefly, illustrating the serrate denarius of L. Roscius Fabatus. He identifies the obverse as Juno Sospita with goatskin headdress (cross-referencing the Procilia entry), and uses Propertius's elegy (lib. IV, on Cynthia and the Lanuvian draco) to illuminate the reverse girl-and-serpent scene. He establishes the gens's plebeian status from L. Roscius OTHO's lex theatralis, but does NOT say Orsini cites Cicero linking Fabatus to the lex theatralis — that would conflate two different Roscii. The Cicero/Asinii Pollionis reference to L. Roscius Fabatus (cited at the start of the next page, p.225) concerns Fabatus as Caesar's legate in Gaul, not the theatrical law.

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head of Jupiter right; DOSSEN behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory standing right holding wreath and palm; L.RVBRI in field
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini describes the first Rubria denarius as having, on the reverse, a Salus ara (altar of Salus) with a Victoria signum added ('Victoriae quoque signum adiectum est'), which he interprets as indicating a military victory of the Rubria gens. He does NOT describe this as a 'Jupiter/triumphal quadriga' type.

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head of Jupiter right; DOSSEN behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Triumphal chariot (quadriga) right with elaborate canopy; L.RVBRI in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini describes the reverse of the second (and third) Rubria denarius as a THENSA (sacred carriage used in circus processions for divine simulacra), which he connects to Rubrius's priestly office or that of his ancestors. He cites Cicero's Verr. III and the letter to Lentulus, and Suetonius Caes. LXXVI on the honors decreed for Caesar including a thensa. The coin does NOT show Juno as part of a Capitoline triad; Orsini's analysis is about sacerdotal imagery.

coins_engraved.obverse: Veiled female head right (Juno or Ceres); DOSS behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Triumphal chariot right with elaborate canopy, drawn by horses; L.RVBRI in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini's analysis for the third denarius is the same THENSA discussion as coin 2 (he groups coins 2 and 3 together). He gives no separate iconographic description for this coin.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory in quadriga right; ROMA above; C·F·L·R·Q·M in exergue (three-moneyer joint issue)
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini (Familiae Romanae p.227): on the fourth denarius of the Rubria plate he notes nothing remarkable "praeter Triumvirorum Monetalium nomina" — i.e. it carries the names of the three moneyers (triumviri monetales), each given by single letters. He places it under Rubria by reading the ambiguous 'L·R' as L. Rubrius, but transparently observes that 'L·R possis etiam L. Roscium interpretari' (it could equally be L. Roscius). He thus correctly recognises the type as the joint three-moneyer issue, flagging the L·R ambiguity himself.

coins_engraved.reverse: Prow of galley right; L.RVBRI / DOSSEN in field

completed.family_note: The Rubrii were a plebeian gens; L. Rubrius Dossenus struck an extensive series of denarii and bronzes (Crawford 348/1-6). The denarii do not feature the Capitoline triad as such in Orsini's analysis; rather, coin 1 has a Salus ara with a Victory signum added; coins 2-3 have THENSAE (sacred carriages) on the reverse, which Orsini connects to Rubrius's sacerdotium or that of his ancestors. The cognomen Dossenus Orsini connects to the comic character, citing Horace's epistola ad Augustum lib. II (where the spelling is 'Dorsenus', the ancient form for 'dossum'). The bronze types include Janiform heads and prow, and an unusual piece showing what appears to be a temple structure. The fourth denarius (Crawford 283/1a) carries only the letters of three moneyers, with L·R ambiguous between L. Rubrius and L. Roscius, as Orsini himself notes.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) presents the series of L. Rubrius Dossenus in detail. He opens by citing Cicero (de claris oratoribus), Appianus (lib. I, bell. ciuil.), and Plutarchus (Ti. et C. Gracchi) for the Rubria gens. He identifies the moneyer with L. Rubrius whom Cicero (in his account from Caesar's civil war writings) describes as a Pompeian partisan, son of Domitius, captured with Corfinius. The cognomen Dossenus he connects to the comic character, citing Horace Ep. II.1 ('Dorsenus'). For coin 1 (first denarius): the reverse shows a Salus ara with a Victoria signum added — Orsini interprets these as symbols of a family military victory. For coins 2 and 3: the reverse shows a THENSA (sacred carriage), which Orsini connects at length to Rubrius's own priesthood or that of his ancestors, citing Cicero (Verr. III and the Lentulus letter), Suetomnius (Caes. cap. LXXVI), and other sources on the thensa as a divine honor. He does NOT describe coins 2-3 as showing Juno or Minerva of a Capitoline triad. Varro is not cited for the Dossenus/Atellan identification.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Mars right; value mark behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Ram walking right; L.RVSTI in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini says the L. Rustius denarius has nothing remarkable except the ram (aries), which he explains as representing the antiquissimum aes signatum — the tradition that earliest Roman coinage depicted livestock, citing Varro de re rustica II.1, Pliny XVIII.3, and Plutarch in Poplicola. He does NOT say the ram is a sacrificial or totemic family emblem.

coins_engraved.obverse: Confronted draped busts of Fortuna Victrix and Fortuna Felix (the two Fortunae); Q·RVSTIVS·FORTVNAE·ANTIAT around
coins_engraved.reverse: Ornamented (garlanded) altar inscribed FOR·RE (Fortunae Reduci); CAESARI·AVGVSTO around; EX·S·C in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies Q. Rustius as Triumvir cudendae monetae sub Augusto. The denarius shows two Fortuna simulacra, struck in honour of Augustus: Fortuna Redux (Dio's ΕΠΑΓΩΓΟΝ) and Fortuna Antiatina (siue Antiatinae). He cites Horace Ode XXXV lib. I for Fortuna at Antium and Macrobius lib. I Saturnalium. He refers to an earlier Mescinia entry for Fortuna Redux.

coins_engraved.reverse_ai: Tabella (voting tablet) inscribed; AVGVSTI / COMES / EX S.C in field

completed.family_note: The Rustii were a gens known from epigraphic evidence (Tibur inscription: C. Rustius C.f. Flavos iter, and a Sutrina table listing L. Rustius L.f. among Pontifices). L. Rustius struck Republican denarii (Crawford 389/1) featuring a ram (aries) on the reverse — Orsini explains the ram as representing the antiquissimum aes signatum (the earliest coined money linked to livestock), citing Varro de re rustica lib. II cap. I, Pliny lib. XVIII cap. III, and Plutarch in Poplicola. This is NOT a family pastoral or sacrificial emblem but the origin-of-money emblem. Under Augustus, Q. Rustius served as Triumvir cudendae monetae, striking bronzes with two Fortuna simulacra — Fortuna Redux and Fortuna Antiatina — in Augustus's honor, connecting the family to Antium. Orsini cites Horace Odes lib. I ode XXXV for Fortuna Antiatina.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini (1577) treats the Rustii with entries for both moneyers. He establishes the gens from a Tibur inscription (C. Rustius Flavos) and a Sutrina table (L. Rustius L.f. among Pontifices), and cites Plutarchus in Crasso and Appianus in Parthico for Rustii serving under Crassus against the Parthians (Surena episode). For coin 1 (L. Rustius, ram): Orsini explicitly says the coin has nothing remarkable ('nihil habet quod notatu magnopere dignum sit') except the ram, which he explains as the antiquissimum aes signatum tradition, citing Varro, Pliny, and Plutarch — NOT a family emblem. For coin 2 (Q. Rustius): identified as Triumvir cudendae monetae under Augustus; the reverse shows two Fortuna simulacra — Fortuna Redux (which Dio calls ΕΠΑΓΩΓΟΝ) and Fortuna Antiatina — citing Horace Odes lib. I ode XXXV and Macrobius lib. I Saturnalium for Antium. Orsini does not speculate about a prosopographic link between the Republican and Augustan moneyers.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; FLAC behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory driving biga right; L.RVTILI below or in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes the denarius to a Rutilius Flaccus whom he could find in no ancient author or inscription; he discusses the gens’s other members (Crassus, Calvus, Rufus, Lupus, Censorinus) from the literary sources instead.

completed.family_note: The Rutilii were a gens duplex — both patrician and plebeian branches are attested (Orsini, p. 228: 'Rutilia gens duplex fuit, patricia scilicet, & plebeia'). The one denarius Orsini engraves is that of L. Rutilius Flaccus (Crawford 387/1, 77 BC), with helmeted head of Roma (FLAC behind) and Victory in biga (L·RVTILI below) — a moneyer otherwise unattested: Orsini himself could find him in no ancient author or inscription. The gens's better-known members — P. Rutilius Rufus (cos. 105 BC, the Stoic exiled after his exemplary Asian administration), Rutilius Lupus, and the Rutilii Crassi and Calvi — are known from the literary record rather than the coinage.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini calls the gens duplex (both patrician and plebeian) and notes that the Flaccus who struck this denarius is otherwise unattested — “nullam in veteribus uel scriptorum uel lapidum monumentis invenire mentionem potui” — while citing other Rutilii from the sources: Rutilius Crassus (Livy IV), Calvus (Livy XLV), Rufus (Cicero, pro Plancio), Lupus (Caesar, BC I; Quintilian I.2), and Censorinus (Valerius Maximus IV.1).

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right (Octavian); C.CAESAR.III.VIR.R.P.C around
coins_engraved.reverse: Ornamented trident, point upward; Q·SALVIVS to left, M·P·COS·DESIG to right

completed.family_note: The Salvii were a plebeian gens of Etruscan origin from Ferentinum. M. Salvius Otho served as IIIvir monetalis under Augustus c. 7 BC (RIC I 431), striking bronze S.C types. He was the grandfather of the Emperor M. Salvius Otho (AD 69). The family rose to senatorial rank through the patronage of Livia. Their coinage is limited to Augustan bronzes.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Salvia briefly, illustrating two coins attributed to M. Salvius Otho. He connects the moneyer to the imperial Othonian dynasty, citing Suetonius on Otho's ancestry. Orsini correctly identifies the IIIvir monetalis title but does not discuss the family's Etruscan origins. His attribution of the first coin is tentative, while the second is firmly identified by its complete legend.

completed.family_note: The Sanquinii were a minor plebeian gens. M. Sanquinius served as IIIvir monetalis under Augustus in 17 BC, the year of the Ludi Saeculares. His coinage (RIC I 340-346) includes silver denarii with Saecular Games types and bronze S.C issues with the OB CIVIS SERVATOS civic crown. The family's prominence was confined to this single Augustan magistracy, and the types reflect the ideological program of Augustan renewal.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Sanquinia with three coins, all attributed to M. Sanquinius as IIIvir monetalis. He connects the coinage to the Ludi Saeculares of 17 BC, noting Tacitus mentions one member of the gens ('Sanquiniae gentis vnus, quòd sciam, Tacitus facit mentionem lib.v.'). Orsini interprets the second coin's stellar head as Caesar's comet-soul rather than a jugate portrait type, citing Suetonius cap. LXXXVIII on the sidus Iulium. He does not cite Horace's Carmen Saeculare or the Acta of the games in this entry.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; numeral behind (XXXXII or similar)
coins_engraved.reverse: She-wolf walking left; ROMA above, P.SATRIE / NVS below
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates this denarius but says the significance of the she-wolf is obscure to him given how little is known of the family: 'quò pertineat, mihi quidem obscurum est.' He draws no connection to the foundation legend.

completed.family_note: The Satrieni were a minor plebeian gens known almost solely from the coinage of P. Satrienus, moneyer c. 77 BC (Crawford 388/1b). His denarius features Roma on the obverse and a she-wolf standing left on the reverse, an allusion to the Lupa Romana and the founding legend of Romulus and Remus. The type is relatively uncommon and the family produced no other known moneyers.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini devotes a brief entry to the gens Satriena, illustrating the single denarius of P. Satrienus. He notes it is the only attestation of the family ('nec alibi, quòd sciam, in ueteribus monumentis mentio extat'). Regarding the she-wolf on the reverse, Orsini explicitly says he does not know what it signifies given the family's obscurity: 'Lupa in altera parte denarii impressa, in tanta Satrienae gentis ignoratione, quò pertineat, mihi quidem obscurum est.' He cites no ancient author and draws no connection to the foundation myth.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X (value mark) behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Victory driving biga right; L.SAV below, ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates this standard Roma/Victory-in-biga denarius, reading the moneyer's abbreviated name as L. Saufeius.

coins_engraved.reverse: Prow right; L.SAVF above, S (value mark) below

completed.family_note: The Saufeii were a minor plebeian gens. L. Saufeius served as moneyer c. 152 BC, striking both denarii (Crawford 204/1) with standard Roma/Victory-in-biga types and associated bronze (Crawford 204/2) with Janus/prow. The family is otherwise obscure in Roman prosopography, though a Saufeius appears as a correspondent of Cicero's friend Atticus.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Saufeia with two coins, both attributed to L. Saufeius. He correctly identifies the standard mid-second-century types and reads the abbreviated legend. Orsini does not provide extensive prosopographic detail but notes the family name in passing. His illustrations show both the silver and bronze denominations of the same moneyer.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
coins_engraved.reverse: The Dioscuri galloping right; C.SCR below, ROMA in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates this early denarius with the standard Roma/Dioscuri type, reading the moneyer as C. Scribonius.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right (Bonus Eventus?); BON EVENT around
coins_engraved.reverse: Puteal Scribonianum (well-head decorated with garland and lyres); PVTEAL / SCRIBON in field
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini depicts the famous Puteal Scribonianum type, connecting it to the sacred well-head in the Forum that bore the Scribonii's family name.

coins_engraved.obverse: Veiled female head right (Concordia); PAVLVS LEPIDVS CONCORDIA around
coins_engraved.reverse: Puteal Scribonianum (well-head); PVTEAL SCRIBON around
coins_engraved.moneyer: L. Aemilius Lepidus Paullus & L. Scribonius Libo
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses this joint issue noting that Paullus Lepidus appears on the other face ('in altera tertii denarii parte, Paullus Lepidus notatus sit, qui Liboni Consuli ex Kal. Iul. suffectus est'), citing it as further evidence that the coin belongs to L. Scribonius Libo as Consul. He discusses the Puteal Scribonianum using Dionysius, Horace, Ovid, and Porphyrio; he does not cite Festus.

completed.family_note: The Scribonii were a plebeian gens prominent from the mid-Republic into the Augustan age. C. Scribonius struck early denarii c. 154 BC (Crawford 201/1) with Roma/Dioscuri types. L. Scribonius Libo (Crawford 416/1a, 62 BC) struck the famous Puteal Scribonianum type, depicting the sacred well-head in the Forum that the family had enclosed with a decorative puteal. The monument marked the spot struck by lightning and was used as a meeting place for legal proceedings. Scribonia, daughter of L. Scribonius Libo, briefly married Octavian.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Scribonia with three coins spanning the mid-Republic to the late Republic. He devotes particular attention to the Puteal Scribonianum, citing Dionysius of Halicarnassus (lib.I) for its location near the Ficus Ruminalis before the Curia, and quoting Horace (Ep.III lib.I: 'Forum, Putealque Libonis / Mandabo siccis') and Ovid on the Praetor's tribunal nearby. He also cites Pomponius Porphyrio on the puteal as a roofed cover over a well ('Puteal tectum illud, quo puteus operitur'), correcting Porphyrio's description. Orsini further cites Pliny (lib. XX XIII cap. VIII) for the Bonus Eventus image on the puteal. He does not cite Festus in this entry. He correctly distinguishes the two Scribonii moneyers and notes the Concordia/Paullus Lepidus obverse on the joint third coin.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind

completed.family_note: The Sempronii were originally a patrician gens, later transferred to plebeian status, as Orsini notes ('Sempronia gens patricia primùm fuit, postea ad plebem traducta, plebebia facta est'). Orsini identifies three distinct families within the gens: the patrician Atratini, the plebeian Gracchi, and the plebeian Pitiones. L. Sempronius Pitio struck the first coin of the tabella, though Orsini says he found nothing about Pitio in literary sources. Ti. Sempronius Gracchus served as one of Caesar's IVviri argento publice signando (not IIIvir monetalis). L. Sempronius Atratinus struck bronze in 718 AUC under Mark Antony. The family's prominence from the second century BC through the Augustan age is reflected in the coinage.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Sempronia extensively, reflecting the family's historical importance. He identifies three sub-families: Atratini (patrician), Gracchi (plebeian), and Pitiones (plebeian). He cites Velleius (lib.II) on Ti. Sempronius Gracchus Triumvir and on C. Gracchus, Quintilianus (lib.I cap.X) on the Gracchi's cognomen spelling, and Tacitus (lib.I) on Sempronius Gracchus who married Julia. He does not cite Plutarch or Appian in this entry. For L. Sempronius Atratinus, Orsini explains the substitution in the consular list citing Dio (lib.XLIX). He discusses six coins connecting them to Caesar's Caesilian colony symbolism and the coloniae Triumviri.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma right; X behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Jupiter in quadriga right; L.SENTI / C.F in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates this denarius with Jupiter in quadriga, reading the full filiation L. Sentius C.f. on the reverse.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head facing left (Roma)
coins_engraved.reverse: Quadriga right; L·SATVRN in exergue
coins_engraved.orsini_error: Orsini places under gens Sentia; moneyer is L. Appuleius Saturninus of gens Appuleia (Crawford 317/1).
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes to gens Sentia based on the cognomen Saturninus, which he connects to the Sentii. Modern attribution may differ.
coins_engraved.obverse_description: Helmeted Roma head right; griffin crest on helmet; detailed helmet decoration.
coins_engraved.reverse_description: Figure in chariot or on horseback right; legend reads approx. L·SATURN or SATURN in field/exergue — Saturn-related iconography.

coins_engraved.obverse: Helmeted head of Roma left; I.S.K or I.S.R visible
coins_engraved.reverse: Bust or head right wearing winged diadem; letter C visible
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini places this coin tentatively under gens Sentia, arguing from the SATVRN legend and referring to C. Sentius Saturninus attested by Velleius and Valerius Maximus. He also discusses a Plutarch passage (Sulla) mentioning a 'Brutius Sura' as praetor's legatus in Macedonia, concluding this name is corrupt since the Brutia gens is unattested. He does not cite Cicero.

completed.family_note: The Sentii were a gens of uncertain status — Orsini says 'incertum patricia ne, an plebeia fuerit.' L. Sentius Saturninus (C.F.) struck the denarii illustrated. The family included C. Sentius Saturninus, who according to Velleius (lib.II) was proscribed by the Triumvirs but later served as legatus in Germania and was Consul with Q. Lucretius Vespillo in year DCCXXXIV. Orsini tentatively attributes two further denarii with the SATVRN legend to this family. Orsini does not identify the family as 'prominent in the late Republic' or call them plebeian.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Sentia with three coins. He correctly identifies L. Sentius Saturninus C.F. from the coin legend. He connects the family to the Saturnini, citing Velleius (lib.II) on C. Sentius Saturninus (proscribed, later legatus in Germany, consul year DCCXXXIV) and Valerius Maximus (lib.VII cap.III) on his courageous conduct as consul. Orsini does not cite Cicero in this entry. He also notes a reference in Plutarch's Sulla to 'Brutius Sura' as praetor's legatus in Macedonia, and argues this is a corrupted name — the Brutia gens being unknown among Roman families — which he uses to support the coin's attribution to Sentia.

coins_engraved.obverse: Laureate head right (Caesar); CAESAR around; star behind
coins_engraved.reverse: Standing figure (Minerva or Venus?) holding Victory and sceptre; P.SEPVLLIVS / MACER around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates Caesar's portrait denarius of P. Sepullius Macer and dates Macer's activity to the period after Caesar's assassination or at the Triumvirate's inception ('Caesare iam rerum potito, uel recens à coniuratis occiso, sub ipso Triumuiratus initio'). He does not specify the Ides of March or the Venus Victrix reverse in this entry.

completed.family_note: The Sepullii were a minor gens known almost solely from P. Sepullius Macer, whose coins (illustrated in the tabella) Orsini dates to the period after Caesar's death or at the very start of the Triumvirate: 'eius, qui Caesare iam rerum potito, uel recens à coniuratis occiso, sub ipso Triumuiratus initio, cudendae praefuit monetae.' No ancient author mentions the gens Sepullia ('nullus, quòd sciam, ueterum scriptorum facit mentionem'). The coins of P. Sepullius Macer are also connected to the Aemiliae Lepidorum family in Orsini's discussion.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini devotes a brief entry to the gens Sepullia. He notes that no ancient writer mentions the family, and that it would be almost forgotten if not for the denarii bearing P. Sepullius Macer's name. He identifies Macer as moneyer at the start of the Triumvirate, also citing his coins alongside those of the Aemiliae Lepidorum family. Orsini does not in this entry discuss the unprecedented nature of Caesar's living portrait, does not call the DICT PERPETVO title unprecedented, and does not cite Suetonius or Dio Cassius.

completed.family_note: The Sergii were a patrician gens claiming descent from the Trojan Sergestus mentioned in Virgil's Aeneid. M. Sergius Silus struck denarii c. 116-115 BC (Crawford 286/1) with Roma/horseman types; the reverse horseman holding a severed head alludes to the heroic exploits of his ancestor M. Sergius Silus in the Second Punic War, who lost his right hand but continued to fight, as described by Pliny. The EX S.C on the obverse indicates senatorial authorization. L. Sergius Catilina, the famous conspirator, was a later member of this gens.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Sergia with the single denarius of M. Sergius Silus. He opens by citing Virgil (Aeneid V) for the Trojan origin claim ('Sergestusq. domus tenet à quo Sergia nomen') and notes the Sili are the only branch attested in coinage despite the gens being patrician and illustrious. He recounts the famous story from Pliny (lib.VII cap.XXVIII) and Solinus (cap.VI) about M. Sergius Silus who lost his right hand and had an iron replacement. He explicitly mentions Catiline as a later member: 'licet pronepos Catilina gratiam nomini deroget.' He interprets the horseman carrying a severed head on the coin's reverse as a reference to these military exploits.

completed.family_note: The Servilii were a patrician gens of great antiquity with multiple branches: Caepiones, Cascae, Rulli, and Gemini. Their coinage spans 141-42 BC. C. Servilius M.f. (Crawford 239/1, 136 BC) and C. Servilius Vatia (Crawford 264/1, 127 BC) struck standard Republican types. P. Servilius Rullus (Crawford 328/1, 100 BC) featured Flora. Several coins relate to the tyrannicide Brutus (born Q. Servilius Caepio), his associate M. Servilius (legatus of Cassius, Crawford 505/2-3), and P. Servilius Casca Longus (Crawford 507/2), first of Caesar's assassins to strike. The family's coinage is among the richest in historical content.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Servilia at great length across two plates. He opens by identifying C. Servilii Ahalae imago on the first coin (p. 240: 'In primo tabellae denario signata est imago C. Seruilii Ahalae'). He connects Brutus to the Servilii through his mother: 'Brutus enim Seruilia matre natus fuit, quae generis sui originem ad C. hunc Ahalam referebat, vt scribit Plutarchus in Bruto.' The second coin he knows others assign to M. Servilius C.F. ('Secundum denarium scio ab aliis referri ad M. Seruilium C.F.') but he himself inclines to attribute coins 1 and 2 to M. Servilius Ahala ('pertinent (ut opinor) ad M. Seruilium Ahalam'). For M. Servilius on the second plate he identifies him not only as Cassius's legatus but also as fleet commander: 'non modo C. Cassii, Caesaris percussoris legatum, sed classis etiam, ex acrostirio, aliisq. rei naualis impressis symbolis, praefectum fuisse intelligimus.' He reads the inscription C. SERVILII C. F. QUI FLORALIA PRIMVS FECIT on one coin and discusses the Floralia at length. The sixth coin he assigns to P. Servilius Rullus and the agrarian law: 'Sextus denarius pertinet ad P. Seruilium Rullum, qui Tr. Pl. anno DCXCLE- gem Agrariam promulgauit.' For P. Servilius Casca he cites Plutarch (Greek) and Suetonius (Caesar cap. LXXXII) on Casca striking Caesar first. The Caepio coin he explicitly leaves uncertain: 'denarius ad quem pertineat Caepionem, mihi quidem obscurum est.' The phrase 'Victory breaking the diadem' does not appear in Orsini's Servilia section; daggers (pugiones) are discussed, not a diadem-breaking Victory.

completed.family_note: The Sestii were a patrician gens; Orsini explicitly states 'SESTIAM gentem patriciā fuiffe (nam Sextiae plebeiae nulla est in denariis mentio) satis ex Liuio constat.' Livy lib. III names P. Sestius Capitolinus as a patrician. L. Sestius struck the coins of this plate as proquaestor (or quaestor — Appian says quaestor, Orsini notes the discrepancy) of Q. Caepionis Brutus in the province of Macedonia. Dio lib. LIII records L. Sestius as suffect consul under Augustus in year DCCXXX.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Sestia with four coins (the plate shows Q·SESTI, two CAEPIO·BRVTVS·PRO·COS types with priestly implements, and L·SESTI·PRO·Q with pyramidal monuments). He identifies L. Sestius as proquaestor of Brutus in Macedonia, citing Livy lib. III for the family's patrician status. He notes that Appian lib. IIII calls Sestius Quaestor not Proquaestor and considers this may be a scribal error ('nisi forte librarii erratu sit, qui Ταμίαν pro Ἀντιταμίαν scripserit'). Orsini cites Dio lib. LIII for Sestius as suffect consul under Augustus. He does not cite Cicero's Pro Sestio in this section; his ancient sources here are Livy, Appian, and Dio.

He connects this to the traditions of Sicinius Dentatus. Orsini does not say 'Roma and caduceus' for this coin.

completed.family_note: The Sicinii were a plebeian gens with frequent mention in the sources. Q. Sicinius struck the silver coins of this plate as Triumvir monetalis; no ancient author known to Orsini mentions him. He may be the son of Cn. Sicinius who was Tribune of the Plebs in year DCLXXVII with Cn. Octavius and C. Scribonius Curio as consuls. The coins display Fortitudo (not Fortuna): the first coin shows Fortitudo's image without a title; the second bears the inscription FORT.P.R. (Fortitudo Populi Romani). The family's most famous member was L. Sicinius Dentatus, Tribune of the Plebs, celebrated for extraordinary military valour.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Sicinia briefly with the two coins of Q. Sicinius. He identifies the type as Fortitudo (not Fortuna): the first coin shows 'Fortitudinis imago sine titulo'; the second shows 'FORT.P.R.' = Fortitudo Populi Romani. He connects this to the legend of L. Sicinius Dentatus, citing Dionysios lib. X, Plinius lib. VII cap. XXVII, Solinus cap. VI, Valerius Max. lib. III cap. VI, and Agellius lib. II cap. XI — not Livy specifically for Dentatus. He does not interpret the caduceus as 'a hope for peace'; the caduceus visible on one coin is not discussed in those terms — his discussion of the palm (from Agellius/Plutarch) is as a victory symbol in contests. No civil war peace interpretation appears in the text.

completed.family_note: The Silii were a plebeian gens, as Orsini establishes from Livy lib. IV. The moneyer of this plate Orsini identifies, with some uncertainty ('ut opinor'), as the man who was Consul in year DCCLXV with L. Munatius Plancus, son of P. Silius who had adopted A. Licinius Nerva (hence 'Silianum dictum') as mentioned by Velleius lib. II. The coin shows a joint issue with Annius Lamia; the types visible on the plate are clasped hands (obverse legend ANNIVS·LAMIA·SILIVS) and a vessel with the IIIvir legend. Orsini does not identify a Pegasus type on this coin.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Silia very briefly. He establishes the family as plebeian from Livy lib. IV, identifying the moneyer as the probable Consul of year DCCLXV. He identifies the joint moneyer Annius Lamia from the legend. He does not describe 'Pegasus and crater types' — the coin visible on the plate shows clasped hands and a ritual vessel with the IIIvir monetalis legend. Orsini does not mention Pegasus, a crater, or P. Silius Nerva consul AD 28 / Tacitus.

completed.family_note: The Spurilii were a very minor gens known solely from the coinage of A. Spurilius, IIIvir monetalis c. 139 BC. His denarius (Crawford 230/1) features the standard Roma/horseman type common in the mid-second century BC. The family left virtually no other trace in Roman prosopography. This is one of the rarest moneyer names in the Republican series.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini devotes a brief entry to the gens Spurilia, citing Livy lib. IIII for a Spurilius as Tribune of the Plebs. For the moneyer name, Orsini notes that Appian lib. II lists among Caesar's assassins a certain M. Spurius, which Orsini believes is a scribal error for Spurilius ('librariorum, ut ego opinor, errore, Spurium, cum scribi debuerit, Spurilium'). He also records that some read the coin legend A.SPVRI. as A. Spurina: 'Quidam A.SPVRI. interpretantur A. Spurinam.' Orsini leaves this reading open — he does not definitively settle the moneyer's name as Spurilius over Spurina.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bare bearded head right (portrait)
coins_engraved.reverse: Scene with standing figures; MVRCVS IMP in field; trophy or captive between figures
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini illustrates Murcus's coin and identifies him as Imperator from the reverse legend MVRCVS·IMP. The plate (p. 248) shows a portrait head obverse and two togated figures on the reverse — not Neptune. Orsini establishes his command from coin legends and Cassius's letter ('In Suriam me profectum esse scito ad L.Murcum...Imperatores'), not from a Neptune type. 'Neptune reflecting his command' is not in Orsini.

completed.family_note: The Statii were a plebeian gens; Cicero mentions it in ep. II ad Q. fratrem lib. I, and Livy lib. II and Dionysios lib. IX. Murcus, who struck this plate's coin, is called L. Statius Murcus by the sources (Orsini notes this name appears in corrupt form in some Cicero manuscripts). Orsini establishes from Cassius's letter (Cicero ep. xi lib. xii) that Murcus held the title Imperator; the coin reverse shows him as MVRCVS·IMP with two togated figures. Dio lib. XLVII records that Murcus was sent to Syria when M. Crispus was Praetor in Bithynia. From Appian lib. III–IV Orsini establishes he had been Caesar's legatus before becoming a Republican commander. He joined Sextus Pompeius and was killed by him in Sicily.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Statia with the single coin of Murcus. He establishes Murcus as Imperator from the coin legend and discusses his career at length from Cassius's letter to Cicero ('In Suriam me profectum esse scito ad L.Murcum, & Q.Crifpum Imperatores'), Dio lib. XLVII, and Appian lib. III–IV. Orsini does not identify Neptune on the coin; the plate shows a portrait and two togated figures (MVRCVS·IMP). He cites Velleius lib. II and Appian lib. II for Murcus joining Sextus Pompeius and being killed in Sicily. The 'Neptune with trident as reference to naval power' is not in Orsini's text.

completed.family_note: The Statilii were a plebeian gens that rose to prominence under Augustus. T. Statilius Taurus was one of Augustus's most trusted generals, holding two consulships and building the first permanent amphitheatre in Rome. As IIIvir monetalis (RIC I 437, c. 7 BC), the bronze with clasped hands (dextrarum iunctio) symbolizes the concordia of the Augustan regime. The names Regulus, Pulcher, and Taurus on the coin represent the three colleagues in the monetary magistracy.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens briefly. He is uncertain whether the coin belongs to T. Statilius Taurus — the proconsul who triumphed from Asia (DCCXIX / 35 BC) and commanded Octavian’s fleet against Sex. Pompeius — or to his son, consul in DCCLXIIII (AD 11) with M. Aemilius Lepidus; and he reads the bull on the moneyer’s coinage as a pun on the Taurus cognomen (“ad Tauri cognomen certè respexit… id animal impressit”).

completed.family_note: The Sulpicii were a patrician gens of great antiquity, one of the most prominent families of the Roman Republic. Multiple moneyers span from 152 BC to AD 68: P. Sulpicius Galba (an early denarius, c. 152 BC) with Apollo/Jupiter types; P. Sulpicius Galba (Crawford 406/1, 69 BC) with priestly implements; C. Sulpicius Platorinus (RIC I 406, 13 BC) as Augustan IIIvir monetalis; and Ser. Sulpicius Galba, the future Emperor Galba (AD 68). The gens produced numerous consuls, and Servius Sulpicius Rufus was one of Rome's greatest jurists.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Sulpicia at length, reflecting its historical importance. He traces the family from the early Republic through the Empire, citing Cicero repeatedly on Servius Sulpicius Rufus the jurist and on the Sulpicii Rufi praenomina. For the Galba coins, Orsini discusses the family's division into patrician Galbae and equestrian Rufi; for the revolt coin he cites Suetonius lib.vii cap.ii. He attributes several coins tentatively, stating of the fifth denarius 'mihi quidem incertum est' which Servius struck it. He connects C. Sulpicius Platorinus to Lavinium (porca and Penates on the coin) and to the Augustan monetary programme. The coin he calls the fourth (aureum nummum) he connects to Ser. Sulpicius who relieved Tusculum from siege, citing Livy lib.vi.

coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies C. Tarquitius on this coin as a supporter of Sertorius in Spain, grounding the attribution in Plutarch's Sertorio and a Sallust fragment quoted by Servius Grammaticus. He does not call it a proconsular issue and does not question its authenticity.

completed.family_note: The Tarquitii were a patrician gens (Orsini: 'gentis patriciae'). L. Tarquitius Flaccus is attested in the Fasti Capitolini as Master of Horse under Dictator L. Quinctius Cincinnatus, anno CCXCV. Tacitus lib.xv mentions a Tarquitius Crescens. C. Tarquitius is identified from the coin as a supporter of Sertorius in Spain, on the authority of Plutarch's Sertorio and a Sallust fragment preserved by Servius Grammaticus lib.i Aeneid. Orsini does not connect the family to the Etruscan Tarquinii, and he does not question the coin's authenticity.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Tarquitia briefly with a single coin attributed to C. Tarquitius. He first establishes the family's attestation in the Fasti Capitolini (L. Tarquitius Flaccus, Magister Equitum under Cincinnatus Dictator, anno CCXCV) and in Tacitus lib.xv (Tarquitius Crescens). He then identifies the coin's moneyer as C. Tarquitius who, per Plutarch's Sertorio, was a supporter of Sertorius in Spain — C. Annius, Sulla's legate, was sent against him. He confirms this with a Sallust fragment quoted by Servius Grammaticus in lib.i Aeneid, which places Tarquitius among Sertorius's circle. Orsini does not call it a proconsular issue, does not question the attribution, and does not suggest it is a fantasy or misreading.

completed.family_note: The Terentii were a plebeian gens (Orsini: 'gens inter plebeias ab antiquis scriptoribus numeratur'). C. Terentius Lucanus is the moneyer of the first coin; Pliny lib.xxxv cap.vii records that he was the first to exhibit gladiatorial paintings publicly. He also adopted P. Terentius Afer (the playwright Terence), according to Donatus. M. Terentius Varro is identified from the third and fourth coins as Pompey's legate in Spain ('Cn. Pompeii in Hispania legatus'), serving also in a proquaestorial role ('Proquaestorio etiam officio'). Orsini identifies the obverse of coin 3 as Iuppiter Terminalis ('Iouis Terminalis caput impressum est'). The reverse of coin 3-4 shows sceptrum and aquila plus dolphin ('sceptrum & aquila in altera denarii parte... delphin ad maris imperium pertinet, quod Cn. Pompeio ex s.c. bello Piratico demandatum est'). Orsini cites Velleius and Suetonius for Varro's role, not Caesar's Bellum Civile.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Terentia with four coins. He identifies the first moneyer as C. Terentius Lucanus, citing Pliny lib.xxxv cap.vii on gladiatorial paintings and Donatus on Terence's adoption by Lucanus. The second coin is also a bronze of C. Terentius Lucanus, whose cognomen Orsini notes is interpreted by some as 'Lucrio' rather than 'Lucanus.' For the third and fourth coins he argues they were struck by M. Terentius Varro when Pompey's legate and proquaestor in Spain; the third shows Iuppiter Terminalis; the reverse shows sceptrum, aquila, and dolphin — the last symbolizing Pompey's maritime command from the Piratic War. Orsini cites Velleius and Suetonius (not Caesar's Bellum Civile) for Pompey's role in Spain. He does not claim to cite Varro's own writings for these coins.

He expands I.S.M.R. as IVNO SOSPITA MAGNA REGINA. He interprets the bull reverse as referring either to the family name (from animal-based nomina per Varro) or to the lex Thoria on public land.

completed.family_note: The Thorii were a plebeian gens. L. Thorius Balbus struck the single denarius Orsini illustrates. The moneyer is identified with the L. Thorius Balbus mentioned by Cicero in de Finibus lib.ii as a Lanuuinus of epicurean bent. Since Balbus was from Lanuvium, Orsini explains, he placed Juno Sospita — whose cult was at Lanuvium — on the reverse ('Iunonis Sospitae simulacrum, quae Lanuuii colebatur'). I.S.M.R. behind the portrait stands for IVNO SOSPITA MAGNA REGINA, as Orsini explains explicitly from Virgilian verses and Ovid's Fasti. The bull on the reverse Orsini takes as either a reference to the family name or to the lex Thoria on public land (Sp. Thorius Tribune of the plebs), citing Cicero de Oratore lib.ii, Lucilius, and Appian.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Thoria with a single denarius of L. Thorius Balbus. He identifies Balbus with the L. Thorius Balbus mentioned by Cicero in de Finibus lib.ii (not Horace's Satires). Since Balbus was from Lanuvium, he placed Juno Sospita on the reverse. Orsini explicitly expands I.S.M.R. as IVNO SOSPITA MAGNA REGINA, citing Virgil and Ovid's Fasti. He discusses the bull on the reverse at length: either it refers to the family name (from animal-based nomina, citing Varro de re rustica lib.ii cap.i) or to the lex Thoria on public land (Sp. Thorius Tribune), citing Cicero de Oratore lib.ii, Lucilius, and Appian lib.i bel. ciuil.

completed.family_note: The Titinii were a gens with both patrician and plebeian families ('gens familias habuit patricias & plebeias'). Livy lib.v attests the patrician branch; Livy lib.iii records M. Titinium as Tribune of the plebs anno CCCIII. C. Titinius, the moneyer, is identified from the XVI mark as a curator of the mint ('denariorum flandorum curator'), struck anno Vrbis DXXXVI — the year when, under Q. Fabius Maximus Dictator (with Hannibal pressing), the denarius was revalued to 16 asses. Orsini draws this from Pliny lib.xxxiii cap.iii. The family also produced notable members attested in Valerius Max lib.iii cap.ii, Appian, and Plutarch.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Titinia, noting it had both patrician and plebeian families. He identifies C. Titinius from the XVI mark as the curator of the mint anno Vrbis DXXXVI, citing Pliny lib.xxxiii cap.iii for the revaluation of the denarius to 16 asses under Q. Fabius Maximus Dictator. He discusses other Titinii attested in Valerius Max lib.iii cap.ii (C. Titinium Minturnensem), Appian lib.iv bel. ciuil., and Plutarch in Bruto (Titinius sent by Cassius at Philippi). The note that Orsini provides only sparse prosopographic detail is incorrect.

completed.family_note: The Titii were a plebeian gens ('gentem plebeiam fuisse, vel ex hoc maxime constat, quod multi ex ea Tribuni plebis extiterunt'). Q. Titius struck the coins in this plate. Orsini does not identify the obverse heads as Mutinus Titinus, Bacchus/Liber, or Ariadne/Libera. He identifies the Pegasus reverse type and notes some scholars connect the coins to Titius the poet (mentioned by Horace Epistles 1.3 to Iulius Florus); Orsini himself prefers to connect the Pegasus to Corinth, as a Caesarian/Augustan colony. The fourth coin is a bronze (Æ). Orsini does not identify specific divine figures on the obverses.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Titia, noting its plebeian character. Q. Titius, whose identity is not well attested in literary sources ('non satis ex scriptoribus constat, quis fuerit'), Orsini tentatively equates with a Marcus Titius named in an inscription from Mytilene. He notes others connected the Pegasus reverse to Titius the poet mentioned by Horace (Epistles 1.3), but he himself prefers the Pegasus to reference Corinth, founded as a Caesarian/Augustan colony. He also identifies Q. Titius who killed Sex. Pompeius in Asia on Antony's orders (Velleius) as a possible family member. Orsini does not mention Mutinus Titinus, Festus, Varro, Bacchus/Liber, Ariadne/Libera, or any identification of the obverse heads as specific deities.

completed.family_note: The Titurii claimed descent from the Sabines through king Titus Tatius. L. Titurius Sabinus struck denarii c. 89 BC (Crawford 344/1-3) featuring scenes from early Sabine-Roman history: the Rape of the Sabine Women, the death of Tarpeia crushed under shields, and Victory in biga. The obverses consistently show the bearded head of king Tatius. These are among the most historically narrative coin types in the Republican series, directly illustrating events from Rome's legendary past. The control marks A.PV and TA indicate different die varieties.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Tituria with four denarii of L. Titurius Sabinus plus a quinarius of P. Sabinus and a bronze of L. Titurio L. f. He identifies the Sabine king Tatius on the obverses and discusses the Rape of the Sabines (citing Livy lib.i and Dionysius Halicarnasseus) and the death of Tarpeia ('De Tarpeia scriptum est in gente Petronia'). He notes L. Titurius Sabinus may be the brother of Q. Titurii Sabini, Caesar's legate in Gaul. The control marks APV and TA (or A monogram) are noted as die markers.
