completed.family_note: The Trebanii are an obscure gens of which Orsini can find no mention in ancient writers. The coin in the plate is a bronze (aereus), not a denarius. Orsini argues at length that the denarius legend L. TREBANI may be a die-engraver's error for L. TREBATI (as a bronze nummus is separately suspected of reading FABRINI for FABRICI Monetalis Triumviri). The family is otherwise known only from Cicero's letters to Trebatius (cited by Orsini: Cicero ad Trebatium lib. VII and the Topica addressed to C. Trebatius) — but those are Trebatii, not Trebanii. Orsini explicitly concludes: 'Trebaniae vero nullus, ut dixi, veterum scriptorum facit mentionem.' The claim in older literature that L. Trebanius was a moneyer c. 135 BC is not established by Orsini; he treats the name as possibly erroneous.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini's central argument is a sustained doubt about whether 'Trebanius' is a real gens at all. He suspects that the denarius legend L. TREBANI is a die-engraver's error for L. TREBATI (Trebatius), just as a bronze nummus apparently reads FABRINI for FABRICI. He cites Cicero ad Trebatium lib. VII and the book of Topica (quem ad C. eundem Trebatium misit) to establish that the name Trebatius is well attested, while Trebanius appears in no ancient writer. He does NOT identify coin type (no Roma/Jupiter description), does NOT read the name from an exergue (the coin in the plate is a bronze, not a denarius, and the legend reads TREBANI / ROMA visible in the engraving). He does not describe the coin as a 'straightforward Republican type' — quite the opposite.

completed.family_note: The Tullii are described by Orsini as a PATRICIAN gens ('Tulliam gentem inter patricias numeratam fuisse, satis ex scriptoribus constat'), not plebeian. The moneyer's coin reads M.TVLLI (visible on the reverse; Orsini says 'M. autem Tullius, qui in hoc denario notatus est'). Orsini proposes two equally possible attributions for the moneyer — either M. Tullius Decula (consul with Cn. Cornelius Dolabella, anno DCLXXII) or M. Tullius Cicero (for a triumph ob res in Cicilia bene gestas) — but he leaves the question explicitly open. No connection to Arpinum is asserted in Orsini's text. The gens's wider prosopography (Cimbori, Longorum, Ruforum, Fabianorum, etc.) is listed from Cicero's own references.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini proposes two equally plausible attributions for the moneyer M. Tullius — M. Tullius Decula (consul with Cn. Cornelius Dolabella, anno DCLXXII) or M. Tullius Cicero (possibly for a triumph ob res in Cicilia bene gestas). He leaves it explicitly open: 'haud facile est, nullo eius adscripto cognomine, ex qua fuerit diuinare.' He does NOT cite Cicero's writings on family origins in Arpinum. He does NOT 'connect the family to the famous orator' — he merely names Cicero as one of two candidates. He lists other Tullia families (Cimbori, Longorum, Ruforum, Seneciorum, Fabianorum) from Cicero as families 'ad quas denarius pertinere potest' but says pursuing all of them 'omnes persequi longum effet.' He also notes Ser. Sulpicius M. Marcello Cos. anno DCCII and the Imperator appellatum from Cicero's Cilician correspondence.

completed.family_note: The Valerii are described by Orsini as of Sabine origin ('Valeriam gentem è Sabinis oriundam, cum T. Tatio rege... tradit Dionysius li. IV'), citing Dionysius of Halicarnassus (not Livy) for the Sabine origin, and Plutarch in Poplicola. The family note correctly names the main moneyers (Acisculus, Flaccus, Messalla, Catullus). The claim that Orsini's table includes eleven coins spanning mid-Republic through Augustan age is broadly right; the table actually comprises two separate plates (one on p. 266 with Republican types and one on p. 269 with late Republican and Augustan bronzes). The Sabine-origin source is Dionysius lib. IV, not Livy.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini cites Dionysius of Halicarnassus (li. IV) and Plutarch (in Poplicola) for the Sabine origin — NOT Livy. He cites Valerius Maximus (lib. III. cap. 1) only for C. Valerius Flaccus's action at Capua. The first three coins in the first plate (Acisculus types) are discussed at length with an etymological digression on Acis/Acisculus, the river Acis from Etna, and the Sirens of Sicily (citing Eustathius in Dionysius, Probus in Catholicis, Ovid Metamorphoses, Hyginus in Fabulis, Servius on Aeneid, Strabo lib. I). Orsini is UNCERTAIN about the Acisculus coin attributions and explicitly says he cannot affirm anything certain: 'quicquà certi afferre possim.' The five Acisculus types noted by Crawford (474/1–5) are accounted for across both tables: three types in the first table plus two Trajanic restorations (quintus and sextus of the second table). Orsini identifies the two restored types as having Solis caput and Apollinis caput respectively — not Hercules. For the Flaccus coins Orsini cites Cicero (orations Pro Quinctio, Pro Rabirio, Pro Flacco, Philippicae) and Fasti. The bronze coins in the second plate are treated as Augustan IIIviri/IIIIviri monetales.

completed.family_note: Orsini describes the gens Vargunteia as uncertain whether patrician or plebeian but thinks patrician: 'Vargunteia gens, incertum patriciane fuerit an plebeia: opinor tamen patriciam fuisse.' The family is attested in ancient inscriptions (a long list of M. Vargunteius dedications is quoted). From this gens was L. Vargunteius (NOT P. Vargunteius) who conspired with Catiline; Sallust's list of conspirators names him L. Vargunteius. Orsini also identifies the moneyer M. Vargunteius as legate of M. Crassus in the Parthian war, from Appian's Parthica.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens at moderate length. He quotes Sallust's list of Catilinarian conspirators naming L. Vargunteius (not P. Vargunteius). He then identifies the moneyer M. Vargunteius as legate of M. Crassus in the Parthian war from Appian's Parthica, noting that 'Βαρύντιος φρεσόφδτής' in Appian is a corrupt rendering of Vargunteius. He supports this identification with an ancient inscription: M.VARGVNTEIVS / VARGVNTEIA. He notes that Cicero in the oration pro Sulla (nominat in oratione pro P. Sulla) also mentions a Vargunteius.

completed.family_note: Orsini identifies the gens Vergilia as plebeian ('fuit plebeia'). The moneyer Vergilius served as curatore denariorum flandorum with Carisius and Ogulnius ('curatorem eum fuisse cum Carifio & Ogulnio denariorum flandorum, ex denarii inscriptione satis constat'). Orsini explicitly says the moneyer's identity and date are unknown ('quis fuerit, quóne tempore vixerit, in tanta antiquitatis ignoratione, difficile est affirmare'). No connection to the poet P. Vergilius Maro is asserted or explored; the poet is mentioned only in a list of ancient inscriptions using both Vergilius and Virgilius as spellings. The 'most famous member' editorial framing is the AI's own addition, not grounded in Orsini.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini says the moneyer's identity is unknowable but that his role as monetary curator with Carisius and Ogulnius is certain from the inscription ('ex denarii inscriptione satis constat'). He does NOT acknowledge difficulty in reading the legend — the difficulty he expresses is about who the man was and when he lived, not about the legend itself. He cites Hirtius (de bello Africo) for a C. Vergilius at Thapsus, but notes the best manuscript reads Petronius not Vergilius there. He cites Cicero in Bruto for a M. Vergilius who as Tribune of the Plebs accused L. Sulla. He discusses the spelling Vergilius/Virgilius from inscriptions naming C. VERGINIVM MARTANVS, M. VERGILIVS NARCISSVS, &C. VERGINIVM RVFVS (consul cum C. Memmio Regulo). Orsini does NOT 'attempt to connect the family to the poet Virgil' — the poet is mentioned only as evidence of the name's two ancient spellings, not as a family member.

completed.family_note: Orsini identifies the gens Vettia as Sabine in origin from the image of T. Tatius on the obverse ('Vettiam gentem Sabinam fuisse, ex T. Tatii Sabini imagine, quae in huius denarii altera parte impressa est, intelligere facile possumus'). The reverse of the coin shows a horseman with the legend IVDEX / T·VETTIVS (visible in the engraving). No 'Rape of the Sabine Women' scene exists on this coin; Orsini does not describe such a scene. There is no mention of C. Annius as a joint moneyer. The moneyer identified by Orsini as the person depicted is L. Vettius (the Catilinarian informant), though the legend reads T. Vettius. The reverse symbol is a spica (ear of grain) connected to an Aedileship of the Vettia gens.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini identifies the obverse portrait as T. Tatius (not a generic 'Sabine king') and explains his reasoning: a Vettius served as Interrex at the election of Numa, attested in Plutarch. The moneyer he connects to historical persons is L. Vettius (in hoc denario notatus est), whose role in exposing the Catilinarian conspiracy Cicero cites — though the legend on the coin reads T. Vettius. Orsini notes 'licet mendose apud eum pro Iudex scriptum fit Index' (Suetonius lib. I, cap. XVII). He cites Suetonius (lib. I cap. XVII and cap. XX), Cicero (in Vatinium), and Dio (lib. XXXVIII) for the Vettius story. He does NOT cite Livy. He does NOT mention C. Annius. The reverse shows a horseman (IVDEX) and a spica connected to a Vettia family Aedileship ('Aedilitatis symbolum spica').

completed.family_note: The Veturia plate (p. 274) shows four engravings in the top row — two obverses and two reverses — representing exactly two coins (one silver, one gold) each shown on both sides. This is Orsini's standard two-sided plate format throughout the work. Orsini's text is unambiguous: 'argenteum alterum, alterum aureum: si modo litterae in argenteo notatae, T I. Veturium indicant.' The four engravings in the top row = two coins × two sides. The four blank circles in the bottom row are unfilled reverse slots. The mapping is not ambiguous: the flag's premise (irresolvable without plate examination) is incorrect.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini identifies the coins as one silver and one gold ('argenteum alterum, alterum aureum'). He cites Livy lib. I for the Roman-Alban treaty formula (not Roman-Samnite), quoting Livy extensively on the fetial ritual and the porca sacrifice. He then quotes Virgil (Aeneid lib. VIII: 'et caesa iungebant foedera porca') and Macrobius (lib. V Saturnal.) on the custom of one-sandalled warriors. He explicitly REJECTS the identification of the foedus depicted with the Caudine Peace (T. Veturius Calvinus): 'Nec enim pacem Caudinam, ut quidam putant, quam T. Veturius Caluinus fecit, propterea quòd ignominiosa populo Romano fuit, significari ea nota credendum est.' He records that others ('alii') connect the pig to the apparition of Aeneas's Penates at Lavinium, though he himself prefers the fetial Romulus–Tatius reading.

completed.family_note: The Vibii were a plebeian gens. In ancient coins only VARI and PANSAE are found (Orsini: "in antiquis denariis VARI tantum, & PANSAE reperiuntur"). C. Vibius Varus struck coins whose types include Concordia, Venus, Hercules, Minerva, and Liber — the Bacchic/Liber type (coin 5) being connected by Orsini to the Liberalia, citing Virgil Bucolicis and Georgics II. C. Vibius Pansa was consul with Hirtius (Orsini: "Consul cum Hirtio anno DCCX") and his coin types relate to the Cereales ludi and the Sicilian origin of the gens. Orsini derives the Vibii's origin from Vibone (Hipponium/Valentia in Bruttium/Lucania), citing Plutarch and Strabo lib.vi. The connection between the cognomen Pansa and the satyr Pan is not made by Orsini.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Vibia across three engraved plates with fourteen coins. He assigns the first five coins (first table) to C. Vibius Varus, noting that literary sources are silent on this moneyer ("nulla extat mentio apud eos scriptores"). He connects coin 1 (M. Lepidus/Concordia) to the triumviral coinage. Coins 3–4 (Hercules/Minerva) point to the Vibii's origin from Vibone, where Hercules and Minerva were especially venerated (citing Strabo lib.vi). Coin 5 (Liber/tiger/thyrsus) is connected to the Liberalia, citing Virgil Bucolicis (Daphnis/tigres) and Georgics II (Non aliam ob culpam Baccho), and Servius. Coins of the second and third plates belong to C. Vibius Pansa: Orsini connects the Ceres-types to the Cereales ludi and the Sicilian origin of the gens ("Vibiae gentis originem e Sicilia"), citing Cicero, Varro de re rustica, Cato, Gellius, and Ovid Fasti. He identifies Jupiter Anxur (coin 9) citing Virgil Aen.vii and Servius/Porphyrio, and the serpent-chariot of Ceres (coin 11) citing Ovid Fasti and Claudianus. The joint reverse with D. Brutus Albinus (inscribed ALBINVS·BRVTI·F) is visible on the third table. Orsini does NOT cite Varro for a Pansa/Pan etymology, and does NOT connect the Phaethon quadriga to the cognomen Pansa.

coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses all three road-inscription coins (coins 2, 3, 4) together as documenting Augustus's road restoration program, citing Suetonius lib.ii.cap.iii and Dio lib.LIII. He quotes Dio in Greek to the effect that when Augustus saw roads neglected he distributed them among senators at their own expense, and took the Via Flaminia for himself specifically because he was about to lead an army along it ('Flaminia, quoniam ea ducturus erat exercitum, ipse procurauit'), immediately restoring it, with statues of Augustus placed on arches on the Tiber bridge and at Ariminum. The triumphal arch with statues and the road-inscription reverse (QVOD VIAE MVN. SVNT) refer to this road-restoration program as a group; Orsini does not single out coin 3 as specifically the Flaminia coin — he treats coins 2–4 collectively as road-restoration types, with Flaminia named as one road among others ('reliquas patrum quibusdam, propriis sumptibus reficiendas mandauit').

completed.family_note: The Vinicii were a plebeian gens. Orsini establishes this from L. Vinicius, who as Tribune of the Plebs interceded when C. Vibius Pansa held the same office ("L. Vinicio constat, qui cum C.Vibio Panfa Tribunus pl. cum effet, ei s.c. intercessit"). This same Vinicius later struck coins as triumvir monetalis under Augustus and was suffect consul from the Kalends of September in year DCCXX AUC. His coins include a Concordia head (coin 1, citing Ovid Fasti VI) and coins recording the restoration of roads at public expense (QVOD VIAE MVNITAE SVNT), with triumphal arches. Orsini cites Suetonius lib.ii.cap.iii and Dio lib.LIII on Augustus's road-building program. Orsini does not mention the Vinicii's origins in Cales or cite Velleius Paterculus.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Vinicia with six coins of L. Vinicius. He quotes Suetonius (on Augustus and Vinicius at dinner with Tiberius) and notes the moneyer's role as triumvir monetalis and suffect consul. He correctly reads the road-restoration inscription (QVOD VIAE MVNITAE SVNT, hoc est quòd uiae munitae sunt) and cites Suetonius lib.ii.cap.iii and Dio lib.LIII on Augustus's road-building program. He notes statues on the Tiber bridge and at Rimini (Ariminum), and interprets the triumphal arch with quadriga and the road-inscription as honoring Augustus for road works from manubial funds. For coin 1, he cites Ovid Fasti VI ('Venit Apollinea longas Concordia lauro / Nexa comas') for the Concordia head laureate. Orsini does NOT mention the Vinicii's origins in Cales, and does NOT cite Velleius Paterculus.

completed.family_note: The Vipsanii were a plebeian gens of equestrian origin, as Cornelius Nepos attests in the Life of Atticus (Orsini: "familia ortus est equestri, ut indicat Cornelius Nepos in Attici uita"). M. Vipsanius Agrippa's coins include joint issues with Augustus struck when Agrippa was consul designate (COS DESIG), a portrait denarius after his third consulship (year 726 AUC), and a bronze with Neptune on the reverse commemorating the naval victory over Sextus Pompeius (Sicilian war), for which Agrippa received the corona rostrata — cited by Velleius lib.II and Pliny lib.xvi.cap.IV. The silver coin (coin 5) carries both rostral and mural crowns. Orsini does not mention the Pantheon, the Aqua Virgo, or Caligula.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Vipsania with five coins of M. Vipsanius Agrippa. He notes that coins 1 and 2 were struck when Agrippa was consul designate only ("nondum primum Consulatum adeptus, sed designatus tantum fuisset"). Coin 3 (Agrippa's portrait) was struck after his third consulship in year 726 AUC when Augustus was his seventh consular colleague; Orsini cites Censorinus De die natali for the date. He cites Velleius lib.II and Pliny lib.xvi.cap.IV for the corona rostrata as a unique honor for the Sicilian and Pompeian naval victory. The bronze coin (coin 4) shows Neptune on the reverse, connected specifically to the Sicilian victory over Sex. Pompeius ("naualem de Siculis & Sex.Pompeio victoriam"). The silver coin (coin 5) has both rostral and mural crowns. Orsini does NOT cite Dio Cassius in the Vipsania section, does NOT identify any coin as a 'posthumous commemorative struck under Caligula,' and does NOT mention IIIvir Cossutius Lentulus.

completed.family_note: The Voconii were a plebeian gens. In ancient denarii only the cognomen VITULORUM (VITVLORVM) family appears (Orsini: "In antiquis uero denariis una tantum VITVLORVM familia reperitur"). Q. Voconius struck coin 1 while Julius Caesar was still alive ("signauit uiuente adhuc Caesare") and coin 2 after Caesar's assassination, as indicated by the title DIVI IVL on it ("interfecto iam a coniuratis Caesare, ab eodem Voconio cusus fuit"). The calf (vitulus) reverse is a visual pun on the cognomen Vitulus. Orsini identifies this moneyer with the Voconius cited by Plutarch in the Life of Cicero and in Cicero's letters to Atticus (Ep.XXIII lib.VIII). He does NOT describe the coins as struck 'under Augustus.'
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Voconia with two coins of Q. Voconius Vitulus. He explains the canting type: the calf (vitulus) on the reverse punning on the moneyer's cognomen Vitulus ("ad quod cognomen respexisse uidetur Q.VOCONIVS is, qui monetam cusit, cum in altera denariorum parte uitulum signauit"). He dates coin 1 to when Julius Caesar was alive and coin 2 to after Caesar's death (DIVI IVL). He does NOT identify 'an Augustan portrait' on either coin — coin 1 has an unspecified portrait struck in Caesar's lifetime and coin 2 has DIVI IVL. The assertion that 'Orsini correctly identifies the Augustan portrait' is false.

Metam. & Claudiani, ex lib.i. de raptu Proserpinae'). Varro and Macrobius are NOT cited anywhere in the Volteia section. Any reference to 'Varro and Macrobius' in the concordance coin-comments for coins 1 or 3 must be removed.

Et iuncti currum dominae subiere leones'), Virgil Aen.vi ('qualis Berecynthia mater / Inuehitur curru Phrygias turrita per urbes'), and Claudianus lib.i de raptu Proserpinae ('Cybelem turrigeam appellauit'). He also cites Diodorus Siculus on lions drawing Cybele's chariot and Varro on their tamed nature. Orsini does NOT name Attis or describe a Phrygian-capped figure anywhere in the Volteia section. The ludi Megalenses connection follows from the overview 'Martis & Cybeles' (Megalesia = Cybele's festival).

He notes the letters S.C.D.T on the tripod as unresolved: "Litteras autem S.C.D.T...fateor me...quid significent, nescire." He speculates that M. Volteius was an xvir sacris faciundis (the priestly college overseeing the Secular Games). Orsini does not mention a 'lyre' on this coin, and does not cite Varro or Macrobius.

coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini: "L. Volteius. L.F.Strabo in altera sexti denarii parte impressit, quò pertineat certi aliquid afferre possim, nisi quòd suspicor, Iouis templum eius procurationis fuisse: a quo quidem deo in taurum uerso abductam Europam in Cretam insulam poetae fabulantur." The coin is by L. Volteius L.F. Strabo (not M. Volteius). Orsini's legend reading is 'L.Volteius.L.F.Strabo,' not 'L.CO.L.F.S.R.R.' The attribution to Volteia is uncertain ('quò pertineat certi aliquid afferre possim' — he cannot say with certainty what it signifies).

completed.family_note: The Volteii were a plebeian or possibly patrician gens (Orsini: "incertum patricia ne fuerit, an plebeia"). No ancient writer mentions M. Volteius who struck the denarii ("M. autem Volteii, qui denarios cusit, nullus meminit ueterum scriptorum"). Orsini identifies the five coin-types by the deity on each: coin 1 = Jupiter (temple, hexastyle); coin 2 = Hercules (Erymanthian boar); coin 3 = Ceres with torches in serpent-drawn chariot; coin 4 = Cybele in lion-drawn chariot; coin 5 = Apollo (tripod, connected to the Saeculares ludi). A sixth coin (coin 6) by L. Volteius L.F. Strabo shows Europa on a bull, which Orsini tentatively connects to Jupiter's procuration role ("suspicor, Iouis templum eius procurationis fuisse"). Orsini cites Virgil, Lucretius, Claudianus, Diodorus Siculus, and Ovid. He does NOT cite Varro or Macrobius in this section.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini treats the gens Volteia with six coins. He identifies the five M. Volteius types by deity: Jupiter/temple (coin 1), Hercules/Erymanthian boar (coin 2), Ceres taedifera in serpent-biga (coin 3), Cybele in lion-drawn chariot (coin 4), Apollo/tripod connected to the Saeculares ludi (coin 5). For coin 5 he explicitly says the tripod belongs to Apollo and connects the type to the Secular Games ("Saeculares ludi fiebant"), NOT to the ludi Apollinares. He notes the S.C.D.T letters on coin 5's tripod as unresolved ("quid significent, nescire"). He cites Lucretius, Virgil, Claudianus, and Diodorus for the Cybele material, and Ovid Metam. and Claudianus for Ceres. He does NOT cite Varro or Macrobius anywhere in the Volteia section. The gens Volteia's patrician/plebeian status is left uncertain. A ludi-framework attribution of coin 2 to 'ludi Plebeii' is not made by Orsini.

coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini discusses coins 1 and 2 together. He identifies them as struck for the restoration of the temples of Capitoline Jupiter (Optimus Maximus) and Vesta, connecting them to Vitellius: 'Restituta vero eorum templa à Vitellio Imp. fuisse, facile adducor ut credam.' He cites Pliny lib. xxxiv cap. vii and Cornelius Tacitus lib. xix. He does not say he cannot identify the coin; he attributes it to Vitellius's temple restorations. The legend VESTA P R QVIRITIVM is discussed at length as evidence for this.

The previous comment's claim that Orsini 'admits he cannot confidently assign' this coin is a direct inversion of the text.

coins_engraved.reverse: Roma standing right, holding Victory and eagle-tipped sceptre; ROM RENASC
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini attributes this coin to Galba: 'Quartū denarium ab Imp. Galba cusum esse, ex renascentis Romae simulacro… coniicere possumus.' He then discusses Bonus Eventus at length, citing Varro (lib. i de re rustica), Pliny (lib. xxxv cap. x), and Euphranor. He does not say 'RENASCES ROMA' as an exact legend — he says 'renascentis Romae simulacro.' He does not say he cannot assign the coin; he attributes it to Galba.

coins_engraved.obverse: Bust of Hercules seen from behind, head turned left; club over shoulder
coins_engraved.reverse: Desultor (rider) left, wearing cuirass; D·S·S and B visible; TI Q text
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies the obverse as Hercules (equated with Semo Sancus / Deus Fidius): 'Quinto denario Herculis, ut uidetur, caput signatum est, quē cum Sanco deo, siue Fidio eundem esse, satis demonstrant Varronis uerba.' The reverse legend D.S.S. he expands as 'Deus Fidius Semo Sancus' (p. 290: 'D.S.S. hoc est, Deus Fidius Semo Sancus'). He draws on Varro, Ovid (Fasti lib. vi), Propertius (lib. iv), Dionysius of Halicarnassus (lib. iv), and a Tiberina inscription (SEMONI SANCO DEO.FIDIO SACRVM…). There is no desultor on this coin; the type is Hercules/Sancus, not a rider performing equestrian feats.

coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini identifies this as the Faustulus type and attributes it to Sex. Pompeius Fostlus: 'Sextus tabellae denarius, in quo Faustulus pastor impressus est cum pico aui, et propè stante cum infantibus lupa, à Sex. Pompeio Fostlo, ut opinor, cusus fuit.' He adds that the Postloria (Frostlora) family took its cognomen from Faustulus. The coin shows a pastor (Faustulus), a woodpecker, and a she-wolf with infants — not an 'early Roma type.' The previous comment's claim that Orsini 'unable to attribute it to a moneyer' is wrong; he attributes it to Sex. Pompeius Fostlus.

coins_engraved.obverse: Head of Libertas right, diademed; LEIBERTAS legend
coins_engraved.reverse: Prow-stem and anchor arranged upright
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: This coin is on the second Incerta plate (p. 291). Orsini attributes the Libertas quinarii on this plate to Caesar's assassins: 'Caesare iam à coniuratis interfecto, libertateq. Reip. restituta, argenteū hunc quinarium à Caesaris percussoribus cusum esse, et ludis Apollinaribus, quos Brutus Praetor populo exhibuit, sparsim fuisse, ex Libertatis signata in eo imagine coniicere facile possumus.' He discusses the PAX ET LIBERTAS legend and the anchor/prow imagery as symbols of recovered liberty. He then discusses Cicero's speech at the temple of Tellus. Attribution is to the percussores of Caesar, not left wholly unidentified.

coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Second Libertas coin on the second Incerta plate. Orsini links the PAX ET LIBERTAS legend to Brutus and the conspirators, citing Cicero's first Philippic ('cuius in lib. i. Philipp. facit his verbis mentionem'). He also notes the corona on the other denarius part as obscure ('mihi quidem obscurum est') since no oak crown is recorded as being decreed to Brutus or Cassius. He does not simply say he cannot assign the coin to a gens; his position is that these coins belong to the percussores of Caesar, with residual uncertainty only about the oak crown motif.

coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Final coin(s) on the second Incerta plate. Orsini closes the entire section by leaving open whether these coins belong to Caesar's assassins or to C. Caesar Triumvir: 'iudicium relinquimus statuendi, sit ne ad Caesaris… interfectores referenda, an ad C. Caesarem Triumuirum R.P.C. qui postea Augustus appellatus fuit.' Earlier he noted that SALVS GENERIS HVMANI appears on an aureus of C. CAESARIS DIVI F. IMP. IIIVIRI R.P.C. and that the Triumviratus-period denarii may be connected. 'Roma Renascens' belongs to coin 4 (Galba), not to this denarius; 'Salus Generis Humani' appears in Orsini only as a comparandum on the gold coin, not as the obverse legend of this denarius.

completed.family_note: Coins that Orsini could not assign to any specific Roman gens because they bear no family name ('nullius prae se ferunt familiae nomen'). He considers them most likely minted for temple dedications and games ('in templorum autem dedicationibus, atq. exhibitionibus ludorum cusos esse coniicere ex iis possumus'). The section spans two plates. Despite the general uncertainty of attribution, Orsini makes confident identifications for most individual coins: coins 1–2 to Vitellius (temple restorations), coin 3 to the Social War ('dubitari non potest'), coin 4 to Galba, coin 5 to Semo Sancus/Hercules, coin 6 to Sex. Pompeius Fostlus, and the second-plate Libertas coins to Caesar's assassins — though he ends with uncertainty whether those last belong to the tyrannicides or to the triumvir C. Caesar.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini opens by explaining these coins bear no family name and were likely minted for temple dedications and games. He then proceeds with specific attributions: (1–2) he connects the Jupiter/Vesta types to Vitellius's temple restorations, citing Pliny (lib. xxxiv, cap. vii) and Tacitus (lib. xix); (3) the Social War type — 'quin ad Italicorum coniurationem pertineat, dubitari non potest' — he is certain; (4) he attributes the Bonus Eventus / ROMA RENASCENS type to Galba ('ab Imp. Galba cusum esse'); (5) he identifies D.S.S. as 'Deus Fidius Semo Sancus' and the obverse head as Hercules/Sancus, drawing on Varro and an inscription from the Tiber island; (6) he attributes the Faustulus type to Sex. Pompeius Fostlus ('à Sex. Pompeio Fostlo, ut opinor, cusus fuit'). On the second plate he attributes the Libertas quinarii to Caesar's assassins ('Caesaris percussoribus cusum esse') distributed at Brutus's Apollinarian games, but ends the whole section by leaving open whether the last coins belong to the tyrannicides or to C. Caesar Triumvir. The AI-generated summary that Orsini generally 'could not confidently assign' coins because 'legends were illegible' or that coins are 'Renaissance collector's pieces' is not grounded in Orsini's text.

He identifies the reverse creature as a tiger sacred to Bacchus ('tigri Baccho sacra'), with thyrsus and other Libera symbols, marking T. Carisius's aedilitas. coins_engraved.obverse: Bare head right; IMP·CAESAR
coins_engraved.reverse: Standing figure left holding staff; legend around
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini places this denarius in the second table of the Clodia gens and also Iulia, because Caesar's portrait is engraved on the obverse ('quòd in eius altera parte Caesaris imago incifa fit'). He identifies P. Clodius as IIIIvir monetae (not IVvir — his exact phrase is 'Quartumuir monetae cudendae'), who struck the coin under Caesar ('sub quo Clodius, ut opinor, Quartumuir monetae cudendae, denarium signauit'). Note: Orsini places it in the 'secunda tabella gentis Clodiae,' not a general Clodia table.

coins_engraved.obverse: Female head right with flowing hair; NT
coins_engraved.reverse: Trophy with shields and armor; CAESAR in field
coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini places this quinarius ('Quintus huius tabellae quinarius') in the third table of the Iulia gens ('in tertia gentis Iuliae tabella reponendus'). He reads the symbols on both sides as relating to Caesar's victories over the Germans: 'habens in utraque parte eadem ferè fymbola, ad indicandas, ut arbitror, Caesaris uictorias de Germaneis, aliisque gentibus deuictis.' This is the fifth coin described in Orsini's plate-1 text, though it stands third in this concordance's numbering; the description is of the Iulia quinarius.

coins_engraved.orsini_comment: Orsini places this denarius in the last table of the Valeria gens, attributing it to the Acisculus branch ('ad familiam Acisculoru'). He misidentifies the types completely: he reads Neptune's head ('Neptuni caput') on the obverse and the sign of Triton ('Tritonis signum') on the reverse, suggesting the coin commemorates either the Acisculus family's curatorship of Neptune's temple or a Roman naval victory. Modern attribution: Jupiter head / anguipede giant (Crawford 474/4).

completed.family_note: Supplementary coins that Orsini discovered or obtained after the main family sections were already engraved. They are presented on two additional plates at the end of the work. This section includes twelve coins spanning families from Carisia to Valeria, demonstrating Orsini's continued collecting and scholarly activity during the publication process. The coins include Republican denarii, Augustan issues, and bronzes, assigned to their respective gentes in the notes.
completed.orsini_text_notes: Orsini presents twelve supplementary coins on two plates at the end of the work ('Numismata Omissa'), explaining that these were obtained or discovered after the main family sections had already been engraved. He provides brief notes assigning each coin to its proper gens in order. Plate 1 (p. 293): T. Carisius (sextertius) → Carisia; P. Clodius denarius → Clodia and Iulia (because it bears Caesar's portrait); P. Cornelius Blasio nummus aereus → Cornelia (postrema tabella); L. Flaminius Chilo denarius reverse → Flaminia (previously badly engraved, here corrected); QUINTVS quinarius → Iulia (tertia tabella), for Caesar's victories over the Germans; SEXTVS denarius → Iulia (postrema tabella), showing the temple of Clementia Caesaris with quotation from Plutarch in Greek. Plate 2 (p. 294): PRIMVS aereus nummus → Maecilia; SECVNDVS denarius → Maria; TERTIVS and QUARTVS → Pinaria; QUINTVS → Plaetoria (secunda tabella); SEXTVS → Valeria (postrema tabella, Acisculorum family), with Orsini misreading the type as Neptuni caput / Tritonis signum. The section 'Omissa in Annotationibus' (p. 295) contains textual addenda to earlier annotations (Antoniorum, Axfiae, Claudiorum), not additional coin plates.
